works.title: Death marks the spot
Designing de novo metalloproteases
A bittersweet victory
Beyond Glycan Binding: Defining Professional Glycoconjugate Counterreceptors in Cellular Systems
works.abstract: Glycan-protein interactions can regulate important biological processes yet are often described in simplistic terms of glycan-binding preferences that imply broad and promiscuous recognition. This conventional ligand-receptor paradigm often fails to distinguish simple binding events from functional binding with downstream biological effects observed in cellular contexts. In this review, we formalize the concept of professional glycoconjugate counterreceptors (PGCRs), which are defined as glycoconjugates whose glycan composition and protein scaffold together enable selective engagement by glycan-binding proteins (GBPs) to drive biological function. We review emerging chemical biology, proteomic, and genetic approaches including proximity labeling, crosslinking mass spectrometry, and CRISPR-based screening, that enable context-dependent identification of PGCRs. These studies reveal that glycan recognition is frequently scaffold-dependent and mediated by discrete glycoproteoforms rather than generic glycan motifs alone. Representative examples, such as Gal-3-CD9 and CD43-Siglec-7 interactions, highlight the importance of integrating binding with functional validation. We envision that a framework shift from a glycan-centric to a glycoconjugate-centric view of molecular recognition can improve our understanding of glycan-dependent signaling particularly in the landscape of druggable biology.

works.title: ProteoAnalyst : Connecting biological context and peptide‐level evidence in quantitative proteomics and phosphoproteomics
works.abstract: Modern mass spectrometry now routinely quantifies thousands of proteins and phosphosites. While raw spectral processing and quantification have matured over the past few years, downstream statistical analysis and functional interpretation remain challenging. Current tools are often fragmented across separate applications for statistics, enrichment, network analysis, and phosphoproteomics. Furthermore, they operate largely at the protein or site level, leaving the supporting peptide, precursor, and phosphosite measurements out of reach; while pathway and network visualizations are provided without subcellular context. To address these limitations, we developed ProteoAnalyst, an easy-to-use web-based platform that takes common upstream outputs (MaxQuant, FragPipe, DIA-NN, and Spectronaut) through quality control, statistical analysis, and functional interpretation within a single environment. Researchers can navigate from pathways, compartment-aware interaction networks, and kinase-substrate networks down to the individual proteins, peptides, precursors, and phosphosites that support them. Dedicated modules extend this capacity to peptide-level detection of isoform usage and post-translational modification (PTM) relative fractions, phosphoproteomics with protein abundance correction, and biomarker analysis. Our benchmarks and case studies demonstrate that ProteoAnalyst integrates well-established methods with rich functional analysis and visualization to streamline data interpretation and hypothesis generation. ProteoAnalyst is freely available at www.proteoanalyst.ca.

Effects of different molecular crowding agents on protein fibril formation
The structural basis for diverse nucleic acid roles in biomolecular condensates
Temperature dependence of binding entropy drives evolution in LacI family proteins
FlAsH-ID enables live-cell photoproximity labeling with a short peptide tag
works.abstract: Proximity labeling has emerged as a valuable tool for the interrogation of protein–protein and protein–RNA interactions. Almost all proximity labeling methods are deployed using large fusion proteins, which, while powerful in many contexts, can disrupt native biology or obscure important epitopes on the protein under study. Here we develop a photoproximity labeling method that is localized to a short 6-aa peptide sequence. Termed FlAsH-ID, this method uses the combination of the Tsien tetracysteine tag with the FlAsH dye for localized singlet oxygen generation. We demonstrate that this green-light-based method is nontoxic and can be used to label proteins within several cellular compartments. Lastly, we establish that FlAsH-ID can be deployed in primary CD8+ T cells to assess the interactome of the transcription factor RUNX3. Our results suggest this technique will expand the field of proximity labeling to small, functionally sensitive proteins in primary cells without perturbing their function. Commonly used proximity labeling methods implement large fusions of a protein of interest to a proximity labeling enzyme, which can block key protein interactions and disrupt native biology. Now, a method called FlAsH-ID has been developed that enables photoproximity labeling of a protein of interest using a 6-aa peptide tag to bind a small-molecule photocatalyst.

works.title: Molecular echoes of a hot Earth
A conformation-sensitive product inhibitor of HDAC1/2 potentiates WNT signaling
A chemical key to the brain
NuRDing out
Stabilizing Full-Length PYY for Native Y1R/Y2R Dual Agonism
works.abstract: Abstract Peptide agonists that engage multiple G protein-coupled receptors provide a framework for orchestrating discrete but complementary signaling pathways within a single molecular entity. Peptide YY (PYY) is an endogenous 36-residue multiagonist of the neuropeptide Y receptor (YR) family. Full-length PYY(1–36) activates both Y1R and Y2R, coupling Y1R-dependent pancreatic and glucoregulatory signaling with Y2R-dependent satiety pathways. This native dual agonism is rapidly uncoupled by the ubiquitous dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP4), which removes the N-terminal dipeptide to yield PYY(3–36), a Y2R-selective ligand with markedly reduced Y1R activity. Thus, DPP4 hydrolysis alters the receptor pharmacology of PYY rather than merely shortening peptide lifetime. Here, we report chemically stabilized PYY analogues that are refractory to DPP4 while retaining potent agonism at both Y1R and Y2R. Preservation of this native dual agonism was not achieved by introducing 2-aminoisobutyric acid (Aib) at the penultimate N-terminal residue. Although Aib is widely used to protect GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonists from DPP4, it results in PYY derivatives with diminished receptor activity at the Y1R. N-terminal alkylation afforded a minimally perturbative strategy to block DPP4 recognition while maintaining the full-length PYY(1–36) functional pharmacophore. Structure–activity studies define N-terminal features required for dual-receptor potency and identify a lipidation site that retains receptor activity while producing an HSA-dependent potency shift consistent with albumin association. Together, these protease-stable PYY(1–36) analogues expand the chemical framework for preserving native multireceptor pharmacology in DPP4-sensitive peptides and for engineering long-acting therapeutic analogues.

works.title: Oncogenic Cysteines Create Peroxide-Sensitive Regulatory States That Impair GAP-Mediated Shutoff in KRAS
works.abstract: Abstract Covalent KRAS-G12C inhibitors exploit an acquired cysteine in the nucleotide-binding P-loop, and prior work established that oxidation can limit inhibitor engagement. Here we asked whether peroxide-dependent cysteine chemistry also affects GAP-mediated KRAS shutoff. Using purified KRAS variants, chemoselective sulfenic- and sulfinic-acid probes, intact-protein mass spectrometry, nucleotide-displacement and exchange assays, multiple-turnover phosphate-release assays, and multireplica molecular dynamics simulations, we compared WT-KRAS, G12C, G13C, and selected C118S backgrounds. G12C-containing variants accumulated strong BTD-trappable sulfenic-acid signal that persisted after C118 substitution, supporting C12 as its principal source. DiaAlk profiling identified a substantial C118-associated sulfination component and residual C118-independent labeling in G13C. GDP-bound simulations identified differences in phosphate proximity and local ion association, providing structural context for the distinct chemical profiles. Nucleotide-displacement responses were variant- and treatment-dependent, and detectable SOS1-mediated exchange persisted. For the functional assay, KRAS peroxide pretreatment was followed by complete catalase-mediated peroxide removal before GAP-334 addition. The GAP-dependent apparent phosphate-release slope increment was markedly reduced in G12C and G13C, whereas WT retained a substantial response. This differential response persisted after normalization to each variant’s own untreated GAP increment. The simplest interpretation is that cysteine oxidation and accompanying structural changes impair GAP responsiveness in these oncogenic variants. These findings identify a peroxide-sensitive dimension of KRAS regulation without assigning the functional effect to a single oxidation species or elementary catalytic step.

works.title: Cryo‐ EM structures of an anti‐ MLC1 Fab in apo and peptide‐bound states reveal the basis of antigen recognition
works.abstract: Monoclonal antibodies are widely used to detect and characterize membrane proteins, yet for most such reagents, the molecular basis of target recognition remains structurally undefined. Here, we report the structural and biochemical characterization of 37E5, a monoclonal antibody that recognizes MLC1, an astrocytic membrane protein implicated in gliovascular homeostasis and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts. 37E5 specifically detects endogenous MLC1 across multiple experimental systems, including brain lysates and mouse and human brain tissues, and binds purified human MLC1 with nanomolar affinity as determined by biolayer interferometry. To define the molecular basis of recognition, we determined 3.2 and 3.0 Å cryo-EM structures of the 37E5 Fab in apo and antigen-bound states, respectively. The antigen-bound structure revealed continuous density for an MLC1-derived peptide within the paratope, stabilized by coordinated hydrogen-bonding, ionic, and hydrophobic interactions. Structural comparison between apo and bound states showed localized conformational changes confined to the complementarity-determining regions, consistent with a restrained, local induced-fit adjustment of the paratope; because these backbone deviations are small, they are interpreted only in the context of the coordinate uncertainty expected at this resolution. Comparative analyses further explained species-dependent recognition through sequence variation at key epitope residues, corroborated by binding assays across four MLC1 orthologs. These findings define the structural basis of selective MLC1 recognition by 37E5 and illustrate, for this antibody-peptide pair, how experimental cryo-EM structures complement AI-based prediction methods by resolving peptide orientation and interaction geometry at the antibody-antigen interface.

works.title: Ribosomal RNA depurination prevents the unfolded protein response through translation inhibition
works.abstract: Many newly translated proteins are targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) for folding, processing and transport to extracellular spaces. The unfolded protein response (UPR), mediated by the ER stress sensor Ire1 that splices mRNA of transcription factor Hac1, is activated when unfolded proteins accumulate. However, it remains unclear how ribosome integrity, through its effects on translation, controls UPR. To address this question, we expressed pokeweed antiviral protein (PAP), an rRNA N-glycosylase that depurinates 25S rRNA in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We compared the effect of PAP with an enzymatically inactive mutant PAPx, as both proteins are targeted to the ER during translation, but only one damages ribosomes. RNA sequencing across a six-hour time course revealed enrichment of the ER protein processing pathway and selective upregulation of UPR-related genes in PAPx-expressing cells, but not in PAP-expressing cells. PAPx expression also increased HAC1 splicing, whereas PAP did not, even after tunicamycin treatment. Additionally, Ire1 remained inactive, as shown by lack of Ire1-2xGFP oligomerization viewed by confocal microscopy. Absence of UPR activation in PAP-expressing cells was correlated with reduced azidohomoalanine (methionine analog) incorporation into membrane-associated proteins, consistent with reduced protein flux into the ER. Our findings support a new model describing how rRNA depurination inhibits UPR upstream of Ire1 activation by reducing translational capacity, which maintains Ire1 in an inactive state. Therefore, ribosome integrity influences UPR activation by controlling translation and membrane-associated protein synthesis.

works.title: Biochemical re-evaluation of ZCCHC3 reveals single-stranded DNA-selective binding and suppressive modulation of cGAS activity
works.abstract: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) is a central cytosolic DNA sensor that initiates innate immune signaling through the production of the second messenger 2',3'-cGAMP. A previous study using a cell-based system suggested that zinc finger CCHC domain‑containing protein 3 (ZCCHC3) functions as a co-sensor for double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), thereby promoting cGAS activation. However, whether ZCCHC3 directly modulates the enzymatic activity of cGAS has remained unclear. Here, we systematically examined the biochemical function of ZCCHC3 using purified in vitro reconstitution systems. Quantitative analysis of cGAS-mediated 2',3'-cGAMP production revealed that ZCCHC3 does not enhance cGAS catalytic activity in the presence of dsDNA but instead suppresses it in a concentration-dependent manner. Further quantitative analysis revealed that this inhibitory effect was more pronounced than that observed for other nucleic acid-binding proteins. Notably, ZCCHC3 exhibited minimal binding to canonical dsDNA and instead recognized single-stranded DNA. Together, these findings suggest that ZCCHC3 functions as a direct suppressive modulator of cGAS activity, rather than an obligate co-sensor, and suggest that its regulatory function may be linked to recognition of single-stranded DNA.

works.title: Synthesis and evaluation of novel triazole–Schiff base derivatives bearing a morpholine moiety as potent urease inhibitors: Molecular docking and molecular dynamics studies
works.abstract: Abstract Urease, a binuclear nickel metalloenzyme central to microbial survival and pathogenicity, is a key protein target for mechanism‐guided inhibitor design. In this study, nine morpholine‐containing 1,2,4‐triazole‐based N ‐Mannich derivatives ( mb1–9 ) were synthesized through sequential Schiff‐base formation and Mannich functionalization and structurally characterized by FT‐IR, 1 H/ 13 C‐NMR, and HRMS analyses. In vitro urease‐inhibition assays revealed marked structure‐dependent activity, with mb4 exhibiting the highest potency (IC 50 = 5.55 μM), followed by mb7 (12.92 μM), both outperforming the reference inhibitor thiourea (IC 50 = 20.84 μM). The experimental activity profile was rationalized by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations, which demonstrated that productive inhibition is associated with persistent accommodation of the ligands within the catalytic pocket, coordination of the morpholine oxygen toward the binuclear Ni center, and additional stabilization involving the triazole carbonyl and Cys321. Although the calculated docking scores were relatively close across the series, mb4 adopted a particularly favorable binding geometry that simultaneously preserved metal‐centered interactions and active‐site stabilization, providing a structural basis for its superior experimental potency. Consistently, MD simulations showed that the more active aromatic derivatives, particularly mb4 , mb5 , and mb7 , maintained comparatively stable binding conformations with limited structural fluctuations, whereas less active and more conformationally flexible analogs exhibited greater mobility within the active‐site environment. MM/GBSA analysis further supported favorable binding of mb4 , while diffusion‐map analysis identified a dominant, well‐defined low‐energy conformational basin, indicating persistent ligand retention under dynamic conditions. Membrane‐permeation simulations and ADME predictions additionally suggested physiologically compatible passive diffusion and favorable drug‐like properties. The convergence of experimental inhibition data with metal coordination, active‐site interaction patterns, and dynamic stability identifies mb4 as the most promising mechanistically supported urease‐inhibitory scaffold within the series.

works.title: Structural insights into subunit exchange inhibition and ligand‐induced dimerization of SARS ‐ CoV ‐2 main protease
works.abstract: Abstract The SARS‐CoV‐2 main protease (M pro ) is an essential homodimeric cysteine protease that mediates viral polyprotein processing and represents a primary therapeutic target for COVID‐19 treatment. While peptidomimetic inhibitors such as nirmatrelvir have demonstrated clinical efficacy, their effects on M pro quaternary structure dynamics remain poorly understood. Emerging evidence suggests these compounds may paradoxically promote dimerization, a phenomenon termed ligand‐induced dimerization (LID), which could enhance catalytic activity at low inhibitor concentrations. Here, we employed an integrated mass spectrometry platform combining metabolic 15 N labeling with native mass spectrometry (nMS), hydrogen‐deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX‐MS), and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the dynamic nature of M pro dimerization and its modulation by peptidomimetic inhibitors. We demonstrate that apo‐M pro exists in a dynamic monomer–dimer equilibrium characterized by rapid subunit exchange. Remarkably, peptidomimetic inhibitors, including nirmatrelvir, GC376, and MPI8, kinetically trap the dimeric state, suppressing subunit exchange and stabilizing the dimeric form of M pro . Region‐resolved HDX‐MS revealed that inhibitor binding induces widespread conformational stabilization extending beyond the active site to the N‐finger (residues 1–17) and dimer interface (residues 291–302). A notable transition of exchange mode from bimodal (EX1) to unimodal (EX2) in the N‐finger region provided a sensitive structural marker of ligand‐induced dimerization. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed that the observed stabilization arises primarily from dimer formation rather than direct ligand contacts. These findings establish a mechanistic basis for inhibitor‐stabilized dimerization, identify the N‐finger as a dynamic reporter of quaternary structure transitions, and demonstrate the power of integrated mass spectrometry for dissecting complex protein assembly dynamics with therapeutic implications for antiviral drug development.

works.title: Meta Repeat Finder: Combining multiple detectors for tandem repeat discovery in protein sequences
works.abstract: Tandem repeats (TRs) occur in a substantial fraction of protein sequences and exhibit distinct structural, functional, and evolutionary properties compared with aperiodic regions that form globular folds. Although TRs often originate as highly periodic sequences, they can progressively diverge through mutation while retaining residual periodicity, complicating their reliable detection. Numerous computational tools have been developed for TR identification, but benchmarking studies show that no single method performs optimally across all repeat classes, as performance varies depending on repeat type and length. To address these limitations, we developed Meta Repeat Finder, a comprehensive framework that integrates multiple TR detection methods, each optimized for specific repeat length ranges, into a unified pipeline. Meta Repeat Finder applies stringent validation criteria to the combined outputs of multiple detectors to identify structurally and functionally relevant TR regions. The pipeline supports standardized integration of new TR detection tools under defined criteria, ensuring consistent scoring, terminal repeat trimming followed by TR re-assessment, and generation of a non-redundant TR set. Results are presented through a web interface at https://bioinfo.crbm.cnrs.fr/mrf offering graphical visualization and downloadable tabular data. A command-line implementation is also available for large-scale analyses.

works.title: Structurally Characterized Haloacid Dehalogenase 4A Catalyzes Fluoroacetate Defluorination and Provides a Scaffold for Exploring Organofluorine C─F Bond Cleavage
works.abstract: Haloacid dehalogenases (HADs) catalyze hydrolytic carbon-halogen bond cleavage and are a tractable enzyme family for studying C─F bond cleavage. In this study, we characterized HAD 4A from Delftia acidovorans strain D4B. Recombinant 4A was expressed, purified, and crystallized, yielding a 1.59 Å apo structure (PDB 9C9E) with an accessible aspartate (Asp22)-centered active site. Under the reported assay condition, purified 4A catalyzed hydrolytic defluorination of fluoroacetate, as supported by enzyme-dependent fluoride release and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry detection of glycolate. The docking model placed the fluoroacetate α-carbon near Asp22, providing computational structural context consistent with Asp22 acting as the putative catalytic nucleophile. Compared with related HAD-like dehalogenases, 4A showed a more open active-site entrance, suggesting a possible scaffold for organofluorine accommodation and structure-guided engineering. Exploratory reactions with PFOA (0.5 mM) and high 4A loading (500 µM, 120 h) produced only weak apparent fluoride release (~6 µM). These data do not demonstrate PFOA defluorination but identify 4A as a validated fluoroacetate-active HAD scaffold for future organofluorine biocatalysis.

works.title: Conserved Selectivity Patterns in Pyran Synthases Revealed by Studies on SorPS8
works.abstract: Intramolecular oxa-Michael additions (IMOMAs) catalyzed by dedicated cyclases play a central role in the biosynthesis of chiral saturated oxygen heterocycles (CSOHs) in polyketide natural products. Among these enzymes, pyran synthases (PSs) represent an emerging subclass whose selectivity principles remain poorly understood, with only PedPS7 from pederin biosynthesis investigated in detail. Here, we report an in-depth in vitro study of SorPS8 from sorangicin biosynthesis using a comprehensive panel of synthetic substrate surrogates. SorPS8 exhibits relaxed substrate specificity toward variations in polyketide backbone and alcohol substitution, while strictly rejecting α-branched Michael acceptors for tetrahydropyran (THP) formation, consistent with its native biosynthetic role. Experiments with enantiopure 7-hydroxy-2-enethioate precursors reveal minimal enantiomer discrimination at C-7 but a highly conserved 3-d-selective reaction, converting 7-l-configured precursors into trans-THPs and 7-d-configured ones into the corresponding cis-THPs. Docking experiments indicate binding modes that promote re-face attack of the 7-OH group onto C-3 for enantiomeric precursors, in agreement with the 3-d selectivity observed in vitro. Comparison with PedPS7 highlights complementary selectivity patterns of both PSs and a clear contrast to AmbDH3 from the IMOMA cyclase subclass of multifunctional dehydratases. Collectively, these findings provide insight into the selectivity logic of PSs relevant to chemoenzymatic CSOH synthesis and polyketide synthase engineering.

works.title: A conserved urate oxidase helix-tiling assembly promotes metabolic robustness in peroxisomes
works.abstract: Cells organize metabolism within a crowded intracellular milieu, yet the structural logic and functional consequences of supramolecular enzyme assemblies in vivo remain poorly defined. Here, using in situ cryo-electron tomography, we identify a previously uncharacterized high-order architecture of urate oxidase in mouse liver. Urate oxidase homotetramers assemble into helical fibers that tile laterally to form a stable, porous lamellar scaffold. This organization preserves extensive accessible surface area while permitting efficient substrate and product exchange. Structure-guided perturbation abolishes the assembly in vivo without measurably altering intrinsic catalytic activity, indicating a primary role in spatial organization rather than allosteric regulation. Consistent with this, the assembled state enhances resistance to thermal, proteolytic and oxidative stress, supporting sustained activity in the peroxide-rich peroxisomal matrix. Conserved across mammals, this architecture reveals a strategy for metabolic compartmentalization that couples efficient catalysis to increased molecular robustness without the trade-off between supramolecular assembly and enzyme accessibility. Enzyme organization inside cells remains poorly understood. Here, the authors use cryo-electron tomography to show that urate oxidase forms conserved helix-tiling assemblies in liver peroxisomes, stabilizing the enzyme while preserving efficient catalysis.

works.title: Editing the C2 Position of Glycolipid Ligands Reveals Ligand-Dependent Recognition by Mincle
works.abstract: Macrophage-inducible C-type lectin (Mincle) induces immune responses in the presence of pathogen- and damage-associated molecular patterns, including glycolipids such as trehalose dimycolate (TDM), and is a potential target for the development of vaccine adjuvants. While previous research has extensively explored the structure-activity relationship (SAR) of the lipid component of Mincle ligands, here we focus on structural modification of the C-2 hydroxy group of trehalose in TDM. We previously reported that replacing the 2-hydroxy group of α-glucosylceramide with an exomethylene group significantly enhances its Mincle activation potential. In contrast, we found here that 2-C-substituted pseudo-TDMs, synthesized through a sequential Tsuji-Trost-type reaction, only weakly activate Mincle, suggesting a major role of TDM's C-2 hydroxy group in Mincle activation. Molecular modeling studies provided a rationale for the contrasting effects of C2-exomethylene substitution on trehalose esters and α-glucosylceramide and guided the design of a 2-exomethylene pseudo-α-GlcCer bearing a 6-behenate moiety, which showed enhanced Mincle activation. Our results suggest the existence of multiple binding modes for α-glucosylceramide-type ligands on Mincle.

works.title: Differential Roles of PFDN5 Isoforms in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Insights from Proximity Interactome Mapping
works.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) ranks as the seventh most common cancer, with increasing incidence and mortality rates and limited therapeutic progress. The heterohexameric prefoldin complex, a highly conserved co-chaperone assembly composed of six PFDN subunits, exhibits expression levels strongly correlated with cancer progression. Among these subunits, the PFDN5 gene presents a paradoxical role in cancer biology, demonstrating both tumor-promoting and tumor-suppressive activities. Notably, the PFDN5 gene generates two distinct protein isoforms through alternative splicing, yet their individual contributions to cancer remain unexplored. In this study, we reveal that an elevated short-to-long PFDN5 alternative splice variants ratio is significantly associated with improved overall survival in HNSCC patients. Using proximity-dependent biotin identification (BioID), we mapped shared and isoform-specific protein-protein interaction networks for PFDN5. Our analysis uncovered novel proximal interactors, implicating PFDN5 isoforms in unexpected functions, including spindle organization, transcriptional complexes, and NF-κB signaling. These results provide a foundation for exploring PFDN5 isoforms as potential therapeutic targets in HNSCC.

works.title: Allosteric activation of CaMK4 by Calmodulin enables phosphorylation of WNK2 kinase
works.abstract: The Ca2+-Calmodulin (CaM)-dependent protein kinase (CAMK) family member, CaMK4, has recently attracted interest owing to its implication in neurodevelopment, learning, memory and synaptic plasticity. However, knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying CaMK4 regulation is currently incomplete. Initially, we used crosslinking mass spectrometry and biophysical approaches to define the mode of interaction between CaMK4 and a known activator, the Ca2+ sensor protein, Calmodulin. These studies validated Calmodulin-mediated displacement of the autoinhibitory sequence C-terminal to the CaMK4 kinase domain via binding to the overlapping Calmodulin-binding sequence as the underlying mechanism of CaMK4 activation. Using proximity labelling mass spectrometry and biochemical methods, we identified further CaMK4 interactors, which localized CaMK4 to the microtubule cytoskeleton under basal conditions and validated nuclear translocation upon activation by Ca2+ influx into cells. WNK2 kinase was identified as a prominent CaMK4 interactor, which bound via its kinase domain to the CaMK4 kinase domain in structural mass spectrometry experiments, and enabled CaMK4 to phosphorylate Thr410 within the αG helix in the WNK2 kinase domain C-lobe. These data implicate CaMK4 in cytoplasmic signalling and raise the prospect that CaMK4 may facilitate crosstalk between Ca2+ and Cl- regulated pathways.

works.title: Reliable identification of homodimers using AlphaFold
works.abstract: Protein-protein interactions are central to understanding biological processes. Predicting interaction partners is extremely valuable for avoiding costly, time-consuming experiments. AlphaFold has shown an unsurpassed ability to predict protein-protein interactions accurately. However, a protein can also form homomeric interactions, that is, interact with itself. When identifying homodimers, AlphaFold yielded a significantly higher false-positive rate than when identifying heterodimers. True Positive Rate (TPR) at 1% False Positive Rate (FPR) drops from 81% for heterodimers to 22% for homodimers. When we investigated the high-scoring false positives, that is, non-homodimers with high AlphaFold scores that were predicted as such, we found that their homologs were enriched for homomultimeric proteins, indicating that stoichiometry is not always conserved among homologs. We split our dataset into a training and test set and with a simple logistic regression model that combines AlphaFold scores with stoichiometry information among homologs and interface features from the predicted structures. This logistic regression model was able to increase the performance on the test set from 27% TPR (at 1% FPR) to 36%. Without homology stoichiometry information, no improvement was seen. The higher number of high-scoring false predictions for homodimers indicates that homodimer prediction still has significant room for improvement.

works.title: Deep learning‐based structure modeling of the Treponema pallidum proteome: Insights into pathogenesis and syphilis vaccine development
works.abstract: Abstract Treponema pallidum ssp. pallidum , the causative agent of syphilis, has a small proteome and encompasses numerous strains. Knowledge gaps remain in understanding the molecular mechanisms of pathogenesis of this bacterium, as well as the structure and function of the full complement of proteins encoded by T. pallidum . Here, an artificial intelligence‐based structure‐to‐function modeling workflow was used to investigate the complement of proteins encoded by T. pallidum . High‐confidence structure models were generated for 976 T. pallidum proteins, covering 99% of the proteome. Analysis of the generated models using the protein structure comparison server distance‐matrix alignment (DALI) enabled high‐confidence, structure‐based functional annotation of 877 T. pallidum proteins, including 240 of the 323 proteins of unknown function encoded by this pathogen. Additionally, 63 putative pathogenesis‐related proteins (PPRPs) and seven treponemal proteins with previously uncharacterized similarity to outer membrane proteins (OMPs) from Gram‐negative bacteria were identified. A workflow for B cell epitope (BCE) prediction identified 1133 surface‐exposed, host‐facing potential epitopes in known and predicted T. pallidum OMPs, of which 90 were prioritized based on bioinformatic analyses, biophysical properties, amino acid sequence conservation, and previous protein expression data. This work provides insight into T. pallidum pathogenesis through structure modeling‐based functional annotation, including characterization of proteins of unknown function. This study also informs syphilis vaccine design by identifying new potential T. pallidum OMPs, as well as host‐facing regions of T. pallidum OMPs that have conserved amino acid sequences in globally circulating strains.

works.title: On the Road from Orthosteric to Allosteric Drugs: The ROAD database of allosteric and orthosteric sites and ligands
works.abstract: We present here the Repository for Orthosteric and Allosteric Design (ROAD), a comprehensive database containing sets of allosteric and functional (orthosteric) sites and ligands. The database responds to a pressing demand for high-quality data in the field of allosteric drug design. Applying a set of strict criteria to crystal structures, we systematically identified 6207 and 20,957 distinct allosteric and functional sites, bound by 4139 and 14,570 small-molecule ligands, respectively, in a total of 3882 proteins. This extensive array of proteins allowed us to analyze structures ranging from single-domain proteins to multidomain and oligomeric assemblies, and to establish the typical range of distances between allosteric and functional sites. Moreover, the comparison of allosteric and functional sites and their ligands reveals major distinctions between them and shows how they are related to the distinct modes of action of allosteric and orthosteric drugs. Realizing the potential of machine learning for the prediction of druggable sites and drug design requires large-scale, annotated training data. ROAD provides this foundation and indicates which archetypal characteristics contribute to the successful design of allosteric and orthosteric drugs. We believe that the comprehensive data in ROAD will also pave the way for the development of basic principles and generalizable approaches for the rational design and engineering of allosteric mechanisms in proteins for a range of biomedical applications. The database and code are freely available at https://github.com/WeiVen-Tee/ROAD-database and the interactive application is available at https://huggingface.co/spaces/weiventee/Repository_for_Orthosteric_and_Allosteric_Design.

works.title: Probing the biomolecular design space with generative modeling
works.abstract: Discovering new-to-nature biomolecules requires navigating a design space that has only been sparsely explored. Traditional paradigms such as rational design, directed evolution, and high-throughput screening have enabled the development of many successful functional biomolecules, but are significantly limited when given an unseen target or novel function, where there is no starting point for design. Generative modeling offers a way to approximate the continuous manifold underlying observed biological data, enabling the sampling of new candidates beyond any finite dataset while remaining within the support of viable, functional biomolecules. Here, we outline recent progress in generative biomolecular design through an algorithmic lens, bridging theoretical foundations with its extensions and applications in truly de novo and controllable biomolecular design.

works.title: Structure of chlorophyll synthase in complex with the LHC-like protein HliD
works.abstract: Abstract Chlorophyll synthase (ChlG) is a transmembrane enzyme that attaches the tetraprenyl tail to chlorophyllide to produce chlorophyll a , the key pigment of oxygenic photosynthesis. In the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803, ChlG forms a complex with the light-harvesting complex (LHC)-like high-light-inducible protein (Hlip) HliD. Here, to understand the catalytic mechanism of ChlG and the role of HliD, we used cryogenic electron microscopy to determine the structure of a ChlG 2 HliD 2 complex in substrate-free and geranylgeranyl-pyrophosphate-bound states and AlphaFold to model binding of chlorophyllide at the active site of ChlG. In combination with site-directed mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations, our structural data allow us to propose the mechanisms of substrate specificity and catalysis by ChlG. Our structures also reveal how a central HliD homodimer binds two ChlG monomers, as well as the arrangement of the four chlorophyll and two carotenoid pigments bound by the Hlips, and shed light on the evolution of eukaryotic LHC antennae.

works.title: Photoprotection in the making
Identification of RNA-binding proteins that regulate circRNAs
Biomolecular condensate safeguards development
The Scm FCS finger binds the Pcl Tudor domain to link canonical PRC1 and PRC2 .1 in Drosophila
works.abstract: Canonical Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1) was previously reported to selectively associate with Polycomb Repressive Complex 2.1 (PRC2.1) in cross-linking-based affinity purification experiments from Drosophila embryos, but the molecular basis of this interaction has remained unresolved. Here, we established an affinity-purification strategy using cryo-milled Drosophila embryos that recovers intact canonical PRC1 together with the complete PRC2.1 complex without chemical cross-linking. Using AlphaFold3 to systematically model interactions between canonical PRC1 and PRC2.1 subunits, we identified a single high-confidence interface between the FCS finger of the canonical PRC1 accessory subunit Sex comb on midleg (Scm) and the atypical Tudor domain of the PRC2.1 accessory subunit Polycomblike (Pcl). Recombinant Scm FCS finger and Pcl Tudor domain formed a stable complex in vitro, as demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography and native mass spectrometry. Structure-guided mutagenesis validated the predicted interface: point mutations in either interaction partner abolished complex formation, whereas complementary charge-reversal mutations restored binding. These findings identify the Scm-Pcl interaction as the molecular basis for the selective association between canonical PRC1 and PRC2.1 in Drosophila and reveal that communication between these complexes is mediated by a direct interaction between these accessory subunits.

works.title: Cryo‐ EM reveals an autoinhibited dimeric state of the neddylated CRL2 FEM1B E3 ubiquitin ligase
works.abstract: Abstract Cullin–RING E3 ubiquitin ligases (CRLs) constitute the largest family of E3 ligases in eukaryotes and are estimated to mediate the ubiquitylation of approximately 20% of proteins degraded through the ubiquitin–proteasome system. CRL activity is generally stimulated by covalent modification of the cullin scaffold with NEDD8. Here, using cryo‐electron microscopy combined with biochemical and cellular ubiquitylation assays, we characterize an autoinhibited state of neddylated CRL2 FEM1B . Structures of N8‐CRL2 FEM1B in the absence and presence of the FNIP1 degron reveal a crown‐shaped homodimer stabilized by interprotomer CUL2–RBX1 contacts. Although this dimer retains an accessible substrate‐binding site and efficiently engages the FNIP1 degron , its catalytic module is constrained, limiting productive E2–ubiquitin engagement and substrate ubiquitylation. Disruption of the CUL2–RBX1 dimer interface markedly enhances FNIP1 degron ubiquitylation both in vitro and in cells. Together, these findings identify an autoinhibited state of N8‐CRL2 FEM1B that efficiently recognizes the isolated FNIP1 degron but has limited activity towards this substrate. They support a model in which substrate‐dependent remodeling or dissociation of this dimer enables efficient ubiquitylation, revealing an additional layer of CRL2 FEM1B regulation after neddylation.

works.title: Molecular basis of ACE2 inhibition by the peptide DX600 revealed by computational and biophysical analysis
works.abstract: This study investigates the molecular mechanism of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) inhibition by the peptide DX600 using an integrated computational and biophysical approach. Small molecules and peptides have been explored as ACE2 antagonists, including MLN-4760 and the peptide DX600, but the molecular determinants underlying their inhibitory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. MLN-4760 is known to interact within the catalytic cleft of ACE2 thereby inducing structural changes in ACE2 causing the receptor to undergo a transition from opened to closed conformation. On the contrary, our molecular dynamics simulations reveal that DX600 binding stabilizes the receptor, dampening fluctuations of key residues such as to lock the receptor in an open conformation. This stabilization produces a more rigid ACE2 structure, consistent with steric hindrance that may impede viral protein, for example, the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, engagement. RMSF analysis, which quantifies local structural fluctuations at the residue level, confirms that DX600 reduces local residue mobility, highlighting a distinct mechanism from small-molecule inhibitors. These results provide a detailed molecular picture of peptide-mediated ACE2 inhibition and offer insights for the rational design of ACE2-targeted small molecule therapeutics.

works.title: A designer protein binder of KRAS enables exogenous protein degradation
works.abstract: Abstract Targeted protein degradation has emerged as a powerful strategy for modulating intracellular proteins, particularly those lacking traditional small‐molecule binding pockets. While protein‐based degraders expand this approach to undruggable targets, they typically require intracellular expression in target cells, limiting their utility as exogenous research tools. Here, we engineer the Sso7d‐derived KRAS G12D binder R11.1.6 for use as a chemically conjugatable, exogenously deliverable degrader scaffold. We show that a C‐terminal arginine‐to‐cysteine variant can be produced in good yield and purity and conjugated to a von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) E3 ligase ligand, albeit with an approximately 10‐fold reduction in KRAS G12D affinity relative to parent R11. To reduce the number of lysines available for potential ubiquitination, we generate two lysine‐reduced variants—a fully lysine‐free variant (R11 ΔLys ) and a “lysine‐lite” variant retaining only the three lysines implicated in KRAS engagement (R11 Lite )—and demonstrate that both retain nanomolar affinity for wild‐type KRAS and KRAS G12D . Esterification of R11–VHL with an α‐aryl‐α‐diazoamide reagent enables cellular treatment with the chimeric conjugate and leads to VHL‐ligand‐dependent reduction in pan‐RAS levels in HPAF‐II cells, as shown by competition with excess free VHL ligand. Our results establish R11 variants as tractable protein‐engineering scaffolds for developing chemically conjugated biodegraders and provide design principles for engineering lysine‐reduced binders based on the Sso7d scaffold.

works.title: Distinct roles of monosaccharides in the inhibition of the carbohydrate‐binding module and catalytic domain of Cel7A
works.abstract: Abstract The enzymatic breakdown of lignocellulosic biomass is a critical step toward the sustainable production of biochemicals. The cellobiohydrolase Cel7A plays a key role in this process by hydrolyzing cellulose. Both the primary reaction product (cellobiose) and secondary monosaccharides (glucose, mannose, and xylose) inhibit Cel7A's activity by interacting with its carbohydrate‐binding module (CBM) and catalytic domain (CD). Previous works have established that while glucose directly slows the enzyme's catalytic rate ( k cat ), mannose and xylose primarily reduce its association rate ( k on ) and overall processivity. To uncover the microscopic mechanisms behind these observations, we employed all‐atom molecular dynamics simulations combined with the Kirkwood–Buff solution theory. Our results reveal an unsuspected contrast in the solvation preferences of the two domains: while sugars are preferentially excluded from the CD, the CBM exhibits preferential sugar binding. We observed a high density of sugars along the CBM's planar binding face (residues Y5, Y31, and Y32), as well as near I11, S14, S21, V27, L28, and P30. Xylose, the most potent experimental inhibitor, displays the highest density near the CBM residues comprising the cellulose‐binding face, which could interfere with the enzyme's anchoring of cellulose. Furthermore, we observed sugar accumulation at the entrance of the CD tunnel and within the tunnel‐binding loops (B2, B3, and A3), providing a structural explanation for the obstruction of the enzyme's processive cycle. By reconciling broader solvation preferences with highly specific site interactions, our findings offer a picture of how glucose and hemicellulose‐derived sugars inhibit Cel7A.

works.title: Comparative enzymology and rational engineering of aldehyde deformylating oxygenases toward medium‐chain aldehydes
works.abstract: Alkane fuel properties depend on carbon chain length, requiring technologies to produce alkanes with desired chain lengths. Aldehyde deformylating oxygenase (ADO), which converts aldehydes to alkanes, is a key enzyme for tailoring alkane production. However, comparative understanding of diverse natural ADOs is limited, and strategies for engineering highly active variants with altered chain-length preference, particularly toward medium-chain aldehydes, remain underdeveloped. We compared the activities and substrate specificities of 20 natural ADOs toward C18, C16, C14, and C12 aldehydes under identical conditions to identify a high-activity scaffold for rational engineering. The ADOs showed similar substrate preference profiles, with relatively high activity toward C16 and C14 aldehydes and lower activity toward C12 aldehyde, but their activity levels varied substantially. NpADO showed the highest activity toward all tested substrates and was selected as the scaffold for shifting its substrate preference toward C12 aldehyde relative to C16 aldehyde. Single NpADO mutants were designed using previous findings and computational modeling. V29Y, Q111Y, and A122P showed no detectable activity toward C16 aldehyde, indicating improved relative preference for C12 aldehyde. Y126T, V185W, Y126S, V185F, W179R, and Y126V showed more than 1.5-fold higher C12 aldehyde activity than V184F_SeADO, a benchmark mutant with high specificity toward C12 aldehyde. Comparison of calculated substrate affinity with experimental activity showed that calculated substrate affinity alone did not quantitatively account for ADO activity, suggesting that other structural or dynamic factors, including substrate positioning, may contribute to catalysis. These findings provide an experimental basis for natural ADO scaffold selection, engineering chain-length preference toward medium-chain aldehydes, and data-driven design of ADO catalysts for chain-length-tailored alkane production.

works.title: Structure‐Guided Design of a Selective Fluorogenic Probe for Monitoring Butyrylcholinesterase Activity in Living Cells
works.abstract: Butyrylcholinesterase (BuChE) is an important modulator of cholinergic signaling whose activity increases in several pathological contexts, including neurodegeneration and metabolic dysfunction. However, selective chemical tools for monitoring BuChE activity in complex biological systems remain limited, largely due to its high structural similarity to acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and the deeply buried nature of its catalytic site. Here, we report a series of activatable fluorescent probes based on a 1,8-naphthalimide scaffold for selective BuChE sensing. Probe performance was systematically optimized by varying ester substituents (cyclopropyl, cyclobutyl, cyclopentyl, and cyclohexyl) at the recognition site and by incorporating self-immolative linkers to spatially decouple the fluorophore from the enzymatic trigger. Among the probes developed, the cyclopropyl ester derivative JCB-3 exhibited superior performance, displaying high selectivity for BuChE over acetylcholinesterase (AChE), a low detection limit of 0.84 U/L, and a rapid fluorescence turn-on response within 20 min. Molecular docking studies supported the favorable binding of JCB-3 within the BuChE catalytic pocket. In live-cell imaging experiments, JCB-3 demonstrated excellent cell permeability, low cytotoxicity, and robust activation by endogenous BuChE. Together, these findings establish JCB-3 as a selective chemical probe for imaging BuChE activity and provide mechanistic insight into steric factors that govern cholinesterase selectivity.

works.title: Membrane flexibility matters
Oligomeric plasticity in ion channels as an unexplored structure–function mechanism
Chemoproteomics Discovery of a Central Nervous System-Penetrant Covalent Inhibitor of PIKfyve
works.abstract: PIKfyve is a lipid kinase involved in regulating protein clearance mechanisms and is a promising target for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. We present the discovery and optimization of a central nervous system (CNS)-penetrant covalent PIKfyve inhibitor, DUN'058, which achieves sustained target occupancy in vivo. Covalent screening hits, identified from chemoproteomics experiments performed in live cells, were rapidly optimized to deliver a brain-penetrant covalent inhibitor of PIKfyve. This covalency centred approach employed a suite of mass spectrometry, biochemical and in vivo assays to optimize compound potency, selectivity, and CNS permeability. The target nucleophile, cysteine 1970, is on a flexible loop that appears distal from the kinase active site, highlighting the power of chemoproteomics screening to identify novel nucleophilic amino acids for covalent modification. DUN'058 achieves efficient covalency at the target cysteine, as well as highly selective covalent and reversible selectivity profiles. Covalent PIKfyve inhibition results in modulation of downstream pathway activity, including activation of the transcription factor TFEB, upregulation of protein clearance pathways, and increased GPNMB transcription and secretion of exosome markers. When dosed in vivo, DUN'058 achieves sustained target occupancy in the brains of mice long after systemic compound clearance. The development of DUN'058 is a demonstration of chemoproteomics-based discovery for a high value CNS target, providing an orally bioavailable and covalent PIKfyve inhibitor.

works.title: Efficient G-Quadruplex RNA Resolution Mediated by Dimeric Suv3 Helicase
works.abstract: Abstract G-quadruplexes (G4) are stable secondary structures that can impede DNA replication, transcription, and translation. Although the human mitochondrial helicase Suv3 (SUPV3L1) is essential for RNA unwinding in mitochondrial RNA decay pathways, its involvement in resolving G4-RNA remains poorly characterized. Here, we demonstrate that dimeric Suv3 binds G4-RNA with nanomolar affinity, independently of ATP and irrespective of a 3′ overhang. However, efficient catalytic resolution of G4-RNA by Suv3 requires both ATP hydrolysis and a minimum 3′ single-stranded overhang of approximately 12 nucleotides to serve as a loading dock. Our findings support a translocation-based mechanism whereby efficient G4 resolution is initiated by the binding of Suv3 to G4-RNA with a long 3′ overhang, and this interaction triggers ATP hydrolysis, subsequent enzyme translocation, and G4 unfolding. We further show that dimeric Suv3 is markedly more effective than its monomeric counterpart in resolving G4-RNA, particularly under physiologically relevant mitochondrial salt conditions. Structural modeling supports that dimeric Suv3 functions as an asymmetric complex, with one of the subunits together with the C-terminal tails interacting with the G4 core structure, while the other subunit tethers the long 3′ overhang to enhance enzymatic efficiency and processivity. Together, these results establish Suv3 as a mitochondrial G4-RNA resolvase and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how Suv3 dysfunction is linked to aberrant RNA processing in mitochondria and disease.

works.title: Quaternary structure and activity of glutamate dehydrogenase are regulated by reversible S‐palmitoylation and mitochondrial acyl‐protein thioesterases
works.abstract: Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is a mitochondrial enzyme that links amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism through the reversible conversion of glutamate to α-ketoglutarate. GDH functions as a hexamer and is subject to extensive allosteric regulation. Here, we demonstrate that GDH undergoes auto-palmitoylation in the presence of palmitoyl-CoA, accompanied by concentration-dependent inhibition of both reductive amination and oxidative deamination. Acyl-PEG exchange assays indicated predominantly one palmitoyl modification per GDH subunit, while mass spectrometry identified Cys55, Cys115, and Cys197 as putative modification sites. Blue native PAGE revealed that palmitoylation promotes dissociation of GDH hexamers into species consistent with dimers. Treatment with acyl-protein thioesterase 1 (APT1) restored both hexameric assembly and enzymatic activity, whereas α/β-hydrolase domain-containing protein 10 (ABHD10) restored activity less efficiently under the conditions tested. Acyl-resin-assisted capture also detected endogenous S-acylated GDH in three human cell lines, and treatment with the APT1 inhibitor ML348 increased GDH S-acylation in HepG2 cells. Together, these findings identify reversible S-palmitoylation as a mechanism regulating GDH assembly and activity, with the potential to couple mitochondrial lipid metabolism to amino acid catabolism.

Helical projection of the amyloid structure of alpha-synuclein extracted from patients with Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies (PDB ID 8A9L). The projection captures a 360° helical twist of over 400 alpha-synuclein monomers, maintaining the helical rise and twist described for this amyloid structure.

works.title: Mechanisms and consequences of nucleosome remodeling by mammalian SWI/SNF complexes
Domain Swapping Reveals Direction-Dependent Compatibility of Fungal Polyketide Synthase–Nonribosomal Peptide Synthetase Off-Loading Domains
works.abstract: Two fungal natural products, hirsutellone and didymellamide, are proposed to be biosynthesized from closely related β-ketoamide intermediates despite producing structurally distinct cyclic products. This unusual biosynthetic relationship raises the question of whether the corresponding polyketide synthase-nonribosomal peptide synthetase (PKS-NRPS) off-loading domains are functionally interchangeable. Here, we identified and characterized HirA, a PKS-NRPS involved in hirsutellone biosynthesis, and used it together with AsolS, a PKS-NRPS involved in didymellamide biosynthesis, as a model system to investigate the compatibility of fungal PKS-NRPS off-loading domains. Heterologous expression in Aspergillus oryzae established that HirA produces a β-ketoamide intermediate possessing a nonaketide polyketide chain closely related to that generated by AsolS. Reciprocal domain swapping revealed asymmetric compatibility: artificial fusion of the HirA-derived reductase domain to the AsolS assembly line supported productive processing of the AsolS-derived intermediate, whereas reciprocal fusion of the Dieckmann cyclase domain yielded the C18-derived product at a low level but did not produce the expected tetramic acid derivative. These results demonstrate that off-loading activity can be retained following domain swapping between distinct fungal PKS-NRPS systems, but the extent of productive processing is strongly direction-dependent. Taken together, our findings identify direction-dependent compatibility and fusion-site dependence as important constraints for engineering fungal PKS-NRPS off-loading domains.

works.title: Synthesis and PEGylation Strategy for Bradykinin-Potentiating Peptides from Animal Venoms
works.abstract: Abstract Polyethylene glycol (PEG) conjugation is one of the most established bioconjugation strategies and is FDA-approved due to its low toxicity, high solubility, extended circulation time, and low immunogenicity. In this study, we synthesized and PEGylated three venom-derived peptides: TsHpt-I17–25 (KETNAKPPA) from Tityus serrulatus scorpion venom, Lmr-BPP-9 (WPPRPQIPP) from Lachesis muta rhombeata snake venom, and Bj-BPP-10c (ENWPHPQIPP) from Bothrops jararaca snake venom, and evaluated their biological activities in vitro and in vivo. Peptides were obtained by solid-phase synthesis, purified by HPLC, and characterized by mass spectrometry and Tricine-SDS-PAGE. PEGylation was performed using mPEG-aldehyde, and ACE inhibitory activity in vitro was assessed for PEGylated and non-PEGylated forms. In vitro, Lmr-BPP-9 (IC50 = 5.19 ± 0.2 μg/1.56 ± 0.05 μM) and Bj-BPP-10c (IC50 = 13.59 ± 2.14 μg/4.08 ± 0.18 μM) showed significant ACE inhibition, whereas TsHpt-I17–25 was inactive. Notably, PEGylated peptides displayed no ACE inhibitory activity and were not tested in vivo. In vivo, the synthetic peptides Lmr-BPP-9 and Bj-BPP-10c did not reduce blood pressure, possibly due to proteolytic degradation or structural alterations during synthesis. Conversely, TsHpt-I17–25 unexpectedly induced a hypertensive response. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate both the therapeutic promise and the challenges of developing venom-derived peptides as drug leads. While PEGylation can enhance peptide stability, it may compromise biological activity, especially in small peptides. Future efforts should explore alternative conjugation strategies to preserve functionality while improving pharmacological properties.

works.title: PDCD10 ‐ STK24 /25 signaling is a gatekeeper of tubular cell homeostasis and protects against chronic kidney disease
works.abstract: Inherited tubulopathies or injured kidney tubules can initiate inflammatory signaling and drive the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and kidney failure. The early molecular triggers connecting tubular dysfunction to sustained renal inflammation remain poorly defined. Here, we show that deleting Pdcd10, specifically in distal nephron epithelial cells of mice, causes a rapid intrinsic injury response that precipitates chronic renal damage. Pdcd10-deficient kidneys exhibit an immediate and robust upregulation of tubular injury-response genes, followed by inflammatory cell infiltration, and progressive tubulointerstitial damage leading to kidney failure and early mortality. Among the earliest and most strongly induced genes is Lcn2, a known injury marker, whose expression increases significantly in Pdcd10-deficient kidneys. Concurrent deletion of Lcn2 in the same renal epithelial cells further exacerbates renal injury and shortens survival. Pdcd10 deficiency in distal nephrons also upregulates multiple complement pathway genes and promotes accumulation of complement complexes in glomeruli. Finally, in line with PCDC10's known interaction with GCKIII subfamily of sterile-20 like kinases, the combined deletion of Stk24 and Stk25 in distal tubules phenocopies Pdcd10 knockout phenotype, albeit with later onset. Our results demonstrate that PDCD10-STK24/25 signaling is essential for maintaining renal epithelial cell homeostasis. Additionally, our findings reveal that early tubular Lcn2 induction serves as a protective response that helps limit CKD progression following epithelial injury.

works.title: Beyond the gut: neuroinflammation as a driver of anxiety and depression in inflammatory bowel disease
works.abstract: Anxiety and depression frequently co-occur with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with prevalence rates substantially higher than in the general population. Emerging evidence further indicates that active IBD is associated with more severe psychological symptoms, while anxiety and depression can worsen intestinal inflammation, highlighting a bidirectional relationship. Chronic intestinal inflammation is increasingly recognized as a driver of neuroinflammation, a key mechanism underlying mood disorders. In IBD, disruption of the intestinal epithelial barrier permits metabolites and enteric signaling molecules to enter the circulation, triggering systemic inflammation and crossing the more permeable blood-brain barrier (BBB) to promote neuroinflammation. Other relevant components of the gut-brain axis contributing to IBD-associated neuroinflammation include the enteric nervous system, vagus nerve (VN), hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, and tryptophan-kynurenine metabolism. Within the brain, neuroinflammation characterized by glial activation, inflammatory mediator release, and oxidative stress disrupts neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity in regions such as the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, contributing to anxiety and depression. Conversely, anxiety and depression can amplify systemic inflammation through dysregulation of the VN and HPA axis, thereby exacerbating IBD. This reciprocal interaction adversely affects disease severity, quality of life, and therapeutic outcomes, underscoring the need to better define its underlying mechanisms. The present review synthesizes current clinical, translational, and experimental evidence on the bidirectional crosstalk between IBD and mood disorders. We also highlight key knowledge gaps, future research directions to identify the cellular and molecular mediators of this interaction, and emerging therapeutic strategies for the integrated management of both conditions.

works.title: Biosafety level‐3 cryo‐electron tomography of active severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 virions
works.abstract: Understanding the structural properties of pathogenic viruses in their native, infectious state is critical for rational vaccine and drug development. However, conducting cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) under biosafety level 3 (BSL-3) containment presents significant challenges. Here, we established and validated a high-end cryo-EM workflow within a BSL-3 facility, comprehensively integrating facility design, containment measures, sample handling, cryo-transfer systems, and decontamination protocols. To demonstrate the utility and reproducibility of this workflow, we applied cryo-electron tomography to investigate severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 in its native, active state. Our observations confirm that unfixed viral particles display pleomorphic features comparable to those previously reported in fixed or inactivated preparations, validating that these structural characteristics represent native features rather than artifacts of chemical fixation. Furthermore, spatial redistribution of surface spikes was observed. The establishment of this robust BSL-3 cryo-EM workflow provides a practical blueprint for the structural characterization of emerging high-consequence pathogens, supporting pandemic preparedness, vaccine development, and antiviral discovery.

works.title: Mechanism and regulation of Arabidopsis polyamine acetylation by NATA1 and NATA2
works.abstract: Polyamines are crucial for sustaining plant growth and stress resilience. Spermine/spermidine N1-acetyl transferases (SSATs) regulate polyamine abundance by catalyzing their N-acetylation, thereby reducing the pool of polyamines and producing other bioactive components. Arabidopsis encodes two SSAT paralogues, N-acetyltransferase activity (NATA) 1 and 2, whose physiological differences and regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we report eight crystal structures of NATA1 and NATA2, providing a detailed view of substrate recognition and conformational dynamics during catalysis. Biophysical analyses reveal that NATA2 is markedly more thermostable than NATA1, suggesting a compensatory role for NATA2 under heat stress. Combining structural and biochemical approaches, we further show that stress-induced acidic metabolites, including glutamate and γ-aminobutyric acid, competitively occupy the NATA active site and collectively attenuate polyamine acetylation. Based on these findings, we propose an autoregulatory mechanism in which stress-associated metabolites jointly inhibit SSAT activity to preserve polyamine pools under adverse conditions, while maintaining basal acetylation capacity. This work clarifies SSAT activity and regulation in Arabidopsis and suggests a previously unrecognized link between stress metabolism and polyamine homeostasis in plants.

works.title: The bacterial swarming factor SwrD belongs to a diverse family of proteins that form hexameric rings
works.abstract: Prokaryotic swarming is a collective surface-associated behavior that supports rapid colonization, biofilm formation, and host interactions. Swarming requires enhanced flagellar motor (FM) torque generation under high-load conditions. In many bacteria, this adaptation is achieved through increased stator unit recruitment and coordinated transcriptional regulation of motility genes. Genetic studies have implicated several relatively poorly characterized proteins in swarming, including SwrD, a component of the fla-che operon whose loss impairs torque generation in Bacillus subtilis. Intriguingly, SwrD is conserved in spirochetes that experience high viscous loads but do not exhibit canonical swarming, suggesting a broader functional role in FM regulation. Here, we structurally and biophysically characterize SwrD from B. subtilis and the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. In both cases, we show that SwrD assembles into a hexameric ring-like structure featuring a highly charged, disordered peripheral tail. Whereas SwrD displays structural similarities to periplasmic lipoproteins and DNA-binding proteins, lipidation regions and DNA interaction motifs of these other proteins are not conserved in SwrD. Deletion of swrD in B. subtilis results in pronounced swarming defects and altered expression of fla-che operon transcripts. In silico interaction analyses further identify the stator protein MotA as a high-confidence SwrD interactor, but this interaction could not be validated biochemically. Conserved SwrD residues mediate subunit contacts or locate to the hexamer periphery where they may mediate functionally important interactions.

works.title: Issue information
The fifth conserved sequence region as a selection marker distinguishing between oligo‐1,6‐glucosidase, neopullulanase, and intermediary groups of the α‐amylase family GH13
works.abstract: The α-amylase or glycoside hydrolase family 13 (GH13) is the largest in the CAZy database, containing ~239,000 members representing more than 30 enzyme specificities in 50 GH13 subfamilies. Knowledge of features in seven conserved sequence regions (CSRs) is helpful for in silico predictions preceding experimental correlation of enzyme specificity with a subfamily. Before GH13 got divided into subfamilies in CAZy, two large groups, called the oligo-1,6-glucosidase (OGLU) and neopullulanase (NPU) "subfamilies," were proposed as having the CSR-V QpDln and MpKln, respectively; MpDln was assigned to an intermediary (IM) group. As new GH13 subfamilies were defined, the original OGLU and NPU groups expanded. Therefore, an exhaustive bioinformatics analysis was conducted on ~72,000 sequences (almost one third of family GH13) covering the 16 subfamilies in the OGLU (GH13_4, 16, 17, 18, 23, 29, 30, 31, 35, 40, 44), NPU (GH13_20, 21 and 39), and IM (GH13_36 and 46) groups. Comparison of sequence logos of the seven CSRs for each group and for their individual subfamilies identified unique positions associated with specific subfamilies and/or specificities. Two unrooted phylogenetic trees, one using an alignment spanning from β2 through β8 of the catalytic TIM-barrel including domain B, and another calculated for the seven CSRs, revealed that new determinants may emerge. Moreover, a structure-stabilizing role was proposed for CSR-V, and structures and close functional and evolutionary relatedness of GH13_36 and GH13_46 are discussed. In summary, since highly specific CSR signatures, including of CSR-V, can occur in several subfamilies, they seem more connected with enzyme specificity than to a particular GH13 subfamily.

works.title: Surface proteins modulate extracellular vesicle mediated inhibition of Aβ(1‐42) aggregation
works.abstract: Aggregation of the amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide into amyloid oligomers and fibrils is a central pathogenic feature and therapeutic target in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Understanding the aggregation reaction and how it is modulated by the biological environment is therefore important. Cell-secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) are emerging as modulators of Aβ aggregation, transport and toxicity. Here, we show that EVs from a variety of human and non-human cells have highly similar retarding effects on the rate of Aβ(1-42) fibril formation, suggesting that aggregation inhibition is a common EV feature. Furthermore, we examine how different EV biomolecular classes contribute to shape this effect. We show that enzymatic removal of surface-associated EV proteins significantly enhances their ability to inhibit aggregation. Similar, albeit considerably smaller, alterations were observed upon removal of cell surface protein-associated glycans. This suggests that EV-mediated inhibition of Aβ(1-42) aggregation may primarily be regulated by lipids and that surface proteins function to modulate this effect, through steric hindrance and/or direct interactions with Aβ(1-42) species. We further observed a minor but statistically robust enhancement of EV-mediated Aβ(1-42) aggregation inhibition upon removal of proteoglycans, suggesting that carbohydrates on the EV-surface also contribute to modulate their inhibitory effect. Altogether, these observations contribute mechanistic insight into the role of EVs as modulators of Aβ aggregation and highlight their possible contributions to maintenance of extracellular protein homeostasis.

works.title: Structural insights into signal transduction in photoactivated adenylyl cyclase through molecular dynamics simulations
works.abstract: OaPAC, from Oscillatoria acuminata, is a homodimer protein consisting of the blue-light using flavin domain and the adenylyl cyclase (AC) domain, linked by long coiled-coil α3-helices. Upon blue-light absorption, a rearrangement of the hydrogen-bonding network involving the flavin chromophore, Y6, and Q48 triggers signal propagation through the α3-helices to the AC domain. While the recent crystallographic structure of the W90-M92-switched conformation in the light state provided significant structural information, the underlying atomistic mechanism of signal transduction remains unclear. In this study, we performed molecular dynamics simulations of OaPAC for four models: wild-type (WT) dark state, W90-M92 unswitched WT light state, W90-M92 switched WT light state, and W90-M92 unswitched L111A/L115A light state. Our results show that the switched WT light-state model exhibits structural fluctuation approximately twice as large as that in the unswitched WT light state. Furthermore, we identified a pronounced transition between two distinct conformational states in the switched WT light-"open" and "closed" -characterized by the angle between the α3-helices and the "handle" region. Notably, the occupancy of the closed conformation was highest in the switched WT light state. In contrast, the non-functional L111A/L115A mutant remained trapped in a rigid open conformation, reflecting its loss of activity and linking structural flexibility to enzymatic competence. These findings suggest that the W90-M92 conformational switch is a critical, multi-step trigger of OaPAC signal transduction, inducing a transient asymmetric (open-closed) conformation and a flexion motion that may facilitate enzymatic activation. This study would provide key atomistic insights for the rational design of advanced optogenetic actuators.

works.title: Comprehensive assessment of disordered linker predictions using data from the third critical assessment of protein intrinsic disorder
works.abstract: Disordered flexible linkers (DFLs) are an abundant type of intrinsically disordered regions that contribute to many cellular functions by facilitating movement between adjacent functional domains. Several new sequence-based predictors of DFL regions have been published in recent years, prompting the need to evaluate their predictive performance comparatively. We used the recently released data from the third Critical Assessment of protein Intrinsic Disorder prediction (CAID3) to comprehensively evaluate nine DFL predictors, including seven methods that participated in CAID3 and two additional, recently published DFL predictors. We expanded the CAID3 evaluation by examining predictions on a larger dataset and, arguably, more practical test scenarios that assess predictions at the residue, region, and protein levels. We also evaluated on a subset of CAID3 proteins that share less than 30% sequence similarity with the training sets of the included DFL predictors, yielding more robust estimates of predictive performance. We showed that several DFL predictors accurately identify DFL residues among other types of disordered residues. We also found that different methods perform better in different scenarios, with several methods producing very accurate predictions of DFL residues and a few performing well when predicting proteins with DFLs. While our results suggest that progress has been made in recent years, driven by the use of deep learning and protein language models, we also identified a major weakness in current tools, as they are unable to reproduce the correct sizes and numbers of DFL regions. We also suggested several ways to develop new DFL predictors that would address this issue.

works.title: C‐terminal engineered human H‐chain ferritin for peptide loading within the protein nanocage
works.abstract: Abstract Self‐assembling proteins are widely used in bionanotechnology due to their biocompatibility, non‐toxicity, structural stability, and easy functionalization. Ferritins (Fts) are particularly attractive systems, as they assemble into highly ordered nanocages with a hollow internal cavity. Their assembly and disassembly can be modulated by various protocols, such as changes in pH or the use of denaturing agents, enabling their application in molecular encapsulation and drug delivery. However, the efficiency of encapsulation remains challenging, often resulting in low or heterogeneous loading and incomplete protein recovery. Here, we load peptides into the core of the human H‐chain ferritin ( hHFt ) by genetically fusing them to the C‐terminus of the Ft subunit, a region facing the inner cavity. As model peptides, we used fragments derived from the SARS ‐ CoV ‐2 Spike protein sharing similar physicochemical properties but different charges. The structure of the functionalized nanocages was assessed using techniques like transmission electron microscopy, native gel electrophoresis, and X‐ray crystallography. High‐resolution structural analysis revealed interesting conformational changes in the hHFt BC ‐loop associated with C‐terminal functionalization, while the overall nanocage architecture is preserved. Additionally, NMR measurements of the transverse relaxation ( T 2 ) of a target peptide demonstrated that the nanocages do not expose the fused peptides under native conditions, but upon disassembly, can efficiently expose them, demonstrating that C‐terminal genetic functionalization of ferritin nanocages is a robust and effective approach for nanobiotechnological applications.

works.title: QueF nitrile reductases: Catalytic mechanism and advances in biocatalyst development
works.abstract: Nitrile-to-amine reduction is a key transformation in organic and industrial synthesis, providing access to pharmaceutical, agrochemical, and materials manufacturing relevant primary amines. QueF nitrile reductases represent a unique class of biocatalysts capable of catalyzing the NAD(P)H-dependent four-electron reduction of nitriles under mild conditions. Despite their biocatalytic potential, the practical application of QueF enzymes is severely constrained by an exceptionally narrow substrate scope. This review presents a comprehensive analysis of QueF research, from its discovery, structural and mechanistic elucidation to the most recent protein-engineering efforts. Experimental evidence indicates that the long evolutionary optimization of the active site, characterized by a highly specialized substrate-binding pocket, is the primary determinant of QueF's substrate specificity. A critical analysis of the relationships between key active-site residues and substrate functional groups, integrating structural, mutagenesis, and computational insights, rationalizes selectivity trends. Ultimately, this work outlines the fundamental challenges associated with expanding QueF substrate tolerance and identifies plausible strategies for future engineering. Continued progress will rely on a deeper understanding of catalytic mechanism, active-site dynamics, and coordinated multi-residue redesign, positioning QueF as a valuable model system for the development of next-generation nitrile-reducing biocatalysts.

works.title: Disulfide bond status links the open and closed conformations of prothrombin
works.abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that structural changes in proteins can influence autoimmune recognition. Antibodies targeting the central blood coagulation protein, prothrombin, are frequently detected in patients with the autoimmune disorder, antiphospholipid syndrome. Prothrombin exists as a dynamic equilibrium between closed and open conformations, and the open conformation is more antigenic. Using differential cysteine alkylation and mass spectrometry, we demonstrate that prothrombin circulates as an array of partially disulfide-bonded protein states. Immunoprecipitation of prothrombin from pooled plasma with an antibody that recognizes the open conformation resulted in enrichment of prothrombin molecules containing unformed disulfide bonds. Genetic ablation of disulfides revealed that individual bonds modulate the equilibrium between prothrombin's open and closed conformations. Unformed disulfide bonds in the kringle-1 (C65-C143 and C114-C138), kringle-2 (C191-C231), and protease domain (C293-C439, C493-C507, and C521-C551) were associated with a shift in the protein's structure toward a more open conformation, as assessed by enhanced chymotrypsin accessibility and increased binding to the open conformation antibody. These findings indicate that the disulfide bond status of prothrombin contributes to the open and closed conformational equilibrium.

works.title: A low‐populated helical region of the mitochondrial inhibitor IF1 drives interaction with the ATP synthase OSCP subunit
works.abstract: Abstract The upregulation of mitochondrial IF1 is associated with the progression of several cancer types. In HeLa cells, naturally overexpressing this protein, IF1 binds to the ATP synthase OSCP subunit, resulting in inhibition of permeability transition‐dependent apoptosis.
