This newly identified protein–protein interaction represents a promising therapeutic target in tumors characterized by IF1 overexpression. However, the rational design of targeted molecules is currently limited by a lack of structural data on the binding mechanism. Here we employed native mass spectrometry and NMR spectroscopy to identify the minimal IF1 segment required to target the OSCP subunit. NMR revealed that the interaction is weak in solution, with an affinity K D in the low millimolar range, consistent with a binding event occurring exclusively when IF1 is overexpressed in cancer cells. These findings guided the design of a model peptide containing the IF1 binding epitope, which was used in molecular dynamics simulations (MD) aimed at investigating its binding mechanism to the OSCP subunit. NMR and MD converged to show that the IF1 binding epitope requires a helical folding for OSCP engagement, consistent with a helical Molecular Recognition Feature (αMoRF) mechanism. Helicity of the epitope is strictly necessary for productive binding, with key contacts involving IF1 residues E30, E31, Y33, F34, and Q37 packing against OSCP helix H3. Structural analysis of the binding complex provided a first molecular framework to inspire the design of molecules capable of displacing IF1 from the OSCP subunit and potentially exerting anticancer activity.

works.title: Cover Image
works.abstract: Helical projection of the amyloid structure of alpha-synuclein extracted from patients with Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies (PDB ID 8A9L). The projection captures a 360° helical twist of over 400 alpha-synuclein monomers, maintaining the helical rise and twist described for this amyloid structure.

works.title: Lipid membrane composition modulates the structural evolution of early‐stage human islet amyloid polypeptide amyloids
works.abstract: Progressive β cell death resulting from the aggregation of human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP) in the pancreas is a molecular driver of type 2 diabetes (T2D). Recent studies from our group have shown that hIAPP forms two distinct amyloid oligomers: on-path donut oligomers (DOs) and off-path round oligomers (ROs). Previous studies have also shown lipids, one of the most abundant classes of biomolecules within cells, alter the kinetics of hIAPP amyloid formation and template structurally distinct hIAPP fibrils. However, the influence of the specific lipid environment on the evolution of early-stage hIAPP amyloids remains unknown. In this study, we employ atomic force microscopy (AFM) and atomic force microscopy Infrared (AFM-IR) spectroscopy to resolve the morphological and structural dynamics of early-stage hIAPP DOs, ROs, and fibrils (FBs) formed in the presence of phosphatidylcholine (PC) or phosphatidylserine (PS). PC-templated DOs with predominantly parallel β-sheet structure, while PS-templated DOs were predominantly antiparallel β-sheet. These DOs were present only during the early stages of aggregation. Conversely, ROs were persistent and their structural evolution was more stochastic irrespective of the lipid environment. The secondary structure of lipid-templated DOs correlated precisely with that of early-stage FBs, highlighting their role as on-path oligomers in hIAPP aggregation. Finally, the lipid environment present during aggregation uniquely altered the structural evolution of FBs, with PC favoring a progressive increase in antiparallel β-sheet FBs and PS favoring an increase in parallel β-sheet. These results provide crucial insight into the mechanisms of hIAPP aggregation in the lipid-rich cellular environment, simultaneously solidifying lipids as critical players in the early stages of hIAPP aggregation.

works.title: Rules of the road for loop-extruding motors: loading, unloading, and crowding
works.abstract: Loop extrusion by structural maintenance of chromosome (SMC) complexes has emerged as a key mechanism of genome organization across domains of life, yet the rules that govern where these motors load, unload, and become enriched remain poorly understood. The canonical model treats cohesin as loading and unloading uniformly but stopping at extrusion barriers. Chromosome architecture is then shaped by where extruding complexes stop. Accumulating evidence broadens this view by uncovering cases of (i) targeted SMC loading across metazoa, plants, and fungi, (ii) sites of specific SMC release, and (iii) domains of crowded loop extrusion. Together, these new Rules of the Road shift the focus from where extruders stop to where they start, end, and dwell-with implications for development, gene regulation, and genome stability.

works.title: Coiled Coils as a Programmable Platform for Computational Biosensor Design
works.abstract: Coiled coils are a versatile class of α-helical protein motifs characterized by recurring sequence patterns that direct their assembly into defined oligomeric bundles and underpin a wide range of biological functions. The well-established sequence-structure relationships governing coiled-coil formation enable predictive control over stability, specificity, and oligomerization state, making them attractive and chemically tractable building blocks for biosensor design in applications ranging from single-molecule detection to synthetic biochemical circuits and functional nanomaterials. After revisiting the theoretical foundations of coiled-coil architecture, this review outlines strategies to engineer programmable binding interfaces that can be rationally tuned to generate orthogonal, high-affinity interaction pairs, enabling flexible and modular biosensor platforms. Particular emphasis is placed on recent advances in computational and data-driven design approaches, including machine-learning and AI-based strategies, alongside established rational and empirical methods for coiled-coil construction. These complementary design principles underpin the development of coiled-coil-based biosensors and are discussed together with selected application examples to illustrate how engineered coiled-coil interactions support sensitive and specific molecular recognition as well as switchable control in synthetic biology and chemical biology. Overall, this review highlights coiled coils as programmable, stable, and highly designable scaffolds at the interface of molecular engineering, computation, and chemical biology.

works.title: Shikonin: From Biosynthesis and Pharmacological Mechanisms to Translational Safety and Drug Delivery
works.abstract: Shikonin (SHK) is a red naphthoquinone produced mainly in the roots of Boraginaceae species and has been investigated for anticancer, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, neuroprotective, cardioprotective, hepatoprotective, and wound-healing activities. This review critically integrates botanical sources and biosynthesis with pharmacological mechanisms, preclinical evidence, safety, and delivery strategies. Across cancer models, SHK converges on redox imbalance and regulated cell-death programmes, including apoptosis, cell-cycle arrest, autophagy, necroptosis, ferroptosis, and immunogenic cell death, while modulating NF-κB, MAPK, PI3K/Akt, and related signalling networks. However, the evidence is dominated by heterogeneous in vitro experiments and small-animal studies, with limited pharmacokinetic standardisation, incomplete assessment of selectivity toward diseased versus normal tissues, and almost no robust clinical evaluation. Poor aqueous solubility, chemical and photochemical instability, rapid metabolism, route-dependent exposure, and a context-dependent therapeutic window remain central translational barriers. Liposomes, polymeric micelles, nanoparticles, nanogels, nanoemulsions, and ligand- or stimulus-responsive systems can improve dispersion, tissue accumulation, controlled release, and combination therapy; nevertheless, their long-term safety, manufacturing reproducibility, and comparative advantage over free SHK require rigorous validation. SHK should therefore be regarded as a mechanistically versatile therapeutic lead rather than a clinically established treatment. Translation will depend on exposure-response studies, standardised formulations, clinically relevant models, and well-designed human trials.

works.title: Beyond Thiol‐Dependent Cyclization of Peptide Libraries: Assessing a Photochemical Alternative
works.abstract: Cyclic peptides are powerful scaffolds for chemical biology and drug discovery. Genetically encoded display (phage, ribosome, mRNA, and yeast) enables high-throughput screening of peptide libraries. Yet expanding their accessible chemical space depends not only on library size but also on the cyclization chemistry, which selects the conformations the library samples and makes linkage choice a primary design variable. Cyclization most often relies on cysteine through disulfides, thiol-reactive linkers, or metal-thiolate bonds. Enzymatic head-to-tail ligation and noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) provide cysteine-free macrocyclization through amide bonds, but each imposes practical limits such as motif constraints or reliance on genetic code expansion. In this perspective, we examine photoinduced aromatic crosslinking as a complementary, cysteine-independent strategy. Recent fluorotryptophan photochemistry shows that irradiation drives diaryl bond formation between fluorinated tryptophan and proximal phenylalanine or tyrosine, generating intrinsically fluorescent macrocycles and enabling an optical readout of cyclization yield. Fluorotryptophan is a conservative modification that can be introduced at native Trp codons, which may avoid the genetic code expansion. Antimicrobial peptides offer a demanding test case: their function depends on backbone rigidity, amphipathic face presentation, and membrane interaction, all of which an aromatic crosslink could influence.

works.title: Effects of POPG and Cholesterol on Freeze–Thawing Mediated Content Exchange and Transcription in Giant Unilamellar Vesicles
works.abstract: Freeze-thaw (F/T)-induced content mixing between artificial cells enables efficient exchange of encapsulated components. However, F/T treatment is often accompanied by vesicle rupture and content loss, and the effects of membrane composition on fusion and reaction efficiency remain unclear. Here, we investigated how cholesterol and the negatively charged phospholipid 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1'-rac-glycerol) (POPG) influence giant unilamellar vesicle (GUV) stability, content mixing, and transcriptional activity after F/T treatment. Cholesterol-containing GUVs exhibited increased vesicle loss and reduced content mixing after F/T treatment. In contrast, POPG markedly improved GUV recovery and suppressed vesicle loss, even in the presence of cholesterol. Membranes containing 20 mol% POPG and 20 mol% cholesterol maintained high cargo retention and efficient content mixing. When DNA-containing liposomes were fused with transcription-reagent-containing liposomes through F/T treatment, this membrane composition also yielded the highest transcriptional activity. Notably, although the combination of POPG and cholesterol inhibited transcription in intact GUVs, it showed the highest transcriptional activity following F/T-mediated content mixing. These findings demonstrate that the effects of membrane composition on encapsulated biochemical reactions depend strongly on whether the reaction components are initially coencapsulated or brought together through F/T-mediated content exchange.

works.title: Visualizing Telokin‐Dependent Regulation of Myosin Filaments by Electron Microscopy
works.abstract: Smooth muscle myosin (SmM) is the primary force-generating motor protein in smooth muscle cells. It undergoes conformational transitions between a compact, inactive folded state (10S) and an extended, filament-forming state (6S). Telokin (Tkn), the noncatalytic C-terminal domain of myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), has been implicated in regulating myosin filament stability. However, the molecular basis of its interaction with SmM remains incompletely understood. In this study, we have employed recombinant human Tkn to investigate its role in SmM filament assembly. Circular dichroism spectroscopy, fluorescence spectroscopy, and chromatographic studies were used to confirm the structural integrity and functional activity of the purified proteins. Remarkably, the presence of Tkn promoted myosin filament assembly even with ATP, a condition that typically favors the folded 10S conformation and inhibits filament formation. Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) micrographs of the resulting filaments showed predominantly non-bipolar filaments that closely resembled the native side-polar smooth muscle thick filaments. Despite sequence variations within the acidic C-terminal region, human Tkn efficiently induced filament assembly of avian SmM, indicating conservation of the underlying filament-promoting mechanism across species. Collectively, these findings provide direct experimental evidence that Tkn acts as a structural regulator of filament assembly and stability. This offers new insights into the mechanisms governing smooth muscle contractility.

works.title: Beyond Inhibition: Emerging Approaches in Ubiquitin–Proteasome‐Mediated Protein Degradation for Precision Targeting
works.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) represents an emerging paradigm in drug discovery, capable of overcoming the limitations of traditional therapeutic strategies based on protein inhibition. Exploiting the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), TPD allows the selective elimination of pathologically relevant proteins. The most established approaches in TPD are proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) and molecular glue (MG) chemical degraders, which feature distinct molecular architectures and mechanisms of action. Although these approaches have proven highly effective in promoting the selective degradation of target proteins, their use is often accompanied by critical issues related to tissue selectivity and biodistribution. To overcome these limitations, advanced strategies have been developed in recent years that exploit endogenous and exogenous triggers, such as antibody-PROTAC conjugates and PROTAC prodrugs that can be activated by enzymes, redox conditions, hypoxia, light, or radiotherapy, allowing for more precise spatial and temporal control of degradation. Alternative approaches, such as hydrophobic tagging, further expand the available repertoire, circumventing the E3 ligase dependency inherent to PROTAC systems for protein destabilization and confirming the versatility of the TPD platform. In this review, an overview of the most effective and promising approaches in TPD is reported, focusing on the most recent technological advances and reporting key case studies.

works.title: Monitoring Enzyme Activity on the Surface of a Self‐Referenced Near‐White Light Emitting Assembly of Atomic Clusters
works.abstract: Sensitive detection of protease activity in complex biological environments remains challenging due to signal instability, background interference, and the lack of internal calibration. Here, we report a self‐referenced, white‐light–emitting surface defect‐engineered nanocluster assembly for selective and ratiometric detection of proteinase K activity and inhibition. Manganese‐doped, zinc‐mediated gold nanocluster (Zn Au NC) assemblies functionalized with bovine serum albumin (BSA) generate tricolor emission from BSA, the nanocluster core, and Mn 2+ , producing near‐white‐light fluorescence that serves as an intrinsic internal reference. Proteinase K induces coordinated spectral changes, including enhanced and blueshifted BSA emission with simultaneous quenching of Zn Au NC and Mn 2+ emissions, resulting in systematic chromaticity shifts and a robust ratiometric response. Mechanistic studies attribute these changes to proteolytic cleavage of BSA and disruption of the nanocluster assembly, corroborated by circular dichroism measurements. The platform exhibits high selectivity for proteinase K , enables inhibitor detection, and performs reliably in fetal bovine serum. This self‐calibrated nanocluster platform provides a versatile strategy for enzyme‐responsive sensing with potential applications in biochemical diagnostics and inhibitor screening.

works.title: RNA Aptamer‐Enabled Development of Heterobifunctionals That Chemically Induce RNA‐FKBP12 Ternary Complexes
works.abstract: Limitations in the druggability of challenging protein targets, coupled with recognition of the diverse roles of noncoding RNAs in cellular regulation and disease have spurred interest in RNA as a druggable macromolecule. The rapidly emerging field of RNA-targeted small-molecule therapeutics is now exploring induced proximity mechanisms in the form of RNA-targeting chimeras that recruit effector proteins to catalyze RNA decay. Inspired by "molecular glue" natural products such as rapamycin and cyclosporin A, which induce protein-protein interactions to sterically modulate protein function, we propose the new application of immunophilin recruitment to alter RNA function. Here in, we report the design and characterization of heterobifunctional molecules that induce highly cooperative RNA-FKBP12 ternary complexes and describe efforts to assess their impact on RNA metabolism. We also evaluate applications and report off-target liabilities associated with the chosen RNA ligand for our heterobifunctional series. Finally, we discuss the challenges faced and highlight opportunities for future success in the RNA space.

works.title: Covalent Ligands that Target the Human Papillomavirus E6 Oncoprotein
works.abstract: The high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) early protein 6 (E6) viral oncoprotein is a key player in HPV-mediated cancers and is the major driver of cervical, anal, and a substantial portion of head and neck cancers. HPV E6 recruits the cellular ubiquitin E3-ligase E6-associated protein (E6AP), also termed UBE3A, and this E6/E6AP complex in turn recruits the tumor suppressor p53, resulting in the ubiquitin-mediated degradation of p53. The cysteine-rich E6 protein presents an attractive target for chemical intervention through covalent, cysteine-reactive chemistries. While previous studies have uncovered peptidic covalent inhibitors of E6, we sought to determine whether we could identify nonpeptidic functional binders. We screened a library of cysteine-reactive covalent ligands and identified a pyrazoline hit, EN218, bearing a chloroacetamide cysteine-reactive warhead. Evaluation of pyrazoline analogs led to the development of an improved molecule, (S)-WX48A, that stereoselectively reacted with C58 on E6 to inhibit E6-mediated p53 ubiquitination. While this molecule is still in an early stage and requires further medicinal chemistry optimization to exert on-target cellular activity, our study demonstrates that E6 can be directly and stereoselectively targeted with a covalent nonpeptidic small-molecule and provides a foundation for developing more drug-like E6 inhibitors for HPV therapy.

works.title: Catalytic DNA for Precision Diagnostics: DNAzyme‐Based Approaches to Single‐Nucleotide Polymorphism Detection
works.abstract: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are the most abundant form of human genetic variation and serve as important biomarkers in disease risk assessment, therapeutic stratification, and precision medicine. Yet accurate detection of low-abundance SNPs in complex biological samples remains difficult with many conventional genotyping methods, which often rely on sophisticated instrumentation and show limited tolerance to matrix interference. DNAzyme-based biosensors offer a promising alternative by coupling programmable nucleic acid recognition with catalytic signal generation under isothermal conditions. This review highlights recent advances in DNAzyme-based SNP detection across optical, electrochemical, and amplification-assisted formats, including fluorescence, colorimetric, chemiluminescent, rolling circle amplification, loop-mediated isothermal amplification, hybridization chain reaction, and catalytic hairpin assembly strategies. We also discuss molecular design principles that enhance single-base discrimination, such as binding-arm engineering, cofactor tuning, and computational sequence design. Finally, we outline current limitations, including nuclease susceptibility, temperature dependence, and performance in complex sample matrices, and consider emerging opportunities for DNAzyme-enabled SNP analysis in point-of-care diagnostics, personalized medicine, and large-scale genomics.

works.title: On the Need to Revise the Amyloid Cascade Hypothesis
works.abstract: Seven million people in the USA are estimated to suffer from Alzheimer's disease (AD), a number expected to double by 2050. Patient care costs >$350 billion/year now but will exceed $1 trillion by 2050, bankrupting our economy. Tremendous progress in understanding and treating AD has been made over the past 4 decades, yet, after >400 clinical trials, no efficacious AD treatments exist. The amyloid cascade hypothesis (ACH), the leading disease model, holds that amyloid β (Aβ) initiates a cascade leading to disease. Alternative processing cleaves APP in the middle of Aβ, producing the C-terminal fragment, p3. Simply put, if the ACH is true, no Aβ means no disease because p3 is believed soluble, non-amyloidogenic, and nontoxic. However, recent studies have shown this to be untrue. In fact, p3 is more amyloidogenic than Aβ, and is neurotoxic. It also forms mixed aggregates with Aβ that have distinct structures and neurotoxicities. ACH has led the AD field to largely ignore these facts. Here, we provide an integrated perspective on how this has come about and urge expansion of the ACH to consider the possible roles of p3 in AD and to refer to it as Amyloid α (Aα), to better reflect its nature.

works.title: Bringing peroxisomes within reach
PerCap isolates native peroxisomes to reveal peroxisomal proteins and regulators
Pol II reshapes DNA damage
Large-scale RNA-binding protein tethering screen discovers modulators of circular RNA metabolism
works.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are emerging as important regulators in mammalian cells and promising substrates for RNA therapeutics, yet the trans-acting factors governing their metabolism remain poorly defined. Here we systematically evaluate 730 RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) using a tethered reporter assay and identify 281 RBPs that significantly modulate circRNA activity. Follow-up assays implicate these RBPs across key stages of the circRNA life cycle, including biogenesis, nuclear export, degradation and translation. We identify seven RBPs for tethered translation enhancement of therapeutically applicable circRNA vectors and highlight LARP4B as a potent enhancer of exogenous circRNA translation across multiple internal ribosomal entry sites and cell types. We uncover an evolutionarily conserved role for RBM15 in circRNA biogenesis in fly, mouse and human, further demonstrating a role in circRNA nuclear retention, and that perturbing RBM15 sites with dCasRx or antisense oligonucleotides modulates endogenous circRNA expression. Together, our study provides a global view of circRNA trans-regulation and describes practical entry points for therapeutic development.

works.title: Genome Mining-Driven Discovery of the Sactipeptide Smithiosin in Probiotic, Thermophilic Strain Bacillus smithii
works.abstract: Sactipeptides are a class of ribosomally synthesised and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs), which have a cyclic topology formed by unique thioether crosslinks called sactionines. Sactionines are introduced by radical S-adenosylmethionine (rSAM) enzymes between cysteine residues and the α-carbon of other amino acids. Genome sequencing has revealed many putative sactipeptide biosynthetic gene clusters; however, few sactipeptides have been isolated and characterised. Here, we use genome mining to identify a novel sactipeptide from Bacillus smithii. The novel sactipeptide, named smithiosin, was extracted from the industrially important thermophile B. smithii and characterised as a novel homologue of the previously characterised sactipeptide subtilosin A from B. subtilis. Furthermore, the smithiosin precursor peptide gene was heterologously expressed in the subtilosin A producer Bacillus subtilis 168 without knockout of the native precursor peptide, successfully leading to the production of both subtilosin A and smithiosin. This demonstrates for the first time that a non-native precursor peptide is able to outcompete the subtilosin A precursor for all of the native biosynthetic enzymes in B. subtilis, including the radical SAM enzyme AlbA. It also opens a potential new opportunity for screening non-native precursor peptides with the subtilosin A biosynthetic enzymes via heterologous expression in B. subtilis.

works.title: Visualization of CryoEM Hydrogen Peaks in the Photosystem II Reaction Center P 680 Chlorophyll Pair
works.abstract: Abstract X-ray crystallography reports only on the electron density (ED) distribution in molecules, and neutron crystallography only describes the distribution of nuclei. CryoEM visualizes both simultaneously and thus can provide unique information about the electronic structures of molecules that neither of its competitors can do alone. Hydrogen peaks in CryoEM maps are an order of magnitude larger than those in X-ray crystallographic maps. This makes it possible to visualize them in CryoEM maps even when they are not fully resolved from the peaks of the heavy atoms to which they are bonded. Here, I report the results obtained when the methods I have developed for locating the hydrogen peaks were applied to photosystem II (PSII) reaction center P680 chlorophyll pair (A404/D404), its protein ligands (D1-H198 and D2-H197), and flanking residues (I192-G204 of the D1 subunit and T191-A202 of D2) in a CryoEM map having a resolution of 1.71 Å. Hydrogen peaks were found at all the chemically expected locations except for two. First, the orientations of the two methylene hydrogen peaks of the vinyl substituent on A404 were found to differ from those of the same vinyl methylene hydrogens of all the other chlorophylls in PSII. They were orthogonal to the expected plane instead of being in-plane. Second, in the backbone I192O–H195N hydrogen-bonding (HB) pair, the hydrogen peak was found to be next to D1-I192O, rather than D1-H195N, which indicates that this hydrogen atom is part of a carboxyl-imide hydrogen bond rather than a carbonyl-amide hydrogen bond.

works.title: N-n-Propylnorapomorphine Inhibits Huntingtin Aggregation and Lipid Membrane Interactions
works.abstract: Abstract Aggregation of mutant huntingtin (HTT) contributes to Huntington’s disease (HD) pathogenesis. Lipid membranes strongly influence this process and can also be damaged by membrane-associated HTT species. N–n-propylnorapomorphine (NPA), an aporphine-derived dopamine agonist, was identified in a polydiacetylene (PDA)-based screen for compounds that reduce HTT-exon1-induced perturbation of lipid vesicles. Here, thioflavin T fluorescence assays, ex situ and in situ atomic force microscopy (AFM), lipid-vesicle binding assays, and supported-lipid-bilayer imaging were used to determine how NPA affects HTT aggregation and membrane interactions. In bulk solution, NPA reduced β-sheet-rich fibril formation in a dose-dependent manner, with high concentrations nearly abolishing fibril growth. AFM imaging further showed that NPA suppresses fibril formation while altering the oligomer morphology and heterogeneity. NPA also destabilized preformed HTT fibrils and suppressed the surface-mediated aggregation of an HTT-derived peptide. Importantly, NPA retained inhibitory activity in the presence of lipid vesicles that either suppressed or accelerated HTT aggregation. NPA reduced HTT association with lipid vesicles in a dose-dependent manner and markedly decreased HTT-induced disruption of supported brain lipid bilayers. Collectively, these observations are consistent with NPA acting at multiple, potentially connected stages of the HTT aggregation pathway by altering early assemblies, destabilizing fibrils, and reducing the formation or persistence of membrane-active species. The present data do not distinguish whether these effects arise from a single shared binding mode or from interactions with multiple HTT conformational states. Although its dopamine agonist activity may limit direct therapeutic application, NPA provides a useful proof-of-concept scaffold for compounds targeting both HTT aggregation and membrane-associated toxicity.

works.title: Transposon mutagenesis identifies lon , csgF , and rfbF as critical genetic determinants of biofilm architecture and adhesion in multidrug‐resistant Salmonella Typhimurium
works.abstract: Salmonella Typhimurium relies on biofilm formation to withstand environmental stressors, resist antimicrobials, and establish persistent host infections. However, the genetic networks governing biofilm development remain poorly understood. Here, we assessed the biofilm-forming capacity of 708 S. Typhimurium isolates. Among them, 88.56% formed biofilms, with 3.81% classified as strong producers associated with extensive multidrug resistance. To elucidate underlying genetic determinants, we performed EZ-Tn5 transposon mutagenesis on a strong biofilm-producing clinical isolate (15E341), generating ~ 5000 mutants. Phenotypic screening and whole-genome sequencing identified three distinct loci-lon, csgF, and rfbF-whose disruption significantly impaired biofilm formation without affecting planktonic growth. Confocal and electron microscopy (LSCM and FESEM) revealed severely compromised 3D biofilm architecture and defective surface colonization. Furthermore, these mutants exhibited significantly reduced adhesion to Caco-2 epithelial cells, glass, and silicone. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a distinct regulatory shift, characterized by marked upregulation of flagellar assembly pathways and downregulation of fimbrial genes. In a murine model, the mutants exhibited attenuated virulence, evidenced by increased host survival and significantly reduced bacterial colonization in the cecum, liver, and spleen. Notably, whereas CsgF is an established curli-assembly factor and Lon is a well-characterized stress and virulence regulator, RfbF, an O-antigen biosynthesis enzyme, emerged as a previously undercharacterized determinant of biofilm capacity in S. Typhimurium. Collectively, these findings highlight multi-gene coordination in biofilm development and identify pathways that warrant further investigation for disrupting persistent Salmonella infections.

works.title: The molecular basis of GshT substrate binding reveals how Streptococcus pneumoniae acquires the antioxidant glutathione
works.abstract: Glutathione is synthesised across all kingdoms of life, but certain bacteria, including the major pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae, import host glutathione instead. Glutathione import is known to involve the substrate-binding protein GshT, but the molecular basis underlying glutathione scavenging by pneumococcal GshT remains incompletely understood. We used isothermal titration calorimetry to demonstrate that pneumococcal GshT binds glutathione with low micromolar affinity. Thermal shift assays with glutathione derivatives demonstrated that two adequately spaced carboxylates in glutathione are essential for binding. Monitoring NMR chemical shift perturbations of mutated GshT variants upon glutathione addition revealed that two conserved positively charged residues lining the ligand-binding pocket determine the ability to bind glutathione. Mutagenesis of these residues in S. pneumoniae abolished GSH uptake, impaired growth and lowered oxidant tolerance. Together, our data demonstrate that a lock-and-key charge complementarity drives the GshT-glutathione interaction. Our findings provide insights into pathogen survival mechanisms that may inform strategies to combat infectious disease.

works.title: Corrigendum to “New methods for drug synergy prediction: A mini-review” [Curr Opin Struct Biol 86 (2024) 102827]
A Small Molecule Inhibitor of the Staphylococcus aureus agr Quorum Sensing System with Low-Nanomolar Potency
works.abstract: The accessory gene regulator (agr) quorum sensing system regulates virulence in certain common Gram-positive bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus. Small molecules that block agr have been reported, but most have modest potencies and warrant further mechanistic characterization. Herein, we report a structure-function study on CP-20, a compound recently shown to inhibit agr in S. aureus by targeting the histidine kinase AgrC. We designed a robust new synthetic route to the CP-20 scaffold, generated a collection of CP-20 analogues, and evaluated their activities in cell-based agr reporter and phenotypic assays. These investigations led to the discovery of a compound, CP-20t, which inhibits agr in S. aureus with low-nanomolar potency and acts on AgrC. CP-20t represents, to our knowledge, the most potent small molecule inhibitor of agr known-bridging the almost 1000-fold potency gap between peptide- and small molecule-based inhibitors-and is a powerful tool to study quorum sensing in S. aureus.

works.title: Glycocalyx Remodeling Shapes Cancer Cell Mechanics
works.abstract: The glycocalyx - a complex meshwork of sugars, proteins, and lipids - coats all human cells and plays a crucial role in cell signaling and immune system regulation. While an understanding of its biochemical functions is emerging, its influence on cell mechanics remains comparably underexplored. Recent evidence suggests that the glycocalyx regulates membrane morphology and cell adhesion, yet its mechanical role has been difficult to study, primarily due to the absence of high-throughput analysis strategies that account for cell-to-cell variability. Here, we overcome this challenge by integrating real-time deformability cytometry (RT-DC) with genetic and chemical glycocalyx engineering to tune the glycocalyx state and assess how cell mechanics are affected. Using this approach, we uncovered mechanical adaptations that contribute to promoting cell migration and metastasis. These findings establish glycocalyx remodeling as a regulator of cancer-cell mechanics and a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

works.title: Lysine-Targeted Covalent Inhibition of eIF4E with an Anionic Electrophile Warhead
works.abstract: Covalent strategies offer a powerful route to expand the druggable proteome, yet selective lysine targeting remains difficult due to the high pKa and protonation of the amine side chain. The translation initiation factor eIF4E, an mRNA cap-binding protein that controls nuclear export and translation of oncogenic transcripts, has long been considered an undruggable RNA-binding protein. We apply an anionic electrophile strategy that converts a carboxylic acid within a reversible eIF4E ligand into a vinyl acylsulfonamide warhead, preserving salt-bridge and hydrogen bonding interactions in the cap-binding pocket and facilitating Lys162 deprotonation to enable site-specific engagement. This single-step transformation yields JL-03, a potent covalent eIF4E inhibitor with excellent stability toward biological nucleophiles, consistent with context-dependent activation of the warhead in the binding site. In cells, JL-03 achieves robust target engagement and suppresses translation of the oncogenic driver cyclin D. JL-03 reduces the viability of HOXA9-high acute myeloid leukemia cells with greater potency than reversible eIF4E inhibitors and synergizes with the menin inhibitor revumenib, demonstrating that coordinated transcriptional and translational blockade exhausts leukemic dependencies. These findings establish eIF4E as a tractable covalent target and highlight anionic electrophile installation as a generalizable strategy for lysine-directed covalent inhibitor design.

works.title: Issue Editorial Masthead
Issue Publication Information
Beyond P ‐values and means: Statistical appreciation in the life sciences
works.abstract: Statistical literacy is frequently treated in undergraduate and graduate life science training as a technical competency peripheral to experimental practice rather than as a central component of scientific reasoning. This separation is especially problematic in life sciences and related disciplines, where biological variability is intrinsic to living systems and often gives rise to heterogeneous, skewed, multiplicative and non-normal data. Consequently, the interpretation of biological measurements depends not only on the data themselves but also on how variability, distributions, measurement scale, uncertainty and inference are understood. This perspective argues that stronger statistical appreciation is urgently needed in the life sciences, particularly during early scientific training. Emphasis is placed on the biological origins of variability, the interpretation of distributions, the importance of multiplicative thinking and lognormality, the appropriate use of means, medians, geometric means and logarithmic transformations, and the distinction between variability, uncertainty and effect size. The article further discusses replication, outliers, the limitations of significance testing and why statistical thinking should be embedded within bioscience education as an integral part of scientific reasoning rather than taught as an isolated analytical skill.

works.title: Artificial intelligence for predicting mutation effects on enzyme kinetics
A selective TNKS2 inhibitor for tumor-restricted WNT suppression
works.abstract: Hyperactive WNT signaling is a potent cancer driver but clinical translation of WNT inhibitors has been hampered by on-target toxicities. WNT signaling can be constrained through inhibition of the PARP-family enzymes tankyrase 1 (TNKS1) and TNKS2; however, existing TNKS inhibitors suppress WNT signaling in both tumor and healthy tissues. In this Article, we show that genomic loss of TNKS1 on chromosome 8p creates a collateral vulnerability that drives a tumor-restricted dependency on TNKS2 for cellular TNKS activity. Through structure-guided design, we identify a flexible loop in TNKS2 that can be exploited to enable TNKS2-selective drug targeting and we generate a first-in-class TNKS2 inhibitor to drive selective WNT inhibition in TNKS1-deficient cell and organoid models. This work demonstrates a targetable cancer-specific vulnerability in multiple cancer types, providing a new approach for WNT-targeted therapies. Through structure-guided rational drug design, a potent and selective tankyrase 2 inhibitor was developed that enables tumor-restricted suppression of oncogenic WNT signaling in cancer cells that have lost one or both copies of chromosome 8p.

works.title: Biosynthetic tailoring of polyene antifungals
Tackling the Tankyrase twins
The transport of protein aggregates to the vacuole suggests a role for lipid droplets in waste disposal in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
works.abstract: Lipid droplets (LDs) are organelles found in all eukaryotic cells, yet their contribution toward proteostasis is still poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that LDs in the model organism Saccharomyces cerevisiae function as transporters to which cytosolic protein aggregates attach for transport to the vacuole for degradation. With the help of chaperones and the yeast prion Rnq1, serving as an aggregation model, and using techniques such as live-cell imaging, super-resolution microscopy, electron microscopy, and biochemical analyses, we demonstrate that protein aggregates bind to LDs, are transported through the cytoplasm, and are ultimately transferred to the insoluble protein deposit (IPOD) on the vacuole surface. The efficiency of this process is highly dependent on the lipid composition of the LDs, with triacylglycerols identified as key determinants for aggregate docking. In LD-deficient cells, we observed severe fragmentation of the aggregates and a complete loss of IPOD, whereas stimulation of LD formation significantly increased the size of IPOD and vacuolar import activity. Overall, our results expand the understanding of cellular protein quality control and link lipid metabolism research to the regulation of protein aggregation. The evidence that LDs act as 'garbage trucks' transporting protein aggregates to the vacuole reveals a new interface between proteostasis and lipid metabolism that could also be significant in higher eukaryotes.

works.title: Structural studies of the spliceosome: emerging insights into diversity and regulatory mechanisms
works.abstract: The spliceosome is a complex macromolecular machine that catalyses the essential cellular process of precursor mRNA (pre-mRNA) splicing. In the past decade, high-resolution structures for numerous stable spliceosome assembly intermediates became available, providing a structural framework for the basic splicing mechanism. However, the field still lags behind in mechanistic understanding of the precise trajectories of individual splicing factors, the regulation and organisation of splicing within the cellular context, and the mechanisms underlying splicing quality control and its links to human disease. In this review, we highlight how recent structural studies have bridged some of these knowledge gaps and brought forward our mechanistic understanding of pre-mRNA splicing. We discuss recent insights into the exon-definition problem, the role of assembly factors in small ribonucleoprotein particle (snRNP) biogenesis, spliceosome-associated quality control and the U12-dependent splicing pathway. We also provide our perspective on the future development of the field.

works.title: GPCR-MAPS: high-resolution functional and allosteric mapping of G-protein-coupled receptor activation functions and bias
works.abstract: Abstract G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are important drug targets. Approaches targeting allosteric modulation and biased signaling, as opposed to the orthosteric pocket, can improve safety profiles of therapeutics. However, rational design of precision therapies is limited by the lack of high-resolution quantitative functional annotation of GPCR structures. Here we present GPCR-MAPS—a fast and general approach to build complete, high-resolution, multimodal functional and allosteric maps of GPCRs. GCPR-MAPS quantifies direct recruitment of proteins and deconvolves the substantial effects of amino acid substitutions on receptor expression. We applied GPCR-MAPS to the β 2 adrenergic receptor to generate >7,500 dose–response curves and reveal a modular receptor architecture, with a core activation network surrounded by residues controlling quantitative parameters and bias. We used this information to identify multiple allosteric surface pockets. The application of this approach across the superfamily of GPCRs could unlock deep understanding of these receptors and enable rational design of precision GPCR therapeutics.

works.title: TF-MAPS: fast high-resolution functional and allosteric mapping of DNA-binding proteins
works.abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) bind specific DNA sequences to control gene expression. Modulating TF activity is of considerable therapeutic interest but very few TFs have been drugged successfully. TF DNA-binding interfaces are large and most TFs have no known allosteric ligands or allosteric sites. Here we introduce TF-MAPs, a scalable and general platform to chart complete functional maps of sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins. We apply TF-MAPS to three human disease TFs: HNF1A, FOXG1 and FOXP1. Allostery in all three proteins is distance-dependent, anisotropic and couples the DNA-binding interface to the protein surface. The allosteric surfaces of FOXG1 and FOXP1 are quite diverged, revealing a potential for protein-specific regulation in protein families. All three TFs have potentially druggable small pockets where mutations affect DNA binding, either within the binding interface or distant from it. Application of TF-MAPS will potentially lead to charting functional and allosteric maps for hundreds of human TFs and other DNA-binding proteins to understand DNA recognition and TF regulation, to interpret clinical variants mechanistically and to guide the development of TF-modulating therapeutics.

works.title: Impressions in biomolecular condensates
Distinct proteomic and acylproteomic adaptations to succinate dehydrogenase loss in two cell contexts
works.abstract: The tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and electron transport chain (ETC) are key metabolic pathways required for cellular ATP production. Though loss of these components impairs cell survival, such defects can paradoxically promote tumorigenesis. One example is loss of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), which functions in both the TCA cycle and as Complex II of the ETC. Mutations in SDH subunits can cause pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), rare hereditary neuroendocrine tumors of chromaffin cells in the adrenal gland and the nerve ganglia. Why tumor formation upon SDH loss is limited to certain tissues remains unclear. We hypothesized that the metabolic and proteomic perturbations resulting from SDH loss are cell-type specific, favoring survival of chromaffin cells. We comprehensively examined the proteomic, acetylproteomic, and succinylproteomic effects of SDH loss in two cell models, immortalized mouse chromaffin cells (imCCs) and immortalized mouse embryonic fibroblasts (iMEFs). Perturbations in metabolite levels were determined by mass spectrometry. Effects of SDH loss on fatty acid β-oxidation (FAO) were assessed by stable isotope tracing and pharmacologic inhibition. SDH-loss imCCs show significant upregulation of mitochondrial proteins, including TCA cycle and FAO enzymes, with pronounced downregulation of nuclear proteins. Both imCCs and iMEFs demonstrate significant energy deficiency upon SDH loss, but FAO activity is uniquely increased in SDH-loss imCCs. While SDH loss increases both lysine-reactive acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA, SDH-loss imCCs and iMEFs show disproportionate hyperacetylation but mixed succinylation. Surprisingly, SDH-loss imCCs, but not iMEFs, display disproportionate hypoacetylation and hyposuccinylation of mitochondrial proteins.

works.title: HDAC inhibition drives NOX5-dependent oxidative stress and sensitizes uveal melanoma cells to SOD1 inhibition
works.abstract: Epigenetic dysregulation and reactive oxygen species (ROS) contribute to melanoma progression and therapeutic resistance, but their interplay in uveal melanoma (UM) remains incompletely understood. Analysis of TCGA data identified UM as expressing the highest levels of NADPH oxidase 5 (NOX5), a superoxide-producing enzyme, among human cancers. HDACi treatment significantly increased NOX5 expression in UM cell lines, accompanied by elevated extracellular ROS, which was abrogated by NOX5 silencing. Inhibition of transcription and translation with actinomycin D and cycloheximide reduced HDACi-induced NOX5 expression, indicating regulation at multiple levels. HDACi treatment also increased acetylation of histones H3 and H4. Consistent with a role for acetylation-dependent transcription, BRD4 knockdown or pharmacological inhibition attenuated NOX5 induction. Similarly, dual silencing of Sp1 and Sp3 reduced both basal and HDACi-induced NOX5 expression. Chromatin immunoprecipitation assays revealed increased recruitment of acetylated histone H3, BRD4, Sp1, Sp3, and phosphorylated RNA polymerase II (Ser2) to the NOX5 promoter following Tacedinaline (HDACi) treatment, supporting acetylation-associated transcriptional activation. Notably, both NOX5 silencing, which reduces ROS production, and HDACi-mediated NOX5 upregulation, which increases ROS, suppressed UM cell growth. However, the lack of a well-established selective NOX5 inhibitor presents a challenge for therapeutically exploiting NOX5 suppression. Conversely, combining Tacedinaline with the superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) inhibitor LCS1 significantly enhanced growth inhibition compared with either agent alone. These findings identify ROS modulation in either direction as a potential UM therapeutic strategy, while highlighting pharmacological ROS elevation through HDAC inhibition and disruption of antioxidant defenses as a potentially more practical approach to exploiting NOX5-driven oxidative vulnerability.

works.title: Differential chromatin enrichment of histone H3K27me3 underlies variable cell responses to estrogen and endocrine treatment
works.abstract: Gene expression heterogeneity generates subpopulations of tumor cells capable of evading therapeutic pressure, as observed in both primary Estrogen Receptor alpha–positive (ERα + ) breast tumors and cell lines. A major source of this variability is the stochastic, burst-like nature of transcription, in which active periods are separated by intervals of inactivity. The estrogen-responsive gene TFF1, expressed in most ERα + tumors, exemplifies such heterogeneity, with transcriptional silencing that can persist several days. Here, we identify chromatin features that distinguish heterogeneous TFF1 activity by examining cells sorted based on TFF1 activity levels. TFF1-inactive (TFF1ˡᵒʷ) cells exhibit a repressive chromatin environment marked by H3K27me3 at both the promoter and enhancer. Although overall ERα binding patterns remain similar, ERα occupancy is selectively reduced at TFF1 regulatory elements in these cells, with fewer active alleles and a markedly lower transcriptional bursting frequency. In contrast, TFF1ʰ ig ʰ cells show increased allele activation, enhanced bursting, and preserved sensitivity to endocrine therapy, whereas TFF1ˡᵒʷ cells display diminished drug responsiveness. Genome-wide analyses reveal that differential H3K27me3 enrichment correlates with variable expression of estrogen-responsive genes, extending this relationship between chromatin state and expression variability. Together, these findings link repressive chromatin dynamics to transcriptional heterogeneity and endocrine resistance in ERα + breast cancer.

works.title: Exogenous antimicrobial straight-chain unsaturated fatty acids promote low-temperature growth of Staphylococcus aureus
works.abstract: The incorporation of oleic acid, a physiologically relevant and relatively non-toxic fatty acid, into membrane phospholipids and glycolipids has major impacts on the membrane biophysical properties of Staphylococcus aureus, including the promotion of low-temperature growth. Inclusion of oleic acid in growth media decreased the minimum growth temperature of S. aureus. It has not been studied yet whether other physiologically relevant, yet more antimicrobial straight-chain unsaturated fatty acids (SCUFAs), elicit similar responses. Here, we report that exogenous addition of these antimicrobial SCUFAs at 12°C led to their incorporation into the membrane lipids in only relatively small amounts, which, however, was sufficient to strongly promote growth at low temperatures. Intriguingly, these SCUFAs showed a preferential incorporation into diglucosyldiacylglyceride (DGDG) over phosphatidyl glycerol, and increased DGDG levels ∼ 4-fold in SCUFA-grown S. aureus. Two glycolipid-deficient mutants lost the growth-enhancing effects of SCUFAs at low temperatures and showed increased susceptibility to SCUFAs at 37°C, suggesting that glycolipids are important membrane components and are required for low-temperature adaptation. The presence of SCUFAs at low temperatures also enhanced the production of the carotenoid staphyloxanthin. Overall, our results suggest that multiple strategies are at play in the membrane lipid remodeling of S. aureus to adapt to the stress of low-temperature growth and likely to other environmental stresses. Incorporation of antimicrobial SCUFAs into membrane lipids may facilitate the insertion of free forms of these SCUFAs into the membrane and be a part of their mode of action.

works.title: Ubiquitin ligase CHFR impairs Tie2 signaling via K48-linked ubiquitylation and degradation of Akt1 in endothelial cells
works.abstract: Vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin is essential for maintaining endothelial junctional barrier integrity. The Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1)/Tie2 axis induced Akt1 activation is crucial for maintaining endothelial junctional barrier by inhibiting FoxO1 and suppressing expression of Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2), a Tie2 antagonist. Systemic inflammatory conditions such as sepsis, Akt1 expression is reduced, whereas FoxO1-dependent Ang-2 expression is increased, resulting in endothelial barrier dysfunction. We previously showed that the TLR4/FoxO1 axis induces the ubiquitin E3 ligase CHFR, which promotes endothelial barrier disruption by targeting VE-cadherin for ubiquitylation and degradation. However, little is known about Akt1 expression during vascular inflammation. Here, we identified FoxO1-dependent CHFR expression as a key mechanism driving K 48 -linked polyubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation of Akt1 in endothelial cells (EC). LPS-induced K 48 -linked ubiquitylation of Akt1 was prevented in CHFR-depleted human EC and in endothelial-specific Chfr knockout ( Chfr ΔEC ) mice. Accordingly, CHFR depletion increased Akt1 and VE-cadherin expression in both human lung EC and Chfr ΔEC mice. Chfr ΔEC mouse lungs also exhibited elevated Ang-1 and Tie2 expression, and Ang-1 stimulation induced sustained Akt1 phosphorylation in CHFR-deficient EC. Moreover, CHFR depletion prevented LPS-induced expression of FoxO1 and Ang-2 in EC. Mechanistically, CHFR interacted with phosphorylated Akt1 and mediated its ubiquitylation at lysine residues K30, K39, K154, and K268. Expression of a ubiquitylation-deficient Akt1 mutant prevented LPS-induced VE-cadherin degradation and vascular injury. Collectively, these findings identify CHFR as a critical regulator of endothelial inflammatory responses by controlling Akt1 stability and VE-cadherin expression during inflammation.

works.title: Copper transport to mitochondria by SLC25A3 contributes to skeletal myoblast differentiation and is required for survival of differentiated myotubes
works.abstract: Differentiation of skeletal muscle is associated with increased mitochondrial biogenesis and reliance of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). The terminal enzyme complex in the electron transport chain, cytochrome c oxidase (COX), requires copper for its assembly and activity, and copper delivery to mitochondria is essential for OXPHOS. However, when mitochondrial copper becomes essential during skeletal myoblast differentiation is not known. Here, we show that genetic deficiency of the mitochondrial copper and phosphate carrier SLC25A3 induced prior to myoblast differentiation leads to the formation of smaller myotubes, but SLC25A3 deficiency induced in mature myotubes leads to cell death and detachment. Both phenotypes are recapitulated upon genetic knockdown of COX17, a critical assembly protein for both COX copper cofactors, or by chemical inhibition of COX. Importantly, myotube death caused by SLC25A3 deficiency is rescued by copper supplementation or expression of an SLC25A3 variant that transports copper but not phosphate. Taken together these data support a model wherein copper transport by SLC25A3 and copper delivery to COX is critical for survival in mature myotubes.

works.title: Intermolecular disulfide bond formation promotes Hsp42 higher-order assembly and shapes client selection in yeast
works.abstract: Cellular redox homeostasis plays a critical role in regulating protein function, including chaperone activity, through reversible oxidation of cysteine and methionine residues. Previously, we found that budding yeast cells experiencing redox imbalance due to inactivated thioredoxin reductase (trr1Δ) activate the heat shock response and induce hyperaccumulation of the small heat shock protein/sequestrase Hsp42 with misfolded proteins. Building on that finding, this study identified cysteine 127 (C127) within Hsp42 as a redox-active residue that becomes oxidized in trr1Δ cells, upon treatment with the powerful oxidant hydrogen peroxide, or by exposure to the cysteine crosslinker divinyl sulfone (DVSF). In trr1Δ cells, C127 oxidation promoted intermolecular disulfide bond formation and contributed to Hsp42 homo-oligomerization. We show that stable oligomerization requires both the prion-like domain (PrLD) and C127 oxidation. While Hsp42-GFP formed prominent persistent foci in trr1Δ cells, replacement of C127 with non-thiol reactive serine decreased foci formation. Furthermore, the C127S mutation diminished Hsp42 oligomerization and sedimentability. Immunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry analysis revealed that Hsp42 in trr1Δ cells preferentially associated with mitochondrial precursor proteins accumulated in the cytoplasm, as well as oxidation-reduction enzymes. The observed client selectivity was altered by the C127S mutation that diversified the spectrum of Hsp42-associated proteins. Collectively, these findings identify Cys127 as a redox-active switch that regulates Hsp42 assembly, foci formation, stability, and client specificity in response to oxidative stress.

works.title: Pyk2 scaffolding relieves Src autoinhibition to coordinate reciprocal kinase activation
works.abstract: Pyk2 and Src are non-receptor tyrosine kinases that assemble into a complex to promote mutual activation. The Pyk2 FERM domain mediates autoinhibition by direct interaction with the kinase. Src autoinhibition is maintained by intramolecular interactions of the SH3 and SH2 domains with internal ligands, including an inhibitory C-terminal phosphotyrosine. FERM disengagement permits Pyk2 autophosphorylation of the FERM-kinase linker to generate a scaffolding site for Src recruitment. Although Src-mediated phosphorylation of the Pyk2 activation loop is well-established, the mechanism by which complex formation activates Src remains unclear. We reconstituted defined phosphorylation and regulatory states of both kinases, combining site-directed mutagenesis with phosphosite-resolved activity profiling to dissect the reciprocal regulation. Src phosphorylates both Pyk2 activation-loop tyrosines by a random, distributive mechanism with negative cooperativity between the sites. Although activated Pyk2 productively phosphorylates the Src activation loop, Pyk2-Src complex formation does not significantly increase activation loop phosphorylation above the rate of Src autophosphorylation alone. Conversely, autoinhibited Src strictly requires Pyk2 scaffolding engagement to productively phosphorylate Pyk2. Pyk2 therefore relieves Src autoinhibition by presenting competing scaffolding sites to disengage intramolecular SH3 and SH2 conformational constraints. The results distinguish activation loop phosphorylation from the conformational competence required for substrate phosphorylation. We propose that autophosphorylated Pyk2 functions principally as a conformational activator and scaffolding platform, opening Src for phosphatase-mediated removal of the inhibitory C-terminal phosphosite and committing both Pyk2 and Src to downstream substrate phosphorylation.

works.title: Sti1 requires its Hsp70-interacting regions to deposit misfolded proteins at the nucleus-vacuole junction
works.abstract: Protein homeostasis, or proteostasis, ensures a properly folded and functional proteome and is essential for cell survival. Proteins often misfold during stress or because of mutations that alter their structure. Proteostasis assembles misfolded proteins into membrane-less protein quality control (PQC) compartments. Many proteins, including chaperones and sequestrases, have been identified as "sorting factors" that target misfolded proteins to different PQC compartments. What makes something a sorting factor for a particular PQC compartment remains unclear. In this study, we used three different model misfolded proteins to help understand how different types of misfolded proteins get to PQC compartments in yeast. We found that the TPR domains of Sti1 are critical for sending soluble misfolded proteins to different cytoplasmic compartments. We show that Sti1 requires interaction with Hsp70 to send soluble misfolded proteins to the nucleus-vacuole junction or for clearance. However, when the misfolded protein is amyloid, Sti1 requires Hsp70 and Hsp90 to either trigger a more robust proteostasis response or to directly target the amyloid protein to a peripheral compartment. This indicates that Sti1 may act as a proteostatic switch not just for protein folding/refolding, but also for misfolded protein sequestration.

works.title: Identification of substrates for the skeletal muscle-specific lysine methyltransferases METTL21C and METTL21E
works.abstract: Protein lysine methylation, catalyzed by S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet)-dependent methyltransferases (MTases), plays important roles in regulating and fine-tuning protein function. The related mammalian lysine-specific MTases METTL21C and METTL21E are predominantly expressed in skeletal muscle, but their substrates have remained unclear and controversial. Here, we found that METTL21C methylated only a single protein, namely fast myosin-binding protein C (fMyBPC; gene: MYBPC2), in METTL21C-deficient mouse skeletal muscle extracts. METTL21C also showed strong activity on recombinant fMyBPC in vitro, introducing trimethylation at Lys-242. This methylation event was also observed in vivo, and abolished by Mettl21c knockout (KO). The observed in vitro activity of METTL21C on fMyBPC was >100-fold stronger than that observed on AARS1 (alanine-tRNA ligase), a previously reported METTL21C substrate. Interestingly, the two other MyBPC paralogs, which are expressed in cardiac and slow skeletal muscle, were not methylated by METTL21C. For METTL21E, we could not detect in vitro activity. However, we found that monomethylation of Lys-35 (K35) in myosin heavy chain (MYH), a methylation event previously reported in various vertebrate muscles, was abolished by Mettl21e KO in mouse muscle, but not by Mettl21c KO. In human muscles, we detected MYH-K35 methylation at a level similar to that observed in mice, suggesting that the current annotation of human METTL21E as a pseudogene (METTL21EP) may be re-evaluated. Taken together, our results provide new insights into protein methylation in skeletal muscle by identifying fMyBPC as a bona fide muscle-specific substrate of METTL21C, and demonstrating that METTL21E is required for MYH-K35 methylation, thus likely representing the responsible MTase.

works.title: Ribonucleotide Reductase Dysregulation in Cancer – Oncogenic Hijacking and Novel Therapies: Teaching an Old Dog New Tricks
works.abstract: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) is the rate-limiting enzyme in deoxyribonucleotide synthesis and is therefore essential for DNA replication, repair, and cell-cycle progression. Because cancer cells rely heavily on nucleotide production to sustain proliferation and genome maintenance, RNR has long been an important therapeutic target. However, while several RNR inhibitors are clinically approved, their utility can be impacted by dose-limiting toxicities, poor pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties, and diverse mechanisms of therapeutic resistance. In this review, we examine emerging mechanisms that regulate RNR in cancer beyond canonical cell-cycle and DNA-damage pathways that could serve as additional targets for blocking RNR. We discuss subunit-specific transcriptional and epigenetic programs, post-translational modifications, protein-protein interactions, and signaling crosstalk that control RRM1, RRM2, and RRM2B expression and activity. We further highlight non-canonical functions of RNR subunits in PI3K/AKT, MAPK/ERK, immune, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), antioxidant, and ferroptosis pathways, emphasizing how these activities may contribute to tumor progression and drug resistance. We summarize mechanisms underlying resistance to conventional RNR inhibitors, including altered drug transport and metabolism, RNR overexpression, and acquisition of stem-like and EMT phenotypes with an emphasis on approaches to overcome these limitations. Lastly, we provide an in-depth summary of preclinical RNR inhibitors, highlighting how they compare to FDA-approved RNR inhibitors and their progression in clinical trials. Collectively, these advances underscore the role of RNR in tumorigenesis and identify opportunities to develop more selective and effective RNR-targeted therapies.

works.title: C-Terminal Dimerization Enables Assembly of Ebola Virus VP30 Oligomers with transcriptional support activity
works.abstract: Ebola virus VP30 is a multifunctional phosphoprotein essential for initiating viral transcription. VP30 functions as a homo-oligomer, where oligomerization is critical for its transcriptional-support activity. While a tetra-leucine motif in the N-terminal region (amino acids (aa) 100–105) mediates oligomerization, the structural determinants and functional relevance of a VP30 dimerization motif in the C-terminus remained poorly defined. Using a novel high-resolution (1.43 Å) crystal structure and biochemical approaches, we identified residues 142 ITLL 145 in the VP30 C-terminal domain (CTD) as key contributors to VP30 dimerization. Alanine conversions of these residues (VP30-CTD 142–145A ) disrupted CTD dimerization, as demonstrated by native mass spectrometry, size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, and split-GFP complementation assays. Notably, VP30-CTD functions as a dominant-negative inhibitor of full-length VP30 in a minigenome assay, whereas the dimerization-deficient mutant VP30-CTD 142–145A does not. Critically, introduction of these mutations into full-length VP30 completely abolished viral transcription in minigenome assays. Recombinant EBOV carrying the VP30 dimerization mutations could not be rescued in cell culture, demonstrating that VP30-CTD dimerization is essential for viral replication. Together, these findings establish that CTD-mediated dimerization is essential for VP30's transcriptional support activity and virus propagation, identifying VP30 dimerization as a previously uncharacterized determinant of the viral replication cycle. Importantly, the dimerization interface is conserved among filoviruses, suggesting it represents a broadly conserved and potentially targetable vulnerability for antiviral intervention.

works.title: Functional differences of two homologous enzymes for LacdiNAc biosynthesis: B4GALNT3 and B4GALNT4
works.abstract: Proteins in mammals are modified with a wide variety of glycans, conferring extensive functional diversity. LacdiNAc (LDN), a unique disaccharide (GalNAcβ1-4GlcNAc) present in N- and O-GalNAc glycans, regulates glycoprotein stability in circulation and suppresses terminal modifications of N-glycans. Although two highly homologous isozymes, B4GALNT3 and B4GALNT4, are known to synthesize LDN, their functional differences remain unclear. Here, we compared their detailed substrate specificity toward N-glycan and glycoproteins, subcellular localization, secretion, and recently discovered lectin functions in their unique PA14 domain. Our enzyme assays and lectin-assisted proteomics revealed that these two enzymes possess different N-glycan branch specificity and substrate protein selectivity. Moreover, B4GALNT4 displayed partial localization in the endoplasmic reticulum and less secretion, compared with predominant Golgi residency and a higher secretion rate of B4GALNT3. In addition, we found that the PA14 domain of B4GALNT4 is also a lectin domain, which selectively binds to sulfated glycans, akin to the B4GALNT3 lectin domain. The addition of a series of sulfated glycan ligands suppressed the activity of both B4GALNT3 and B4GALNT4 in vitro, albeit with slightly different inhibition profiles. In addition, the intracellular activity of B4GALNT4 was less enhanced by blocking sulfation than that of B4GALNT3, suggesting that these two enzymes are negatively regulated by sulfated glycans in distinct ways. Collectively, our findings indicate that the two isoenzymes for LDN synthesis, B4GALNT3 and B4GALNT4, share some functions and behaviors but differ in others, providing insights into the mechanism by which LDN biosynthesis is regulated.

works.title: BMP2 and BMP6 prodomains are essential to generate heterodimers in liver endothelial cells and associate with ligands after cleavage and secretion
works.abstract: Liver endothelial cell (LEC)-derived bone morphogenetic proteins (BMP)2 and BMP6 coordinately regulate hepatocyte hepcidin production to control systemic iron homeostasis, but the mechanisms are uncertain. BMPs are homodimeric or heterodimeric proteins that are generated as precursors comprised of a non-signaling prodomain and an active ligand released by proteolytic cleavage. Although prodomains do not signal, they play pleiotropic roles in ligand generation and activity. Here, we used LEC- and hepatocyte-derived cell cultures to explore how BMP2 and BMP6 prodomains and proteolytic cleavage impact homodimer formation, heterodimer formation, and hepcidin regulation. We show that when co-expressed in LECs, BMP2 and BMP6 form heterodimers, which more potently induce hepcidin versus homodimers. Proteolytic cleavage of BMP2 precursors at two furin consensus sites is required to generate fully active BMP2/6 heterodimers, although cleavage at either site generates partially active heterodimers. Uncleavable BMP6 precursors fail to generate fully active BMP2/6 heterodimers and dominant negatively inhibit BMP2 homodimer formation. We also show that in LECs, cognate BMP2 and BMP6 prodomains are essential for homodimer and heterodimer formation. Finally, both prodomains remain noncovalently associated with BMP2/6 heterodimers after cleavage and secretion. BMP6 prodomains also remain associated with BMP6 homodimers, whereas the association of BMP2 prodomains with BMP2 homodimers is influenced by the presence of the linker region between the cleavage sites. Our findings suggest that BMP2/6 heterodimers are likely the primary endogenous ligand that regulates hepcidin and iron homeostasis, and both BMP2 and BMP6 prodomains are critical to functional BMP2/6 formation in LECs.

works.title: IL-6 Trans-Signaling Promotes Posterior Capsule Repopulation by Lens Epithelial Cells Through JAK-STAT3 Signaling
works.abstract: Posterior capsule opacification (PCO) is the most common long-term complication following cataract surgery and results from the persistence, survival, and migration of residual lens epithelial cells (LECs). Although inflammatory cytokines remain elevated in the aqueous humor years after surgery, their functional role in PCO remains unclear. Here, we investigated the contribution of interleukin-6 (IL-6) trans-signaling to LEC behavior. Human aqueous humor samples demonstrated significantly elevated soluble IL-6 receptor (sIL-6R) levels 3-12 years after cataract surgery, suggesting sustained activation of IL-6 trans-signaling in the post-surgical ocular environment. In cultured human LECs, IL-6 alone failed to activate signaling, whereas IL-6 trans-signaling induced robust STAT3 and p38 MAPK phosphorylation. Functionally, IL-6 trans-signaling enhanced LEC survival and significantly promoted cell migration. Mechanistically, IL-6 trans-signaling induced the migration-associated proteins ICAM-1 and MCP-1. Pharmacological inhibition of JAK1/2 with ruxolitinib or STAT3 with Stattic completely abolished ICAM-1 and MCP-1 induction, whereas inhibition of p38 MAPK or NF-κB had no effect, establishing JAK-STAT3 as the primary signaling pathway. In contrast, IL-6 trans-signaling neither induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition nor altered TGF-β2-mediated fibrotic responses. In an ex vivo porcine cataract surgery model, Hyper-IL-6 markedly accelerated posterior capsule repopulation, whereas the selective IL-6 trans-signaling inhibitor sgp130 effectively suppressed this response. Collectively, these findings identify IL-6 trans-signaling as a previously unrecognized regulator of LEC survival and migration and suggest that selective inhibition of IL-6 trans-signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for preventing PCO following cataract surgery.

works.title: Mouse macrophages lacking both Pak1 and Pak2 exhibit preserved chemotaxis despite a strikingly altered migration mode
works.abstract: Macrophages migrate directionally along chemoattractant gradients through repeated cycles of membrane protrusion and trailing-end retraction. Chemoattractant receptor signaling activates the Rho GTPases Rac1, Rac2, and Cdc42 at the leading edge, which stimulate actin polymerization via actin-nucleating factors, such as the Arp2/3 complex. Simultaneously, these Rho GTPases stabilize membrane protrusions by activating p21-activated kinases (PAKs), which inhibit the actin-depolymerizing ADF/cofilin family through activation of LIM motif-containing kinases. Here, we used myeloid-restricted Pak2 conditional knockout (cKO), Pak1 / Pak2 double knockout (dKO), and Pak1 knockout ( Pak1 –/– ) mouse models to determine whether PAKs are required for chemotactic navigation. In real-time chemotaxis assays, macrophages lacking Pak1 are indistinguishable from control cells, whereas Pak2 cKO macrophages frequently adopt a dendritic morphology and exhibit modestly impaired chemotaxis and cell velocity. In contrast, macrophages lacking both Pak1 and Pak2 exhibit robust chemotaxis and markedly increased cell velocity. Strikingly, Pak1 / Pak2 dKO cells adopt a distinct, chemoattractant-induced rounded morphology, characterized by extensive membrane ruffling at the leading edge, which is rich in transverse actin fibers, and a compact trailing end, although these cells intermittently transition to slower, partially spread out or elongated morphologies. Phospho-cofilin (Ser3) levels are reduced in complement C5a-induced polarized dKO cells compared with control cells, whereas total cofilin levels are unchanged. In summary, whereas loss of Pak2 alone modestly impairs chemotaxis, combined deletion of Pak1 and Pak2 preserves directional navigation while enhancing cell motility, likely through reduced inhibition of ADF/cofilin and increased actin turnover at the leading edge.

works.title: A Novel Drp1-Golph2 Tether Mediates Mitochondria-Golgi Spatial Association to Orchestrate Mitochondrial Function and Hepatic Lipid Catabolism Across Vertebrates
works.abstract: Mitochondria-organelle contact sites are fundamental to cellular homeostasis; however, the molecular mechanisms and physiological significance of mitochondria-Golgi spatial communication remain elusive. To address this, we employed a cross-species approach using hepatocyte models from humans, mice, chickens, and frogs, combined with in vivo and in vitro studies in grass carp fed diets with varying lipid and chlorogenic acid (CGA). This strategy enabled us to systematically delineate the molecular machinery governing mitochondria-Golgi coupling and its role in hepatic lipid metabolism. The key findings were: (1) A candidate cross-species functional module: We identify a novel spatial association between mitochondria and the Golgi apparatus, formed by a direct protein-protein interaction between dynamin-1-like protein (Drp1) (via Leu639) and golgi membrane protein 1 (Golph2). Although Drp1 Leu639 is highly conserved across vertebrates, the corresponding Golph2 interacting site exhibits substantial sequence divergence among species, and this module exhibits functional conservation rather than sequence conservation. (2) A mechanistic link between structure and metabolism: This Drp1/Golph2-mediated mitochondria-Golgi spatial association serves as a critical regulatory node, where its disruption impairs Drp1 phosphorylation and mitochondrial fission, leading to enhanced mitochondrial β-oxidation and altered hepatic lipid metabolism. (3) A nutri-physiological regulatory axis: The nutritional compound CGA alleviates hepatic steatosis by transcriptionally downregulating Drp1 via a peroxisome proliferator activated receptor gamma (pparγ)-binding promoter element, thereby normalizing excessive mitochondria-Golgi juxtaposition. Significantly, this study reveals that Drp1/Golph2-mediated mitochondria-Golgi spatial association represents a regulatory axis with functionally conserved outputs from fish to mammals, establishing this complex as both a fundamental coordinator of mitochondrial dynamics and a promising target for treating hepatic lipid disorders.

works.title: Ligand identity and oncogenic mutations alter the oligomerization behavior of EGFR: insights from concentration-dependent brightness measurements
works.abstract: Fluorescence fluctuation techniques are increasingly being used to study the dynamics of membrane receptors in live cells. Here we probe the oligomerization of EGFR, tagged with YFP, in the plasma membrane of live cells in response to three of its ligands, EGF, TGFα, and EREG. By measuring EGFR-YFP molecular brightness, we find that the EGFR oligomerization state varies, depending on the identity of the ligand and its concentration. The L834R oncogenic mutation increases the apparent oligomer order of EGFR. These findings reveal complexities in EGFR oligomerization behavior that are not anticipated based on classical views of signal transduction across the plasma membrane. We further probe for possible correlations between EGFR oligomerization status and the phosphorylation of two EGFR tyrosines, Y1068 and Y1173. We find that larger EGFR oligomers are correlated with higher Y1068 phosphorylation but are uncorrelated with the degree of Y1173 phosphorylation. This suggests that changes in EGFR oligomerization status may lead to selective modulation of some downstream signaling cascades to re-wire EGFR signaling.

works.title: Hypoxia alters the synthesis and post-translational modification of collagens in human coronary artery smooth muscle cells
works.abstract: (250 words) Considerable data support the hypothesis that hypoxia plays a central role in the development of atherosclerotic plaques and cardiovascular disease. Hypoxia may modulate the pool of proteins within cells, including vascular smooth muscle cells of the artery wall, and drive phenotypic changes. Here we report a detailed liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) study of changes induced in human coronary artery smooth muscle cells (HCASMC) on transfer from an atmosphere of 20 to 1% O 2 (hypoxia) for 1 and 7 days. Exposure to 1% O 2 resulted in marked changes in the HCASMC proteome with 755 proteins (of 5,842 total) altered in abundance after 1 day, and 2874 (1234 up, 1640 down) after 7 days of hypoxia. Significant changes in specific collagens, and collagen-modifying hydroxylases and cross-linking enzymes were detected (lysyl oxidases and related species, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases), with most of these upregulated by hypoxia. These data are consistent with significant extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling under hypoxia and increased collagen synthesis, processing, secretion and incorporation into ECM. Analysis of protein post translational modifications (hydroxylations) indicates enhanced hydroxylation of multiple collagen peptides, particularly within the helical coil regions. Immunoblotting and ELISA data support these ECM changes.
