Comparison with proteomic data obtained from advanced symptomatic human carotid artery atherosclerotic plaques and control artery samples, provides evidence for a similar pattern of changes, particularly with regard to collagen-modifying and processing enzymes, consistent with the presence of hypoxic regions within human plaques. Together, the data indicate that hypoxia plays a significant role in collagen-focused ECM remodeling.

works.title: Human adenine nucleotide translocator isoforms mediate functionally redundant mitochondrial ADP/ATP exchange
works.abstract: The adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT) is essential for cellular energy metabolism, mediating the exchange of ADP and ATP across the inner mitochondrial membrane. While mammals express multiple ANT isoforms, it remains unclear whether they possess distinct properties or whether their diverse expression patterns reflect functional specialization as widely posited. In this study, we employed a controlled human cell system to directly compare the transport kinetics and bioenergetic contributions of individual human ANT isoforms. By evaluating endogenous knockout cells and systematically re-expressing each isoform, we demonstrate that ANT1, ANT2, and ANT3 are functionally redundant. The three ANT isoforms exhibited near-identical transport rates in both forward (ADPin/ATPout) and reverse (ATPin/ADPout) exchanges. While transport kinetics were equivalent, cells solely expressing ANT2 or ANT3 exhibited slightly different resilience to respiratory inhibition, suggesting isoform-specific roles that may be related to non-transport functions. Our findings provide a refined view of ANT-mediated mitochondrial nucleotide flux and suggest that ANT isoform-specific differences, if they exist, are likely subtle and not innately tied to ADP/ATP exchange.

works.title: Structural basis of phospholipid sensing nuclear receptor LRH-1 recognition by carboxylic acid bioisosteres reveals an alternative ligand interaction site
works.abstract: Liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1; NR5A2) is a phospholipid-sensing nuclear receptor that regulates metabolic and steroidogenic pathways in the liver, intestine, and pancreas. Previously, we showed that small-molecule LRH-1 agonists with carboxylic acid "tails" mimic endogenous phospholipid contacts at the mouth of the ligand-binding pocket, enhancing receptor activation. To improve metabolic stability while preserving these key interactions, we designed a series of agonists in which the carboxylate was replaced with bioisosteric polar groups. Substituting a tetrazole for the carboxylate in a lead agonist preserved high affinity LRH-1 binding, improved potency in cellular reporter assays, and promoted stronger target gene induction. Incorporation of a sulfamide moiety to promote interactions in the deep part of the LRH-1 binding pocket yielded a dual-modified agonist (6NTet) with further gains in affinity and activity. Crystal structures, molecular dynamics simulations, and mutational analyses revealed that the 6NTet tetrazole tail dynamically samples two distinct interaction sites within the LRH-1 ligand-binding pocket. One site corresponds to a previously characterized region engaged by phospholipid ligands and synthetic carboxylate-containing agonists (site 1), whereas the second represents a previously unrecognized interaction site (site 2). Mutational analyses demonstrated that both sites contribute to agonist-induced receptor activation, while site 2 additionally influences basal LRH-1 activity. Together, these findings establish tetrazole substitution as an effective strategy for improving phospholipid-mimetic LRH-1 agonists and identify 6NTet as a promising lead compound. The discovery of a novel ligand interaction site further expands our understanding of LRH-1 activation and provides a framework for next-generation agonist design.

works.title: Structural basis for dAMP specificity of the anti-phage deaminase KomA
works.abstract: The bacterial enzyme KomA is a recently discovered adenosine deaminase (ADA) homolog whose activity initiates an anti-phage defense pathway. Here, we show that KomA preferentially deaminates dAMP over AMP, with no detectable activity toward N6-methyl-AMP or the corresponding nucleosides. KomA has a Michaelis constant ( K m) of ∼5-6 μM for dAMP, consistent with efficient substrate recognition. We determined structures of KomA in the apo form, bound to the transition-state analog pentostatin 5′-monophosphate (PMP), and bound to inosine monophosphate (IMP), a reaction product of AMP. KomA retains the conserved Zn 2+ -dependent active-site architecture of the ADA family while possessing distinct features that confer nucleotide and deoxyribose specificity. Structural comparisons reveal active-site closure upon PMP binding and partial reopening in the IMP-bound state, providing a framework for substrate recognition and product release. Substitutions of active-site residues R68 with alanine (R68A) and Y60 with valine (Y60V) reduced or abolished dAMP deamination, whereas alanine mutations of surface residues E145 and Y146 increased activity. These findings establish KomA as a specialized dAMP deaminase and provide a structural framework for understanding its catalytic cycle and substrate specificity.

works.title: A small molecule inhibitor of human ARV1 sterol-binding protein blocks lipid binding
works.abstract: ARV1 ( are2 required for viability 1) sterol-binding protein is conserved across eukaryotic species and binds cholesterol, phospholipids, and phosphoinositides. Mutations in hARV1 are linked to epileptic encephalitis. mArv1 -deficient mice show resistance to diet-induced obesity. Scarv1Δ cells have defects in glycosylphosphatidylinositol biosynthesis, sterol distribution and sphingolipid biosynthesis. ARV1 knockdown in human cells leads to endoplasmic reticulum cholesterol accumulation. How ARV1 regulates lipid movement is not understood. The development of inhibitors targeting the ability of ARV1 to bind lipid will provide valuable insights into its function. Employing a homogenous time-resolved fluorescence high throughput screening assay, we identified VB-84133 as an inhibitor of human ARV1 lipid binding with an IC 50 of 3.2 + 0.21 μM. VB-84133 blocks the interaction of the ARV1 homology domain (AHD) with cholesterol, phosphatidylserine and other phospholipids in liposome binding assays. This inhibition was specific to ARV1 interaction, since VB-84133 did not block binding of phosphatidylserine to Annexin A2 or A5. We demonstrated that ARV1 moves phosphatidylserine between inner and outer membranes using an in vitro fluorescence-based liposome quenching assay, and that movement was inhibited by VB-84133. In phenotypic studies, S. cerevisi a e ARV1 cells undergo arv1 -associated cell death in the presence of VB-84133. VB-84133 constitutively activates the unfolded protein response (UPR) and XBP1 splicing in HepG2 cells but does not synergize with loss of ARV1 gene expression in further progressing splicing. VB-84133 also inhibits NBD-cholesterol localization to lipid droplets. Overall, VB-84133 specifically targets ARV1, evidenced by its capacity to bind ARV1 and trigger loss-of-function events associated with ARV1 deficiency.

works.title: Bifunctional cytochrome P450/ferredoxin is required for fungal phytochrome assembly at mitochondria
works.abstract: Mitochondria act as dynamic signaling hubs intertwining cellular metabolism and environmental perception in fungi. Here, we elucidate the assembly of the red-light sensing phytochrome (FphA) at the mitochondrial outer membrane in Alternaria alternata. Phytochrome photoconversion strictly relies on biliverdin biosynthesis by heme oxygenases. While mammalian and plant heme oxygenases localize to the endoplasmic reticulum or chloroplasts, the fungal system uniquely repurposes the outer mitochondrial membrane. We demonstrate that the fungal heme oxygenases HoxA and HoxB form a heteromeric complex integrated into the membrane via mitochondrial import machinery components Mim1 and Mim2. At the mitochondrial surface, only HoxA binds directly to FphA. Genomic screening identified Bifunctional Cytochrome P450 Reductase/Ferredoxin A (BcfA) as the essential physiological electron donor. Quantitative kinetics established that BcfA operates as an asymmetric hub, displaying higher affinity for HoxB than HoxA. HoxB functions as a high-affinity kinetic tether locking the donor at the membrane boundary. Consequently, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of bcfA disrupts red-light signalling. Thus, a multi-protein mitochondrial complex evolved in fungi to wire light perception through spatial compartmentalization.

works.title: Becoming Messengers: cAMP, Ca2+, and the Emergence of Cellular Control
works.abstract: How do molecules become messengers? This Review follows the intertwined histories of cAMP and Ca 2+ , two variables that now anchor intracellular signaling yet reached that status through different experimental and conceptual routes. cAMP became legible within hormone biology, where trace extracellular signals demanded explanations for coordination, amplification, and specificity. Its path depended on assayable membrane systems, adenylyl cyclase, and the eventual biochemical resolution of the membrane apparatus into receptor, transducer, and amplifier. Ca 2+ followed a slower, more elusive path into the messenger vocabulary. Long recognized as essential for contraction, excitability, and fertilization, it was not recognized as a bona fide messenger until considerably later than cAMP, as experiments revealed regulated intracellular dynamics, defined release mechanisms, and identified cellular readers able to interpret Ca 2+ changes. Read together, these histories show that messenger status emerged when molecules became experimentally visible, mechanistically connected to cellular responses, and conceptually placed within a language of control.

works.title: Transfer of carotenoids to mitochondria by GRAMD1B improves resilience to photo-oxidative stress in 661W cone photoreceptor cells
works.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central drivers of photoreceptor degeneration in retinal diseases. Cone photoreceptors are particularly susceptible because of their high metabolic demands and dependence on mitochondrial energy production and metabolism. Primate cone photoreceptors uniquely accumulate carotenoids, yet the mechanism by which these pigments support photoreceptor function and maintenance has remained elusive. We recently identified GRAMD1B, a non-vesicular lipid transport protein that is highly expressed in human photoreceptors and mediates the delivery of carotenoids to mitochondria. We therefore hypothesized that mitochondrial targeting of zeaxanthin enhances the resilience of photoreceptors to oxidative stress. To test this hypothesis, we established a gain-of-function model by expressing human GRAMD1B in 661W murine cone photoreceptor cells, which lack endogenous GRAMD1B. GRAMD1B expression was associated with reduced plasma membrane and increased mitochondrial zeaxanthin and fundamentally reshaped the transcriptional response to blue light-induced stress. Mitochondrial zeaxanthin targeting preferentially activated pathways involved in oxidative phosphorylation, ferroptosis, sphingolipid metabolism, and mitochondrial stress adaptation. Functionally, GRAMD1B-mediated carotenoid transport altered mitochondrial membrane potential, enhanced adaptive redox signaling through the NRF2-HO-1 pathway, and improved cell survival following photo-oxidative stress. In contrast, parental 661W cells contained lower mitochondrial zeaxanthin and mounted primarily extra-mitochondrial stress responses. Together, these findings identify a novel function of GRAMD1B and carotenoids in mitochondrial biology with important implications for retinal health and disease.

works.title: Targeting CLDN3 Enhances PD-1 Blockade Efficacy in Gastric Cancer by Disrupting the NF-κB/p65–CXCL1–PD-L1 Immune Evasion Axis
works.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Claudin 3 (CLDN3), a tight junction protein aberrantly expressed in multiple malignancies, has been implicated in tumor progression. However, its functional significance and therapeutic relevance in GC remain incompletely defined. Therefore, we systematically evaluated the functional role and underlying mechanisms of CLDN3 in GC using clinical cohort analysis, in vitro and in vivo experiments, immune co-culture systems, and transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Using hybridoma technology, we also generated a monoclonal antibody against CLDN3 and assessed its antitumor efficacy, both as monotherapy and in combination with anti-PD-1 blockade, in vitro and in vivo . CLDN3 was upregulated in GC tissues and was associated with poor prognosis, aggressive clinicopathological features, and decreased intratumoral CD8 + T-cell infiltration. Mechanistically, CLDN3 activated the NF-κB pathway by promoting p65 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, thereby enhancing CXCL1 transcription and consequently driving GC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Furthermore, CLDN3 upregulated PD-L1 expression in a CXCL1-dependent manner, leading to decreased CD8 + T-cell infiltration and attenuated CD8 + T-cell-mediated tumor cell killing. Notably, the anti-CLDN3 monoclonal antibody demonstrated high binding affinity and specificity, significantly suppressed tumor growth and metastasis in vivo , and enhanced the antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 blockade, accompanied by increased CD8 + T-cell infiltration. Collectively, these findings indicate that CLDN3 promotes GC progression and immune evasion by activating the NF-κB/p65–CXCL1–PD-L1 signaling axis, and CLDN3 blockade combined with PD-1 inhibition may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for GC.

works.title: Modulation of G6PD-mediated Vitamin C Sensitivity in Small Cell Lung Cancer by the AKT/NRF2 axis
works.abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) remains a highly lethal malignancy with limited therapeutic advances. Although high-dose vitamin C (Vc) exhibits anti-tumor activity in various cancers, its therapeutic potential and underlying resistance mechanisms in SCLC remain poorly understood. Here, we identified heterogeneous responses to Vc among SCLC cell lines and found that Vc-resistant cells acquire enhanced antioxidant capacity to tolerate Vc-induced oxidative stress. Through transcriptomic, multi-omics, and functional analyses, we identified glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) as a critical determinant of Vc resistance. Mechanistically, Vc activates the p-AKT/p-GSK3β/NRF2 signaling axis in resistant cells, leading to NRF2-dependent transcriptional upregulation of G6PD and activation of antioxidant adaptation programs. Integrated analyses of transcriptomic, proteomic, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomic datasets further supported the involvement of the NRF2-G6PD axis in oxidative stress adaptation in SCLC. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of G6PD with RRx-001 restored Vc sensitivity and synergistically suppressed SCLC growth in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism underlying Vc resistance in SCLC and demonstrate that co-targeting G6PD provides a potential strategy to enhance the therapeutic efficacy of Vc.

works.title: KLHDC3-mediated degradation of transcriptional repressor SCAND1 is regulated by Hsp90
works.abstract: The ubiquitin-proteasome system and the stress response pathway are highly integrated in order to maintain proteostasis. C-degron E3 ligase substrate adapters recognize certain proteotoxic substrates, although their integration with the cellular stress response has not been previously investigated. Here, we evaluate the C-degron E3 ligases KLHDC3 and APPBP2 for their substrates and pathway dependencies with chemical inhibitors. KLHDC3 and APPBP2 downregulated SCAN-domain containing transcriptional regulators SCAND1 and ZSCAN18, respectively. A bioactive compound screen in reporter cell lines revealed inhibition of KLHDC3 by a panel of Hsp90 inhibitors. KLHDC3 post-translationally downregulated SCAND1 across multiple cell lines, leading to changes in cell viability in endometrial cancer cell lines. SCAND1 overexpression in MFE-296 cells repressed gene targets that drive proliferation and immune responses. This work reveals a mechanism where constitutive post-translational suppression of a transcription factor is released on Hsp90 inhibition, establishing C-degron E3 ligases and their substrates as mediators of the cellular stress response and expanding the known functions and proteostasis implications of a C-degron E3 ligase.

Multisensing photoreceptors: a cross-kingdom perspective
works.abstract: Photoreceptors are classically depicted as monochromatic switches governed strictly by light. However, emerging biophysical and structural insights reveal that these proteins act as dynamic, multisensory hubs across kingdoms of life. Drawing primarily on plant and fungal systems, where mechanisms are most extensively characterized, this review synthesizes how photoreceptors integrate ambient temperature and cellular oxidative state alongside photon flux, with cross-kingdom examples extending this framework to bacteria. Thermal energy modulates dark reversion rates, quaternary assembly, and photobody phase separation, whereas reactive oxygen species alter the photocycle and trigger structural shifts through direct redox sensing. Under a 'stress-first' evolutionary model, ancestral stress-sensing scaffolds could be retrofitted with chromophores via exaptation, providing a unified biophysical rationale for how cells decode complex, fluctuating environments.

Deciphering molecular mechanisms of synergistic growth reduction in kinase inhibitor combinations
works.abstract: Targeted kinase inhibitors often yield transient or incomplete responses because tumour cells buffer pathway blockade through signalling cross-talk, motivating synergistic drug combinations. However, it remains unclear whether synergy typically arises from engaging new signalling programs or from reinforcing the dominant effects of each monotherapy at shared downstream control points. Here we analyse two synergistic inhibitor pairs in AGS gastric adenocarcinoma cells: PI3K inhibition combined with inhibition of either MEK (MAP2K1, MAP2K2) or TAK1 (MAP3K7). Using time-resolved phosphoproteomics and transcriptomics after single-agent and combination treatment, we track signalling and transcriptional rewiring from 30 minutes to 24 h and partition combination responses into monotherapy-like versus combination-specific components. We show that global phosphorylation and gene expression changes under both combinations largely mirror those of the monotherapies, with limited evidence for uniquely engaged kinase programs. Instead, synergy concentrates at pathway convergence nodes, where combined perturbation amplifies downstream regulation of growth and survival circuitry, including transcriptional control through MYC and CREB1. Both combinations produce stronger suppression of MYC-linked proliferative programs and CREB1-associated survival signalling than either single agent, consistent with reinforced constraint on cell-fate decisions. At the transcriptional level, the combinations uniquely repress nucleotide metabolism and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, consistent with reduced mTOR activity. Together, these results indicate that synergistic growth inhibition can arise primarily from strengthened pathway convergence rather than recruitment of new signalling routes. Our approach provides insights into the molecular mechanisms affected by the PI3Ki-TAK1i and PI3Ki-MEKi combinations and can serve as a flexible framework for dissecting drug combination responses based on multi-omics measurements.

works.title: EGFR/TBK1-dependent mitochondrial quality control contributes to acquired resistance to temozolomide
works.abstract: Acquisition of secondary resistance to chemotherapy in cancer cells is an ill-characterized multi-step process. We conducted an unbiased, longitudinal proteomic analysis of U251 glioma cells treated by temozolomide as they transit from drug-sensitive to tolerant and then resistant states. This unprecedented analysis revealed key mitochondrial evolutions throughout the process. Following an early stress substantiated by a transient peak of reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial quality control mechanisms enable emergence of the resistant population. We combined genome editing, targeted protein degradation via PROTAC, and pharmacologic inhibitors to investigate the mechanisms underlying stress resolution both at population and single cell scales (including microscopic evaluation and in-situ proximity ligation assays). These studies unravel a Src-activated EGFR and TBK1 axis that initiates autophagic recycling of mitochondria as a necessary step to the emergence of the resistant population.

works.title: Region-resolved multi-layer proteomics reveals proteostasis-centered post-translational remodeling during mouse brain aging
works.abstract: Brain aging is a spatially heterogeneous and multi-layered process, yet how protein abundance and post-translational modifications (PTMs) are coordinated across brain regions and over time remains incompletely understood. Here, we present a brain-region-resolved, multi-layer proteomics atlas of mouse brain aging, integrating the proteome, phosphoproteome, acetylome, and ubiquitinome across 11 anatomical regions and five time points spanning from young adulthood to senescence. Using dia-PASEF with PTM-optimized acquisition, we quantified 11,460 proteins with 29,225 phosphorylation sites, 5345 acetylation sites, and 5197 ubiquitination sites across 628 injections, enabling systematic analysis of age-associated molecular trajectories. We find that aging patterns are highly region-specific at both the protein and PTM levels, and the pons emerges as a region with marked phosphorylation-level alterations in aging-related signaling pathways. Notably, we uncover a proteostasis-centered regulatory axis in the aging hippocampus, where reduced ubiquitination and increased acetylation converge on Tau, potentially impairing its degradation. Using a telomerase-deficient mouse model (Tert KO), we show that telomere dysfunction perturbs aging-associated molecular trajectories and induces a divergent proteostasis and stress-response state distinct from physiological brain aging. Together, our study provides a spatiotemporal multi-layer proteomics resource of brain aging and reveals a proteostasis-centered landscape of post-translational remodeling associated with region-specific vulnerability and Tau dysregulation.

works.title: Optimized Super-SILAC Normalization Enables Enhanced Profiling of Histone Post-Translational Modification Changes Associated with Microbiota and Acute Inflammation
works.abstract: The gut microbiota produces metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that modulate histone acylation and serve as precursors for non-acetyl acyl marks, representing a mechanism in host-microbiome epigenetic crosstalk. However, the reliable quantification of these low-abundance modifications in complex tissues remains challenging. Here, we established an optimized, non-acetyl histone acylation-focused super-SILAC strategy for profiling histone post-translational modifications (HPTM) in the gut epithelium. We generated a functionally optimized internal standard from heavy-labeled colon cancer cells (HCT-116 and Caco-2) treated with propionate, butyrate, and crotonate, thereby enriching the standard in non-canonical acylations. This custom super-SILAC mixture enabled robust normalization and improved the quantification of low-abundance histone acylations in biological tissues. Our in vitro characterization revealed that SCFAs induced distinct and overlapping acylation profiles, with propionate leading to the most pronounced changes, including increased H3K14pr and H4K16pr. Applying this method to mouse models, we found that antibiotic-induced microbiota depletion led to the loss of marks associated with active chromatin (H3K14pr and H4K16pr) and a concurrent increase in heterochromatin-associated marks (H3K9me2/3). In contrast, Dextran Sodium Sulfate (DSS)-induced early-stage intestinal inflammation caused H4 hyperacetylation, increased H3K14pr, and reduced H3K27ac. In conclusion, the super-SILAC method enables robust identification and quantification of low-abundance histone acylations in cells and tissues under both physiological and disease conditions.

works.title: High-Throughput Plasma Proteomic Profiling Identifies Novel Biomarker Candidates in Parkinson’s Disease with Cognitive Decline
works.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disease diagnosed based on its cardinal motor features. Many PD patients experience non-motor symptoms, including cognitive decline, which can be particularly debilitating. Fluid biomarkers in PD are lacking, but modern proteomic techniques have allowed for high-throughput studies which have generated promising results. Mass spectrometry provides an unbiased approach to biomarker discovery, and the plasma proteome reflects ongoing disease processes throughout the body, including the central nervous system. Plasma samples from 198 individuals (130 PD and 68 controls) from the Swedish Biopark cohort were TMT-tagged, pre-fractionated, and analysed using untargeted mass spectrometry. Robust peptides from candidate biomarkers were technically verified using parallel reaction monitoring (PRM). The analyses focused on PD diagnosis and cognitive decline. Results were compared with plasma Neurofilament light chain levels analysed on the SIMOA platform. Several promising candidate biomarkers were discovered for PD diagnosis, cognitive decline, and motor impairment in the discovery phase. Peptides from six of the 12 proteins quantified with PRM correlated with quantifications from the discovery phase. Following PRM verification, it was found that peptides from C9 and APOC3 had altered levels in PD compared with controls. Additionally, SAA1 was found to be associated with both cognitive and motor impairment. Neurofilament light chain levels were elevated in PD with cognitive impairment but showed a weaker correlation with cognitive function than SAA1. In conclusion, untargeted mass spectrometry is a viable method for generating novel candidate biomarkers in PD plasma, several of which were technically verified with PRM including SAA1, C9, and APOC3.

works.title: Complex antennal modifications of silkworm N-glycans as potential baculovirus ligands
works.abstract: The domesticated silkworm Bombyx mori evolved from a wild species almost 5000 years ago and is the basis for sericulture practised especially in some Asian countries, while silkworm cell lines as well as silkworm larvae are used in biotechnology. Silkworms are affected by a number of viral pathogens, including baculoviruses; thus, molecular mechanisms of viral infection are of interest in sericulture and virology. As any eukaryotes, many silkworm proteins are N-glycosylated. In this study, the N-glycomes of B. mori larvae, including strains either susceptible or resistant to a silkworm virus, were examined using an LC-MS/MS approach which revealed not only which proteins are N-glycosylated, but indicated that the N-glycomes contain novel glucuronylated, xylosylated and phosphorylcholine-modified glycans, including examples with masses of over 3000 Da due to extended antennae, in addition to typical oligomannosidic and fucosylated structures. Western blotting and glycoproteomic analyses indicate that specific glycoproteins are modified with phosphorylcholine, whereby this epitope is also recognised by human C-reactive protein and other innate immune proteins when the natural glycans were printed in a microarray format. Binding data indicate that N-glycans and phosphorylcholine may play a role in recognition of silkworm proteins by the B. mori nucleopolyhedrosis virus. Our data not only demonstrate the complexity of the silkworm N-glycome, unsurpassed by other insects studied thus far, but indicate the challenges facing glycoengineering to refine the use of insect systems as biotechnological factories for therapeutic proteins.

works.title: A simplified high-pressure freezing workflow in Autogrids
works.abstract: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) enables structural analysis of biological samples in near-native states, yet vitrification of thick and complex specimens remains challenging. High-pressure freezing (HPF) can vitrify up to ∼200 μm thick specimens, but its seamless integration into cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) workflows is hindered by planchettes that are not optimized for EM grids, resulting in extensive handling, reliance on user experience, and frequent grid damage. Here, we present a streamlined HPF workflow based on newly designed planchettes that directly accommodate clipped EM Autogrids. Interchangeable lids control sample thickness and support vitrification of diverse specimens, including single-celled eukaryotes and tissue biopsies, while minimizing post-freezing handling. We demonstrate that these planchettes enable reliable preservation of cellular ultrastructure and macromolecular integrity, as assessed by cryo-ET and subtomogram averaging. This resource provides a practical solution for integrating HPF into modern cryo-ET pipelines, expanding access to structurally complex specimens and supporting future clinical applications.

works.title: Covalent remodeling of CRBN creates a non-canonical neosubstrate interface with NTAQ1
A step toward molecular-scale views of human synapses: Cryo-ET of human induced neurons on EM grids
Quantum crystallography: A new frontier in structural biology
Meet the author: Albert Guskov
Dynamic ring rearrangements underlie transport by MCE proteins
works.abstract: Mammalian cell entry (MCE) proteins mediate hydrophobic substrate transport between bacterial membranes, yet the dynamics underlying substrate translocation remain poorly understood. Here, we present the structural characterization of B. bacteriovorus Bd1152, revealing a rare two-MCE-ring architecture. Integrating X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy and continuous flexibility analysis, we uncover pronounced shearing and twisting motions between its MCE rings. Analysis of E. coli PqiB reveals that this conformational plasticity extends across distinct MCE architectures, with coordinated inter-ring rearrangements coupled to constriction and dilation of the central transport channel. These dynamics support a peristaltic model for substrate translocation through MCE proteins. Furthermore, a conserved loss-of-function PqiB mutant adopts a collapsed channel conformation, disrupting formation of a continuous transport conduit. Together, our findings establish inter-ring conformational plasticity as a conserved feature of MCE proteins and reveal how coordinated MCE-domain and pore rearrangements may facilitate lipid transport across the bacterial periplasm.

works.title: High resolution structures of rat brain V-ATPase with concanamycin
A novel rare splice variant of the human voltage‐dependent proton channel hH V 1
works.abstract: Diversity among human voltage‐gated proton channels (hH V 1) arises exclusively from alternative splicing or post‐translational modification. In addition to the canonical 273‐amino acid form (hH V 1‐l), two shorter isoforms, HVCN1 S and H V 1Sper, have been described, both characterized by truncated N‐terminal domains. To date, isoforms longer than hH V 1‐l were unidentified in humans. Here, we report a novel ‘very‐long’ hH V 1 splice variant (hH V 1‐vl) containing a 47 amino acid N‐terminal insertion derived from alternative splicing of exon 12 of the HVCN1 gene . The additional amino acid sequence is predicted to be largely unstructured and contains several potential phosphorylation sites. Molecular dynamics simulations further suggest that the conserved poly‐glutamate motif downstream of Thr29 can interact with cytosolic arginine residues at the base of the S4 segment. Nested PCR unambiguously identified hH V 1‐vl in healthy tissues (pons and choroid plexus epithelial cells) as well as in three different types of lymphoma. However, quantitative PCR showed that hH V 1‐vl is expressed at low levels in the analyzed tissues, 0.3–2% of the total HVCN1 transcripts. Heterologous expression of hH V 1‐vl followed by patch‐clamp recordings demonstrated that this isoform retains the key properties of proton channels, including high proton selectivity and voltage‐ and pH‐dependent conductance. Compared with the canonical 273‐amino acid hH V 1‐l isoform, hH V 1‐vl exhibits similar gating parameters, including proton selectivity, ΔpH‐dependent gating, conductance density, g H – V relationship, and closing kinetics, but shows markedly slower activation kinetics.

works.title: Rotation of the N-terminal helix triggers Gα activation
works.abstract: Heterotrimeric G proteins, activated by G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), are central mediators of cellular signaling. Activation requires GDP release from the Gα subunit, a step attributed largely to the C-terminal α5 helix, the primary GPCR-interacting region. Contributions from other Gα regions have remained unclear. Here we show that the N-terminal helix (αN) of Gαs promotes GDP release through a rotational conformational change. Diffracted X-ray tracking revealed that engagement with an active GPCR increases αN conformational displacement. Biochemical assays and molecular dynamics simulations showed that counterclockwise rotation of αN, viewed from the extracellular side, facilitates GDP release, whereas clockwise rotation does not. Mechanistically, this αN-mediated pathway acts synergistically with α5 conformational changes and propagates through the β-sheet network within the Ras homology domain to the P-loop and the αG helix. These findings identify an αN-driven activation pathway and extend the mechanistic framework for GPCR-triggered G protein activation. Receptor engagement rotates the N-terminal helix of the G protein alpha subunit, and this motion is relayed through the protein to release bound GDP, revealing an activation pathway that works together with the long-studied C-terminal route.

works.title: EMC chaperone activity is required for cotranslational calcium channel assembly
works.abstract: Nearly half of the ~5,000 human membrane proteins need to assemble into stoichiometric complexes as part of their biogenesis at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. How ER-resident biogenesis factors coordinate membrane insertion, folding and assembly is not well understood. Here we demonstrate that the human ER membrane protein complex (EMC) insertase additionally acts as a chaperone to facilitate the assembly of heterotrimeric voltage-gated calcium channels (Cav). Using function-separating mutations and inhibitory nanobodies, we show that nascent Cav channels are degraded prematurely when EMC’s chaperone function is selectively perturbed. Blocking EMC’s chaperone function impaired Cav-dependent cardiomyocyte contraction. EMC engagement of the pore-forming Cav α-subunit occurred cotranslationally and required the Cav α-subunit’s first transmembrane domain bundle to protrude from the nascent ribosome–multipass translocon complex. Our findings establish a chaperone function for the EMC and suggest that biogenesis of multibundle membrane proteins may require a highly orchestrated, cotranslational interplay among ER biogenesis factors. Stanton et al. show that the human endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein complex (EMC) engages nascent calcium channels cotranslationally as a chaperone as part of a large ribosome–multipass translocon–EMC supercomplex. Loss of this function impairs channel biogenesis and disrupts cardiomyocyte contraction.

works.title: Correction: Identification and functional characterization of an mRNA Cap3 methyltransferase from Acanthamoeba castellani medusavirusi
Mapping the Sequence Preference of the Generalist Class II Lanthipeptide Synthetase ProcM by mRNA Display
works.abstract: The biosynthetic machineries of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are often substrate tolerant. A remarkable example is the class II lanthipeptide synthetase ProcM, which naturally functions as a generalist enzyme that has not evolved to use a specific substrate during its evolutionary history. Although ProcM has been studied extensively, the sequence features associated with productive modification remain underexplored. In this study, we use the ultrahigh-throughput mRNA display technique to map the sequence compatibility of ProcM across a focused library. This approach expands the landscape of ProcM reactivity beyond native substrates and individually characterized variants. Machine learning (ML) analysis revealed that the dataset contains sequence patterns associated with ProcM reactivity, with models achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.73. This moderate predictive performance contrasts with the near-perfect accuracy reported for specialized enzymes. This finding suggests that predicting substrate compatibility for generalist enzymes is more challenging due to uneven representation of reactive and nonreactive sequences and limitations of the available data. Our results provide a high-throughput view of ProcM reactivity and highlight differences with previous high-throughput studies on substrate selectivity of RiPP modification enzymes. Future studies will need to assess whether these differences are common when comparing generalist with specialist enzymes.

works.title: Amyloid-β42 Drives Collagen-Independent Activation of Discoidin Domain Receptor 2 in Alzheimer’s Disease
works.abstract: Abstract Discoidin domain receptor 2 (DDR2), a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) family member, plays a pivotal role in collagen-mediated signaling, influencing several key cellular processes. In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), DDR2 expression and activity are significantly upregulated. While collagens, the endogenous ligands of DDR2, either remain unchanged or are downregulated in AD-like conditions, Amyloid-beta 42 (Aβ42) has been found to activate DDR2 noncanonically in the absence of collagen. Additionally, DDR2 naturally translocates to the nucleus in the neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y, and the nuclear pool of DDR2 further increases in the presence of Aβ42, suggesting a novel pathological role for DDR2 in AD. The E113K mutant of DDR2, where the collagen-binding site has been compromised, fails to get activated by collagen, whereas Aβ42 could still activate it. Furthermore, the DDR2 inhibitor WRG-28 effectively inhibits Aβ42 induced phosphorylation of the protein. We have modeled the ectodomain of DDR2 in silico, extending it through the transmembrane helix and subsequently docked the Aβ42 pentamer to provide a structural hypothesis for elucidating the mechanistic basis of Aβ-mediated kinase activation. Additionally, we analyzed WRG-28 binding by forming a ternary complex among DDR2, Aβ42, and WRG-28. Our structural analyses offer key insights into the molecular mechanisms governing DDR2 activation by Aβ42 and its inhibition by WRG-28 in the AD cell model, providing a foundation for targeted therapeutic strategies.

works.title: A Role for Janus Cyclohexyl Ring Motifs in Medicinal Chemistry. Incorporation Into G‐Quadruplex Ligands and Anti‐ Trypanosoma brucei Activity
works.abstract: The naphthalene diimide (NDI) ring system is recognized as a privileged motif for binding to G‐quadruplex DNA. Accordingly, compounds with peripheral groups attached to the NDI core are being explored as antiparasitic and anticancer candidates. In this study, we have synthesized and explored a series of NDIs with peripheral all‐ cis ring fluorinated cyclohexyl rings to assess their relative stabilization potential for G‐quadruplex and double‐stranded DNA. This was explored through FRET melting experiments and measuring changes in melting temperatures (Δ T m ). Compounds were also assayed against Trypanosoma brucei to assess their in vitro potency (EC 50 ) against the causative parasite of human African trypanosomiasis or African Sleeping Sickness. The study revealed significant differences in activity when changing the nature of fluorine substitutions on the cyclohexane ring and also the length and nature (ether (O) or methylene (CH 2 )) of the linker to the core aromatic motif. The most active compound of the series was ether 12a which displayed nanomolar activity (EC 50 = 40 nM) against T. brucei although with a modest selectivity (14‐fold) for the parasite over HeLa (human model) cells. The study reveals good prospects for exploring fluorinated Janus cyclohexanes in a medicinal chemistry context.

works.title: Exploring the Chemistry, Biological Mechanisms, and Therapeutic Potential of Squalamine and Trodusquemine
works.abstract: This review highlights the chemistry and therapeutic potential of the shark-derived aminosterols squalamine and trodusquemine. It surveys the evolution of synthetic strategies developed to access these structurally unique natural products, with emphasis on stereoselective and more efficient routes to squalamine. It also examines their broad spectrum of biological activities, including antiangiogenic, antimicrobial, antiparasitic and antiviral effects, together with the anti-obesity properties of trodusquemine and the emerging interest of both aminosterols in neurodegenerative disorders. Altogether, these studies position aminosterols as promising membrane-active scaffolds for future drug discovery, even though no compound from this class has yet reached the market.

works.title: Expression of Human CYP2D6 in Artificial Cells Based on Polymer‐Lipid Hybrid Vesicles
works.abstract: Artificial cells with the ability to express functional, biomedically relevant enzymes have long been a goal in the field of bottom-up synthetic biology. Here, we demonstrate the expression of human cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) within the lumen of giant hybrid vesicle-based artificial cells using a cell-free protein expression system based on the protozoan Leishmania tarentolae. The vesicle membranes comprise 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine and amphiphilic block copolymers containing poly(cholesteryl methacrylate-co-butyl methacrylate) with either poly(galactose methacrylate) (pGalacMA) or poly(carboxyethyl acrylate) as the hydrophilic block. The amount and composition of the block copolymer incorporated into the giant hybrid vesicle membrane altered the artificial cells' ability to support functional protein expression, likely through changes in membrane properties. In particular, giant hybrid vesicles containing pGalacMA supported production of enzymatically active CYP2D6. Overall, the reported approach advances the development of artificial cells capable of producing functional, biomedically relevant enzymes. Further, the effort highlights complex interplay between polymer properties and performance of biological components in the functional complexity achievable in polymer-lipid hybrid vesicles.

works.title: Beyond Static Structures: New Opportunities to Model the Dynamic Interactions of Cell‐Surface Proteins
works.abstract: Recent advances in AI-driven structure prediction have transformed structural biology but remain limited for cell-surface proteins mediating transient, context-dependent interactions. Multidomain architectures, flexible linkers, and coupled cis- and trans-interactions challenge current models, leading to inaccurate predictions for key adhesion molecules. These limitations highlight the need to incorporate cellular context, conformational dynamics, and multivalent interactions. Emerging strategies, including MD-informed machine learning, generative models, and multiscale simulations integrated with experimental restraints, offer promising solutions. Together, these approaches aim to bridge static structure prediction with dynamic, physiologically relevant modeling of protein interactions at cell-cell interfaces.

works.title: In vivo-compatible spatial multi-omics via hydrogen peroxide-independent APEX2 labeling
Q&A with Bil Clemons
Withdrawal: Abstract 4318 Identifying the Effects of N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N′-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine quinone on Aquatic Amphibian Gene Expression
A BromoTag-Based Toolkit for Rapid Modulation of Chemically Induced Proximity
works.abstract: Mammalian cells control a wide range of essential processes via protein-protein interactions (PPIs), including signal transduction, gene expression, cell cycle regulation, and metabolism. Pathologic alterations in PPIs have been linked to many human diseases. Thus, the ability to rapidly and selectively induce PPIs in cultured cells is crucial for many fields of biological research. One proven approach is the use of synthetic bivalent chemical ligands to selectively recruit protein domains with engineered mutations (i.e., "bump-and-hole"). Developing new PPI chemical inducers with unique protein domains enables multiplexing and potentially expands the breadth of recruitable proteins. Herein, we describe the design and characterization of a BromoTag- and dTAG-based toolkit to induce protein homo- and heterodimerization. Using a NanoBiT split-luciferase assay, we characterized a library of BromoTag-based homo- (BromoTag/BromoTag) and heterobivalent (BromoTag/dTAG) compounds for their ability to induce neo-PPIs. Compounds were evaluated for activity across multiple cellular applications, including caspase-9 and c-Kit tyrosine kinase activation, with comparable activity to other dimerizer systems. This BromoTag-based protein dimerization toolkit provides a useful alternative to current controlled dimerization systems that will enable robust prototyping of chemically induced proximity.

works.title: A 1,2-Dioxetane-Based Chemiluminescent Probe for In Vivo Copper Imaging
works.abstract: Copper is involved in healthy physiology and aberrant pathology with prominent roles in Wilson's and Menkes diseases. Tracking its reactivity in living systems is crucial to understanding its biological function and could be helpful in identifying targeted therapies. We developed a turn-on chemiluminescent copper probe CpCL, which was designed by linking a picolinic acid moiety to the phenolic substituent of a spiroadamantane 1,2-dioxetane. Reaction of CpCL with copper results in formation of a copper complex intermediate that releases the phenolate upon hydrolysis, followed by initiation of a chemiluminescence reaction for light emission. The probe displayed excellent selectivity for Cu2+ compared to other competitive metal ions, with a sensitive limit of detection of 360 nM. The mechanism was studied using initial rate kinetics to provide an estimated pseudo-first-order rate constant of 5.18 ± 0.38 × 10-5 s-1 for the hydrolysis of the copper-bound probe. The probe was then validated in living mice using the copper chelator ATN-224 as a negative control, demonstrating that it can be used to monitor copper ions in vivo.

works.title: Breaking the ice: multiple origins of ice‐binding/antifreeze proteins
works.abstract: Ice-binding proteins (IBPs) enable organisms to survive freezing environments by binding to ice and inhibiting crystal growth. Their remarkable structural, taxonomic, and evolutionary diversity makes them an exceptional system for studying protein evolution. This review examines the origins, structures, and distribution of IBPs across fishes, arthropods, plants, microorganisms, and other taxa. Comparative genomic analyses have revealed the progenitor genes of all known fish antifreeze proteins (AFPs), with the alanine-rich α-helical AFPs demonstrating repeated convergent evolution from diverse progenitors. β-solenoid IBPs have arisen repeatedly in arthropods, plants, fungi, and microorganisms. Although these proteins share the ability to bind ice, they can have different functions and their structures differ substantially in fold, architecture, and ice-binding surface composition. Horizontal gene transfer has also played a major role in IBP evolution, including transfer of type II AFP genes among fishes, DUF3494 IBPs among bacteria and numerous eukaryotes, and likely transfer of a hyperactive β-solenoid AFP between distantly related beetle lineages. The identification of IBPs presents significant experimental challenges, requiring rigorous verification through thermal hysteresis or ice recrystallization inhibition measurements together with recombinant expression. Nevertheless, advances in genome sequencing, transcriptomics, protein purification, and structural prediction are rapidly accelerating IBP discovery. Collectively, IBPs demonstrate the extraordinary diversity of evolutionary solutions to a common environmental challenge and provide a powerful model for investigating the mechanisms by which novel protein functions arise.

works.title: Bacterial sialidases subvert the complement system through desialylation
works.abstract: Bacterial sialidases (neuraminidases) are widely studied virulence factors, yet their impact on the complement system, a central component of innate immunity, remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the effects of six sialidases from five human pathogens, including Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium perfringens, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola, and Vibrio cholerae on complement immunity using an integrated approach combining genetics, biochemistry, glycobiology, mass spectrometry, and structural biology. We show that major complement proteins, including C1q, C4, and C5, as well as complement regulators Factor I, Factor H, and C4BP, are modified by terminal sialic acids (sialylation) and undergo terminal desialylation by all six sialidases. Using the oral pathogen T. denticola and its sialidase NanH as a representative model, we demonstrate that sialidase-mediated desialylation suppresses complement activation and surface deposition, promoting complement evasion. Structural analyses of T. denticola NanH in complex with an inhibitor, sialic acid, and native glycans, together with comparisons to other sialidase structures, reveal the molecular basis of substrate recognition and catalysis. Despite substantial sequence diversity, all six exo-α-sialidases share a conserved six-bladed β-propeller catalytic domain and cleave both N-acetylneuraminic acid and N-glycolylneuraminic acid, the predominant mammalian sialic acids. Together, these findings establish a conserved structural and functional mechanism by which diverse bacterial pathogens desialylate complement components to impair innate immune defense.

works.title: Harnessing artificial intelligence to understand enzyme catalysis and discover new enzymes
works.abstract: Molecular simulations have been central to our understanding of how enzymes work, and the ongoing explosion of artificial intelligence/ML (AI/ML) approaches is greatly expanding the scope of problems that can be addressed using simulations. The speed of development of the field is tremendous, with the near-constant development of new approaches and successful applications. This review aims to give a higher-level overview of four key areas where AI/ML approaches are significantly transforming computational enzymology (both understanding and design), specifically (1) enzyme discovery and functional annotation, (2) kinetic parameter prediction, (3) understanding of protein dynamics and enzyme reaction mechanisms, and (4) decoding protein allostery. We also discuss some of the outstanding technical challenges in this research space, and efforts being made to overcome them.

works.title: The dynamics of large biomolecular assemblies
works.abstract: With recent advances in cryo-electron microscopy/cryo-electron tomography (cryoEM/cryoET), computational capabilities and machine learning, there has been an incredible increase in the speed of structure determination for large biomolecular assemblies. In order to connect these static descriptions with biological function, one needs reliable and accurate approaches to quantify the factors that regulate dynamics. For this, models that employ simplified energetics and/or coarse-grained representations have become indispensable tools for integrating structural insights, biochemical analyses and physical principles. Here we discuss examples where molecular simulations have provided a framework for understanding dynamics in assemblies of increasing size and complexity. We focus on three classes for which there have been notable advances in recent years: ribosomes, viral capsids and nuclear pore complexes. Each possesses unique physical attributes that have required distinct theoretical and computational strategies. Together, these studies provide a rich conceptual and technical foundation that can help shape our perspective on the machinery of the cell.

This study expands the targeted protein degradation toolkit by validating several structurally simple peptide recruiters. While wild-type 431 monomeric and dimeric peptides serve as effective IGF2R-specific modules, the optimized L4 variant emerges as a highly potent alternative that engages alternative endocytic pathways. By bridging extracellular targets to these respective receptors, these peptide-based degraders drive robust endosomal internalization and subsequent lysosomal degradation.

works.title: ADP-ribose induces neuronal ferroptosis through ENT2-mediated nucleotide rewiring
A nanoscale map of the human cell surface proteome reveals spatial and functional organization
Structural mechanism of programmable gene integration by the R2 retrotransposon coupled with CRISPR–Cas9
Small-Molecule Inhibitors of Cholesterol Sulfotransferase as Immunomodulatory Agents
works.abstract: Though immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy has been a promising advance in cancer treatment, response rates to ICB are low owing to other mechanisms that cancers employ to evade the immune system. SULT2B1b is an enzyme known to produce cholesterol sulfate (CS), an immunosuppressive metabolite that inhibits T-cell migration. Cancers expressing high levels of SULT2B1b thus generate a tumor microenvironment that excludes T cells, which leads to increased tumor growth and renders ICB therapy ineffective. Here, we identify a novel class of azasteroid SULT2B1b inhibitors with greater potency and selectivity than previously identified compounds. X-ray co-crystal structures indicate that these inhibitors bind in a conformation different from that of native substrates, enabling inhibition without acting as a substrate. Additionally, these new compounds effectively reduce CS levels in tumors in mice and, as such, have potential as cancer therapeutics in combination with ICB therapy.

works.title: Directed Evolution of the Cbx1 Chromodomain Generates a High-Affinity Trimethyllysine-Binding Variant
works.abstract: Directed evolution is a powerful and versatile strategy for engineering proteins with enhanced affinity and tailored molecular recognition properties. Here, we applied phage display-guided directed evolution to enhance the binding of the wild-type Cbx1 chromodomain (Cbx1-CD) to an H3K9me3-containing peptide. Screening a soft-randomized library targeting residues surrounding the aromatic cage yielded C29, which bound the H3K9me3 peptide with a KD of 57 nM and exhibited an approximately 14-fold lower dissociation rate constant than Cbx1-CD. Across an H3K9me3-derived alanine-scanning series and a peptide panel, C29 showed stronger binding signals than Cbx1-CD for multiple peptides containing trimethyllysine (Kme3), suggesting lower flanking-sequence dependence for C29 than for Cbx1-CD. An AlphaFold3 model of the C29-H3K9me3 complex suggested local changes in the hydrophobic and electrostatic environment surrounding the Kme3-binding pocket, providing a mechanistic hypothesis for C29's enhanced affinity and reduced flanking-sequence dependence. When two Kme3-containing peptides were spiked into a 100-fold molar excess of unmodified background peptides, C29-conjugated beads effectively enriched both Kme3 peptides relative to the unmodified background. These findings define C29 as a high-affinity Kme3-binding Cbx1 chromodomain variant and support its further evaluation as an affinity reagent for Kme3-containing peptide enrichment.

works.title: Oxidized 5-Methylcytosines and Nucleosome Architecture Cooperatively Influence Thymine DNA Glycosylase Activity
works.abstract: Active DNA demethylation is a fundamental epigenetic process in which the iterative oxidation of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) by TET dioxygenases generates diverse combinations of oxidized 5-methylcytosines within CpG dinucleotides before their excision by thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG). Although heterogeneous CpG oxidation states are expected to arise frequently during this process, how the modification state of the opposing cytosine influences TDG activity remains poorly understood. Here, we developed a chemically defined panel of CpG substrates containing cytosine, 5mC, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), 5-formylcytosine (5fC), and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC) opposite a target 5fC and systematically examined TDG-mediated excision in both naked DNA and nucleosome core particles (NCPs). In naked DNA, opposing-strand cytosine modifications exerted only modest effects on TDG activity when a single excisable base was present within the CpG dyad, whereas dual-substrate CpGs exhibited unexpected differences in strand utilization. In contrast, nucleosome assembly profoundly altered TDG activity, revealing modification-dependent effects that were largely absent in naked DNA and dramatically redistributing strand utilization within dual-substrate CpGs. Together, these findings demonstrate that the oxidation-state composition of a CpG dyad and nucleosome architecture cooperatively regulate TDG activity, establishing heterogeneous CpG oxidation states as functionally distinct substrates for TDG and providing a biochemical framework for understanding how chromatin structure regulates active DNA demethylation.

works.title: Structural and Biochemical Characterization of a Type II Arabinogalactan Fucosyltransferase 4 from Arabidopsis thaliana
works.abstract: Plant cell walls are made of complex polymeric networks of diverse polysaccharides, proteins, polyphenolics, and glycoproteins called hydroxyproline-rich glycoproteins (HRGPs), like arabinogalactan proteins or AGPs. Approximately 90 to 98% of the mass of AGPs is composed of polysaccharide components, which are synthesized by a group of enzymes known as glycosyltransferases (GTs). One subset of these enzymes comprises a family of fucosyltransferases (FUTs) that transfer fucose (Fuc) residues to the arabinose (Ara) moiety of AGP. Ten FUTs involved in plant cell wall polymer synthesis have been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana, three of which have been characterized: AtFUT1, a xyloglucan-specific FUT, and AtFUT4 and AtFUT6, which are AGP-specific FUTs. In this study, we determined the crystal structure of AtFUT4 to gain insights into its substrate specificity toward GDP-Fuc (donor substrate) and AGP-based oligo- and polysaccharides (acceptor substrates). Through integrated bioinformatics and biochemical analyses, we identified key features that define acceptor- and donor-specificities. We tested two acceptors, AGPs and the pseudo-substrate arabinotetrose, and identified critical residues that contribute to acceptor recognition. In addition to identifying residue-level interactions, our analysis highlights the importance of structural flexibility: tighter binding of GDP-fucose by AtFUT4 likely enables broader acceptor specificity compared with AtFUT1, while also increasing donor hydrolysis in the absence of acceptor. Overall, the study advances understanding of the structure-function relationship of AtFUT4 in AGP fucosylation and provides a foundation for rational engineering of GTs, particularly FUTs, development of inhibitors, studies of cell wall polysaccharide interactions, and exploration of the roles of AtFUT4 in plant physiology.

works.title: Structural conservation and expanded functionality of hyper‐stable human serum albumin variants
works.abstract: Human serum albumin (hSA) is the most abundant protein in human plasma, and its pharmacological properties, such as long plasma half-life mediated by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) and its ability to bind endogenous and exogenous molecules, make it attractive for biotechnological applications. Currently, most wild type (WT) SAs are derived from human or bovine serum or produced in yeast and mammalian cells. Although well established, these methods are costly, difficult to reproduce, and not environmentally sustainable. Building on a previous study to design highly mutated hSA sequences, we extend the validation through an in-depth analysis of three engineered hSA variants: hSA1, hSA2, and hSA3, containing 16, 25, or 73 amino acid substitutions, respectively. These variants were designed for enhanced solubility, stability, and expression in Escherichia coli. All three variants showed low micromolar affinities for hFcRn at pH 5.5, and negligible binding at pH 7.4. In a human endothelial cell-based recycling assay (HERA), the engineered hSA variants were recycled by hFcRn to the same extent as hSA isolated from serum. Exploring the properties of canonical drug-binding sites, warfarin affinity was comparable to WT hSA, whereas ibuprofen binding differed. Complementary cytotoxicity assays on human macrophages confirmed negligible toxicity and biocompatibility. The cryo-electron microscopy structure of hSA3 revealed that, despite extensive engineering, the native heart-shape of hSA, folding of domains, and its open conformation were preserved. These findings validate the structural integrity and functional adaptability of engineered hSA variants, underscoring their potential as versatile, animal-free solutions for next-generation therapeutics and biotechnological applications.

works.title: Dissecting the molecular basis of reduced stability in staphylokinase variant 42D
works.abstract: Staphylokinase (SAK) is a highly fibrin-specific plasminogen activator with considerable potential as a thrombolytic agent. Among the three naturally occurring SAK variants, STAR and 42D exhibit comparable fibrinolytic activities but markedly different thermal stabilities. Although the reduced stability of 42D has been experimentally demonstrated, the molecular basis underlying this destabilization remains unclear. To identify residues responsible for the decreased stability of 42D, we systematically reconstructed the mutational transition from STAR to 42D by generating all corresponding single- and double-point mutants. Variants were characterized using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), a fibrin matrix lysis assay, FoldX stability calculations, and molecular dynamics simulations. DSC measurements revealed that the G36R substitution is the principal determinant of the reduced thermal stability of 42D, decreasing the melting temperature by 11.9°C relative to STAR, whereas H43R exerts a compensatory stabilizing effect. FoldX calculations identified increased backbone conformational entropy penalties and van der Waals clashes as prominent energetic features associated with G36R-mediated destabilization. Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated that G36R does not induce global unfolding but rather causes localized perturbations in secondary-structure organization. Importantly, the naturally occurring 42D variant exhibited a similar pattern of localized structural perturbations, supporting a major contribution of G36R to its reduced stability. Despite substantial differences in thermal stability, most variants retained fibrinolytic activities comparable to that of STAR, suggesting only a partial overlap between the determinants governing stability and function. Collectively, our results resolve the individual contributions of the three substitutions underlying the stability difference between STAR and 42D and identify G36R as the principal destabilizing mutation. These findings improve our understanding of sequence-stability relationships in SAK and may facilitate the rational engineering of thrombolytic proteins with enhanced developability and therapeutic potential.

works.title: Editorial overview: 3D Genome and Subcellular Organization
The relationship between local frustration and protein function
works.abstract: Energy landscape theory is the accepted theoretical framework for understanding protein folding based on minimizing frustration. The theory provides an algorithm to learn the energy of amino acid interactions within a folded protein structure that also allows evaluation of localized regions of frustration. Most amino acid contacts are minimally frustrated or neutral, but patches of amino acid contacts are highly frustrated. These energetically unfavorable interactions are mostly found on the protein surface and have been linked to protein function in various ways. This review highlights experimental and computational exploration of how localized energetic frustration is linked to protein function.

works.title: Modulation of pre-mRNA splicing by small molecules
works.abstract: Alternative splicing of mRNA precursors is an important mechanism of gene regulation, which is frequently altered in a variety of pathologies. Recent advances demonstrate that modulating splice-site selection can offer new therapeutic options for unmet medical needs. Here, we review structural and functional data that help explain basic principles of splice site selection and their modulation by small molecules. These include selective effects of inhibitors of branch point recognition, as well as the effects of intercalating compounds that serve to repair imperfect base-pairing interactions important for 5' splice site recognition. The remarkable complexity and versatility of the spliceosome, which removes introns with high precision despite the diversity of splice-site sequences, can offer unique opportunities to selectively modulate splice-site selection for gene regulation and therapeutic applications.

works.title: Characterization and Molecular Engineering of a Thermostable Amino Acid Dehydrogenase for Enhanced ( S )‐2‐Amino‐1‐Butanol Synthesis
works.abstract: ( S )‐2‐Amino‐1‐butanol, a key intermediate for ethambutol hydrochloride synthesis, is currently produced via heavy metal‐catalyzed processes or enzymatic resolution with limited theoretical yields. While amine dehydrogenases (AmDHs) offer sustainable alternatives for asymmetric reductive amination, their applicability is often restricted by narrow substrate scope. Here, we report the discovery of a thermostable amino acid dehydrogenase from Thermoactinomyces daqus ( Td AADH) that exhibits optimal activity at pH 9.0 and 55 °C with exceptional thermostability ( t 1/2 = 21 days at 40 °C). Although inactive toward the non‐native substrate 1‐hydroxy‐2‐butanone, structure‐guided engineering via site‐directed and iterative saturation mutagenesis (ISM) successfully endowed the enzyme with desired functionality: the initial double mutant K93S/N288L (M1) acquired de novo amination activity, while subsequent evolution to the quintuple mutant M4 (incorporating L136T/T139D/M141R) enhanced specific activity by 2.75‐fold (5.38 U·g −1 ) without compromising enantioselectivity ( ee > 99%). Mechanistic investigations via molecular docking suggest that these mutations plausibly reshape the substrate‐binding pocket, alleviate steric hindrance, and optimize electrostatic interactions to accommodate the hydroxyketone substrate. Preparative‐scale biotransformation (40 °C, 30 mM substrate, coupled with GDH/glucose for cofactor recycling) achieved quantitative conversion (≥99%) within 36 h. This work expands the enzymatic toolbox for thermostable AmDHs.

works.title: The Dual Nature of RNA Ligation and Degradation by T4 RNA Ligase 1: Insights Into an AMP‐Driven, Nucleobase‐Dependent Reverse Reaction
works.abstract: T4 RNA Ligase 1 (Rnl1) catalyzes the ligation of a 5'-phosphate to a 3'-hydroxyl in single-stranded RNA and is widely used in RNA biotechnology for applications such as RNA library preparation and 3'-adapter ligation. In addition to ligation reaction, Rnl1 catalyzes the reverse reaction, leading to RNA degradation. However, how RNA sequence affects susceptibility to this reverse reaction remains unclear, and practical strategies for controlling it through buffer conditions have not been established. Previous studies showed that AMP promotes and ATP suppresses the reverse reaction; we confirmed these effects by electrophoretic analysis of FAM-labeled RNA homopolymers, a substrate not previously examined. Furthermore, using miRNA substrates, we demonstrated that the reverse reaction can occur under conditions that more closely resemble the practical conditions in which Rnl1 is used, thereby extending the relevance of previous findings. Additionally, we showed that the Rnl1-mediated reverse reaction exhibits pronounced nucleobase preference. The reverse reaction is suppressed by elevated temperature and duplex formation. Furthermore, experimental results combined with stochastic simulations indicate that Rnl1-mediated degradation proceeds via an endonucleolytic mechanism. These findings define how reaction conditions and nucleobase difference influence reverse reaction efficiency and provide practical guidance for minimizing RNA degradation while maintaining ligation efficiency.

works.title: Development of Highly Efficient Lysosome‐Targeting Peptide Ligands for the Internalization of Extracellular Proteins
works.abstract: Lysosome-targeting chimeras (LYTACs) induce the internalization of extracellular and membrane-associated proteins by routing them to lysosomes via endogenous receptors, such as the insulin-like growth factor-2 receptor (IGF2R), also known as cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor. While current IGF2R ligands are effective, expanding the LYTAC toolkit with structurally simple and synthetically accessible ligands remains a practical necessity. Here, we first validated that previously reported dimeric and monomeric peptides induce robust internalization, establishing them as effective IGF2R-targeting LYTAC ligands. To further optimize the peptide architecture, we performed systematic mutational scanning on its monomeric sequence to simplify the peptide architecture. We identified the L4 variant, which features a single leucine substitution at the fourth position. This optimized monomer induces greater internalization efficiency than the previously reported wild-type monomeric peptide ligand. To demonstrate its utility, we conjugated the L4 recruiter to a specific PCSK9 binder. The resulting bifunctional molecule successfully induced the dose- and time-dependent internalization of PCSK9. Collectively, these findings establish several peptide variants as practical and highly effective building blocks for the development of extracellular protein internalization platforms.

works.title: Explorations of the Hydrogenation of D 2 by Nitrogenase
works.abstract: A non‐physiological substrate of the enzyme nitrogenase, D 2 , is doubly hydrogenated by the enzyme to produce 2HD. This ‘HD reaction’ is in competition with the native function of the enzyme, hydrogenating N 2 to NH 3 . At the active site of the enzyme, a gallery of H atom donors is identified, and the proposed complete cycle mechanism for the N 2 reaction uses these donors eight times to generate the 2NH 3 + H 2 products. Here, the functionality of these H atom donors in hydrogenating D 2 to 2HD is investigated, applying density functional simulations to a 480+ atom model of the active site including all important surrounds. Many possible reaction trajectories were explored, and a revised mechanism for the HD reaction is presented. The mechanisms for hydrogenation of D 2 and of N 2 have common components, accounting for their experimentally known competition. Consideration of ten items of relevant experimental data about the HD reaction shows how the proposed mechanism complies with and interprets these data, although two experimental observations are still to be checked.

works.title: Integrative biophysical illumination of the 3D GPCRome dynamics
works.abstract: Abstract Insights into the dynamics of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) remain limited. Here we present an integrative strategy that bridges computational and experimental biophysical methods for probing protein dynamics. To illustrate its potential, we developed GPCRmd-NMR, a platform that synergistically combines molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy across the three-dimensional GPCRome. The resulting dataset enables structure-resolved analysis by applying the strategy across multiple GPCRs. We provide access to underexplored functional GPCR dynamics, receptor states and sites, including microswitches, hidden ligand entrance gateways and intrinsically disordered regions. Our integrated framework offers a solution to challenges faced by both experimental and computational researchers including the MD–NMR timescale gap.

works.title: Pharmacological ON/OFF Regulation of CAR T Cells through Estrogen Receptor-Based Stabilization and Targeted Degradation
works.abstract: Regulation of therapeutic cell response is important for safe and effective therapy, particularly for immunotherapy. Ideally, the regulators should be based on human proteins using compounds that have already been approved for human use. Regulation of protein degradation by small molecules enables fast cellular response and a small genetic footprint of genetic constructs. Here, we present a clinically compatible strategy for reversible pharmacological control of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell function using human estrogen receptor (ER)-based degron domains and FDA-approved small molecules. By fusing tamoxifen-responsive ER ligand-binding domains to CARs, we generate ligand-inducible ON-switch CARs whose stability, signaling, and effector functions are precisely controlled by 4-hydroxytamoxifen. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ER-tagged CARs can be selectively degraded using the FDA-approved ER-targeting PROTAC ARV-471, establishing a complementary OFF-switch mechanism that suppresses CAR expression and effector function. Notably, these results expand the ON-OFF switch platform for post-translational control of therapeutic proteins, offering new opportunities to improve the safety and precision of cellular immunotherapies.

works.title: Site-Selective Bioconjugations of Distinct Methionine Residues in a Protein via Reactivity-Based Reagent Control
works.abstract: The reaction of thioethers in biological macromolecules with oxaziridines enables their functionalization with moieties having utility in both basic and applied science. Exploitation of that reaction has advantages over common bioconjugations due to the relatively low abundance and weak reactivity of thioethers. Herein, we report a novel and improved route to 1-ureal piperidine,3-aryl oxaziridines that enables the preparation of bioconjugation reagents that are either electronically activated or deactivated. We leveraged the differential reactivities of the oxaziridine reagents and engineered methionine residues in distinct environments within a therapeutically relevant antibody fragment (Fab) to effect site-selective bioconjugations. We capitalized on this novel means of kinetic resolution to effect dual functionalization of a HER2-targeted Fab with distinct fluorophores for imaging receptor internalization. This work broadens the scope of what is possible in bioconjugations of thioethers and demonstrates that site-selective bioconjugations of the same residue at more than one site in a protein can be realized via reactivity-based reagent control.

works.title: G-Tract Length Shapes the Fate of G-Quadruplexes
works.abstract: Guanine (G)-rich DNA sequences can form unusual secondary structures known as G-quadruplexes (or G4s). The stability of these structures, whose folding is mainly driven by the formation and stacking of G-quartets, is influenced by several factors, foremost among them the nature of the sequence itself, particularly the nucleobases flanking the G-tracts, and the loops connecting them. A considerable effort has been devoted to understanding how the size, position, and composition of each loop and flanking sequences affect the stability of the resulting G4 fold. However, most of these studies have been restricted to sequences forming a three G-quartet G4 core. To better understand how the length of the G-tracts (from three to five Gs) and loops (from one to seven nucleotides) act in concert, we studied a set of 261 different sequences covering different possible combinations. A systematic biophysical analysis suggests that sequences with longer G-tracts tend to form more stable G4s, but also a mixture of species; it further shows that loop composition and position also influence the topology and stability of the resulting G4s. Collectively, this work provides an unprecedented view on how G4-forming sequences fold upon themselves and of the structural features that govern the stability of the resulting G4s.

works.title: Recovery of a Minor Cryo-EM Particle Population Reveals Conformational Equilibria Linking Cofactor Loading, Turnover, and Reactivation in Methionine Synthase
works.abstract: Abstract Cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase (MetH) is a highly dynamic enzyme that requires large-scale domain rearrangements to facilitate turnover and reactivation. Despite significant biochemical and structural efforts, a full picture of the conformational changes underlying the transition between MetH turnover and reactivation has remained elusive. Here, we leverage state-of-the-art cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) methods to reanalyze an old dataset and gain new insights into these changes. By utilizing a neural-network particle picker, performing careful classification of particles, and incorporating high-resolution information to determine initial particle orientations, we uncovered and reconstructed a minor population of reactivation-state MetH (∼4.5–5 Å resolution) from a dataset that is dominated by resting-state MetH. This structure represents the first fully intact structure of the enzyme with a physiological cobalamin cofactor bound. These findings highlight the potential for improved cryo-EM methodology to uncover previously hidden details about enzyme function and deepen our understanding of structural ensembles.

works.title: Redox Cofactor Diversity in Biological Hydride Transfer Reactions
works.abstract: Abstract Hydride-transfer reactions play central roles in biological redox chemistry across all domains of life. These transformations rely on specialized cofactors that enable the efficient transfer of reducing equivalents in oxidoreductive reactions. Nature has evolved several cofactors for this purpose, including nicotinamides, flavins, F420, pyrroloquinolone quinone (PQQ), and mycofactocin (MFT). Although these cofactors perform related functions, they differ in their structure, redox properties, reaction mechanisms, and biological distribution.
