This Review outlines these cofactors, highlighting common themes in hydride transfer mechanisms and how cofactor chemistry is linked to their biological function. In particular, F420, PQQ, and MFT are niche cofactors that expand our understanding of the diversity of cofactors and redox metabolism. Ultimately, understanding the chemistry and biology of redox cofactors offers broader applications in biotechnology and biocatalysis.

works.title: From Monomer to Mesh: The Biochemical Maturation of Gel-Forming Mucin Glycoproteins
works.abstract: Abstract Secreted mucin glycoproteins, which form the scaffolds of the mucus hydrogels coating tissue epithelia, are among the most complex molecules in nature. Mucin protein backbones are typically more than 5000 amino acids in length, become stapled into domain folds by over 100 disulfide bonds, and contain thousands of potential sites for O-glycosylation. The glycans added to these sites vary in chemical composition, length, and degree of branching, producing mucins with diverse biochemical and biophysical properties. In addition to this chemical complexity, structural heterogeneity arises via hinges between domains, long segments of natively disordered polypeptide, and intrinsic glycan flexibility. Though mucin backbone amino acid sequences are encoded in the genome, the ultimate properties of mucins depend heavily on glycosylation, which is shaped dynamically by the sets of glycosyltransferases expressed in individual mucus-producing cells. The substantial energy and intracellular organization required to produce mucin glycoproteins pays off in their crucial and versatile biological functions, ranging from cleaning tissue surfaces to lubrication to microbiome management. Mucins are of particular interest in human health due to their roles in protecting the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts and their dysfunction in various diseases. Studying the elaborate maturation process during mucin biosynthesis and polymerization, decoration with glycans, and formation of interpolymer interactions may help identify vulnerabilities that can be overcome nutritionally or medically. Understanding the principles of mucin construction will provide the framework for strengthening mucus hydrogels both physically and functionally.

works.title: Kinetic signatures of RAS–BRAF engagement reveal isoform selectivity, oncogenic amplification, and mutation‐dependent inhibitor resistance
works.abstract: The RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK (MAPK) signaling cascade is a central regulator of cellular proliferation and differentiation, and its dysregulation is a frequent driver of oncogenesis. RAF activation requires recruitment by GTP‐bound RAS at the plasma membrane; however, the precise molecular determinants governing RAS–RAF engagement remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that the BRAF N‐terminal region forms a cooperative BSR–CRD autoinhibitory gate that restricts RAS engagement and encodes isoform‐specific kinetic behavior. Using Open Surface Plasmon Resonance (OpenSPR) and Bio‐Layer Interferometry (BLI), together with NanoBiT cellular assays, we reveal a kinetic encoding mechanism in which KRAS and NRAS define distinct regimes of BRAF engagement: KRAS exhibits stability‐driven, long‐lived complex formation, whereas NRAS displays frequency‐driven, transient interactions. Oncogenic mutations reshape these regimes by selectively stabilizing RAS–BRAF association without uniformly increasing affinity, amplifying isoform‐specific kinetic signatures. Pharmacological profiling further reveals isoform‐dependent sensitivity of RAS–RAF disruption governed by nucleotide state and compatibility with the BSR–CRD gate. Together, these findings establish that KRAS and NRAS operate through distinct kinetic regimes of BRAF engagement governed by a structurally gated N‐terminal regulatory architecture encoding temporal and pharmacological specificity in MAPK signaling.

works.title: The physiological roles and pathological implications of metabolic communication via tunneling nanotubes in immune cells
works.abstract: The traditional paradigm of intercellular communication is rapidly evolving. Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) represent a distinct mode of intercellular communication, enabling the transfer of organelles, signaling molecules, and metabolic resources between spatially separated cells. Unlike soluble factor-mediated communication, TNTs establish direct physical connections that can support rapid and directional cargo transport, including mitochondrial transfer, with consequences for recipient-cell metabolism and function. In the immune system, TNT-mediated mitochondrial and other cargo transfer has been implicated in macrophage functional polarization, T-cell metabolic fitness, and natural killer (NK) cell-mediated immunity. In this review, we summarize the molecular characteristics of TNTs in immune cells, the regulation of their formation under inflammatory and metabolic stress, and the mechanisms and consequences of cargo transfer. We further examine the context-dependent nature of TNT-mediated communication, including its potential roles in host defense, tissue repair, tumor immune evasion, and pathogen dissemination. Finally, we critically evaluate transfer kinetics, quantitative scale, prevalence, in vivo evidence, and the technical limitations that currently constrain causal attribution and therapeutic translation.

works.title: Structural and functional insights into rhodopsin‐like and secretin‐like GPCR –arrestin interactions and regulation
works.abstract: Structural and functional studies of arrestins have revealed their essential role as multifunctional regulators of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling, desensitization, and trafficking. Despite significant challenges in capturing the dynamic nature of GPCR-arrestin interactions, great progress has been made in recent years, particularly through cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and X-ray crystallography that allowed structural characterization of arrestins in both their basal and GPCR-bound-like conformation and of GPCR-arrestin complexes in fully and partially engaged conformations. These structural insights have advanced our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying arrestin transition to the GPCR-bound conformation and its selective engagement by different GPCRs. The phosphorylation-dependent 'barcode' hypothesis further explains how specific patterns of receptor phosphorylation can encode differential arrestin recruitment and functional specificity. We discussed various biophysical techniques including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), and fluorescence-based assays that have been used to investigate arrestin conformational dynamics and GPCR interactions in vitro and in live cells.

works.title: RLIM ‐associated neurodevelopmental disorders: From clinical spectrum to molecular mechanisms
works.abstract: The E3 ubiquitin ligase RLIM (also known as RNF12) plays a central role in ubiquitin-dependent signaling pathways that regulate mammalian development. Missense variants in the RLIM gene cause Tønne-Kalscheuer syndrome (TOKAS), an X-linked recessive neurodevelopmental disorder affecting males, characterized by intellectual disability, developmental delay, and congenital abnormalities affecting the craniofacial, urogenital, ocular, and skeletal systems, as well as congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Additionally, RLIM duplications lead to a similar neurodevelopmental disorder, Chromosome Xq13 duplication syndrome. That both loss and gain of RLIM function produce overlapping neurodevelopmental phenotypes highlights the dosage sensitivity of this E3 ligase and points to its tightly regulated roles in human development. Despite an increasing number of reported cases, RLIM-associated disorders remain underdiagnosed and poorly understood, with no cure or targeted treatments, largely due to limited insight into the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying their pathogenesis. Here, we review current knowledge of RLIM biology across molecular, cellular, and genetic levels. We summarize the genetic basis, diagnostic criteria, and clinical spectrum of RLIM-associated disorders and integrate this with current understanding of RLIM-dependent ubiquitin signaling. By bringing together insights from biochemistry, cell signaling, and genetics, this review aimed to serve as a mechanistically informed reference for researchers and clinicians working on RLIM variants. We rank candidate RLIM substrates by the strength of the evidence linking them to disease. Finally, we discuss the key open questions that must be addressed to achieve a comprehensive cellular and molecular understanding of RLIM-associated disorders and thus lay the foundation for future therapeutic interventions.

works.title: Uncovering KRAS -mutant allele-specific biology and vulnerabilities in non-small cell lung cancer
works.abstract: KRAS (Kirsten-Ras) mutations are the most commonly occurring oncogenic drivers in non-small cell lung cancer. Despite the discovery of KRAS inhibitors representing a translational breakthrough for KRAS-driven cancers, resistance remains a major clinical challenge. We believe that to circumvent resistance, an in-depth understanding of the biological differences and therapeutic vulnerabilities specific to KRAS mutations is critical to inform rational combination partners with either mutant-selective or broad-spectrum (K)RAS inhibitors. The present review draws upon insights from both preclinical and clinical studies exploring KRAS-mutant allele-specific behaviours and therapeutic vulnerabilities. We will also highlight studies in which targeting of these vulnerabilities was combined with (K)RAS inhibitors, offering contextual examples of KRAS-mutant allele-tailored therapeutic strategies.

works.title: Geometry‐aware modeling with cellPACK for evaluating spatial trends in intracellular organization
works.abstract: Cells appear extraordinarily complex, yet aspects of their organization may arise from a small number of influences acting within geometric constraints. Here, we extend and use cellPACK, an open-source framework for rule-based spatial modeling, to compare observed and simulated 3D distributions of peroxisomes and endosomes (puncta) in human induced pluripotent stem cells. Simulations conditioned on observed cell and nuclear geometries along with puncta counts show that geometric variation can generate apparent structure in organelle localization, highlighting the need to account for geometry when interpreting spatial statistics. We therefore employ an occupancy-based metric that normalizes puncta density by available intracellular volume, revealing modest enrichment near the nuclear surface against an otherwise near-uniform cytoplasmic distribution. We use these occupancy patterns to fit combinations of predefined spatial bias models and evaluate the resulting 3D packings against observed data. To support open and reproducible modeling while enabling a more intuitive visual exploration, we present cellPACK Studio, a browser-based interface that allows users to generate, modify, and visualize the 3D cell packings used in this study (available at cellpack.allencell.org). Together, these results and tools illustrate how spatial modeling can transform descriptive imaging data into testable, interpretable hypotheses of intracellular organization.

works.title: The X‐ray crystallographic structure of a designed, self‐assembling, and heme‐binding protein
works.abstract: Abstract De novo heme‐binding proteins offer powerful minimal scaffolds for elucidating how sequence, oligomerization, and environment rule cofactor coordination, yet high‐resolution structural data for these systems remain scarce. Here, we report the high‐resolution crystal structure of a designed, self‐assembling α‐helical and heme‐binding protein determined at 1.9 Å resolution, that undergoes a pronounced pH‐ and cofactor‐driven reorganization. The structure crystallized in the orthorhombic P2 1 2 1 2 1 space group ( a = 44.8 Å, b = 46.3 Å, c = 101.2 Å), with one tetramer per asymmetric unit and refinement statistics of R fac / R free = 23.5/25.5%. The apo protein folds into a three‐stranded coiled coil, whereas heme binding under strongly basic conditions disrupts register‐specific interactions and drives a major helix shift. This transition yields a four‐stranded coiled coil with an out‐of‐register ABAB arrangement that accommodates two bis‐histidine‐ligated hemes. Cofactors are His‐coordinated via the ε‐nitrogen (Fe‐N His ≈ 2.0 Å), separated by 38 Å (tetrapyrroles edge‐to‐edge) and arranged nearly coplanar with a 67° rotation offset relative to one another. Imidazole dihedral angles (99° and 108°) indicate near‐orthogonal geometry for the His axial ligands to the heme. Crystallization is promoted by a heme‐templated packing in which interactions between macrocycles of neighboring assemblies and several salt‐bridges generate an extended supramolecular lattice. These results demonstrate how heme binding and proton concentration reshape oligomeric topology and promote ordered assembly in minimal protein systems, highlighting the varied structural effects of heme binding and providing principles for stabilizing specific coordination and exploiting cofactor–cofactor interactions to guide high‐order organization in de novo metalloproteins.

works.title: Author Correction: HERC4-mediated ubiquitination licenses RIPK1 to initiate TNF-induced cell death
works.abstract: Correction to: Nature Structural & Molecular Biology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41594-026-01871-y , published online 28 September 2026.

works.title: Conjugation of a Cell-Penetrating Peptide to the Lasso Peptides Citrocin and Microcin J25 Enhances Antimicrobial Activity
works.abstract: A subset of lasso peptides function as antibiotics against Gram-negative bacteria by inhibition of the bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP), including microcin J25 (MccJ25) and citrocin. These peptides interact with specific transporters in the inner and outer membranes of bacteria to gain access to the cytoplasm. The reliance on transporters limits the breadth of spectrum of these lasso peptide antibiotics and opens up paths to drug resistance. Here, we detail a strategy to overcome the transport limitations of lasso peptides: covalent conjugation of the lasso peptide to a cell penetrating peptide (CPP). Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP conjugates were synthesized by attaching the CPP to the loop of the lasso peptide and tested for antimicrobial activity against the ESKAPE pathogens. Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP have antimicrobial activity against all four Gram-negative ESKAPE pathogens, a broader spectrum of activity than the parent lasso peptides. Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP also exhibit more potent activity than the parent lasso peptides, with minimum inhibitory concentrations in the high nanomolar to single micromolar range. The uptake of citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP was also studied in Escherichia coli revealing that the conjugates are internalized via both transporter-dependent and transporter-independent pathways.

works.title: Slower Motions and Dramatic Conformational Populations Present in A:G Mismatched DNA Phosphates
works.abstract: Abstract Mismatches such as A:G base pairs arise in DNA primarily due to improper nucleotide incorporation during replication as well as formation of a heteroduplex. Repair of these mismatches and prevention of deleterious mutations is vital to an organism’s survival. Mismatch Repair (MMR) is the primary repair pathway for general DNA mismatches and follows replication to maintain genomic integrity; however, some details of mismatch recognition are unknown. Repair invariably requires precise and localized DNA–protein interactions and binding processes that depend on the specific properties, such as conformational structure and dynamics, of the repair protein and the damaged dsDNA substrate. Therefore, it is likely that the conformational properties of damaged, mismatched or modified DNAs will be different than canonical duplexed DNA. The work herein demonstrates a dramatic shift in time scale of motions and conformational populations for the phosphate flanking an A:G mismatched base pair. 31P NMR results show the motions are in the intermediate time scale (10–3 s), which is orders of magnitude slower than prior results (10–5–10–9 s), and the population of the BII substate shifts to ∼ 99%. These perturbations could be utilized in a phosphate tracking mechanism during indirect readout by repair enzymes such as MutS.

works.title: Distributed Structural Elements of DWORF Coordinate Activation of the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum Calcium Pump SERCA
works.abstract: Many physiological processes are controlled by changes in cytosolic calcium, including muscle contraction, neuronal transmission, and cell proliferation. In muscle, the sarco-endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA) restores resting cytosolic calcium by transporting calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, thereby promoting relaxation. In cardiac muscle, SERCA is regulated by phospholamban (PLN) and dwarf open reading frame (DWORF), which inhibit and activate SERCA, respectively. To investigate the mechanism of DWORF-mediated activation, we focused on Trp22, an unusual tryptophan residue positioned near the center of the DWORF transmembrane domain. This position resembles the recently identified transmembrane binding site for small-molecule SERCA activators, suggesting that Trp22 may play a direct role in activation. Consistent with this hypothesis, calcium-dependent ATPase measurements in reconstituted membranes showed that a Trp22-Ala substitution completely abolished SERCA activation. We next tested whether residues outside the central transmembrane region contribute to activation by modulating SERCA-DWORF interactions. Phosphomimetic substitutions at the N-terminal residues Ser7, Thr8, and Ser10 eliminated SERCA activation, suggesting that the N-terminus modulates DWORF positioning. More strikingly, substitutions within the C-terminal motif Tyr31, Val32, Phe34, and Ser35 profoundly altered function. Tyr31-Ala, Val32-Ala, and Phe34-Ala converted DWORF from an activator to an inhibitor, whereas Ser35-Ala and Ser35-Pro caused loss of activation. Together, these results support a coordinated mechanism in which Trp22 acts as a critical determinant of SERCA activation, the N-terminus provides the potential for reversible regulation, and the C-terminus constrains the DWORF transmembrane helix in an activation-competent state.

works.title: Broadening the Substrate Specificity of a Sugar Kinase to Span l - and d -Sugars for Coupled Activation Reactions
works.abstract: Abstract Sugar-1-phosphates are key intermediates in the synthesis of nucleotide sugars, which serve as essential building blocks for glycans from prokaryotes to eukaryotes. Compared to mammalian glycomes, those of microbes are enriched in deoxy l-sugars, many of which are activated as nucleotide β-l-sugars in the cell. The in vitro and cellular construction of many biologically relevant microbial polysaccharides, natural product glycoconjugates, surface glycoproteins, and antigens relies on nucleotide β-l-sugars. Yet, there remain few efficient chemical or biochemical routes toward the activated forms of these sugars or their sugar-1-phosphate starting materials. Here, we perform rational and unbiased engineering of the sugar kinase domain of the microbial l-fucose salvage enzyme FKP (Fucokinase/GDP-fucose pyrophosphorylase) and expand its substrate scope to span noncanonical l- and d-monosaccharides. We show that point mutations outside of the active site enable efficient phosphorylation of the prokaryote-specific sugar 6-deoxy-l-talose, and an active site mutation facilitates the phosphorylation of d-glucose. Coupling of FKP and its mutants with nucleotidyltransferases facilitates the production of diverse nucleotide sugars in one pot, highlighting facile in vitro methods to produce necessary starting materials that can be used in the enzymatic production of microbial and eukaryotic glycans.

works.title: Vitamin B 12 ‐Functionalized Nanogels for pH‐, and Redox‐Responsive Doxorubicin Delivery
works.abstract: Rapidly proliferating cancer cells display an elevated demand for vitamin B 12 , rendering this bacterial‐derived cofactor an attractive targeting motif for nanotherapeutic drug delivery. Herein, we report a concise two‐step synthesis of a polymerizable 5′‐modified vitamin B 12 ‐monomer that enables the covalent integration of B 12 into pH‐ and redox‐responsive nanogels. The resulting nanogels efficiently encapsulate doxorubicin through electrostatic interactions between the cationic drug and the anionic nanogel network, while enabling stimuli‐responsive drug release under tumor‐relevant conditions. In vitro studies revealed that DOX@B 12 ‐nanogels retain potent antiproliferative activity against HT‐29 colorectal cancer cells (IC 50 = 0.878 ± 0.102 μM), while decreasing cytotoxicity toward healthy CCD 841 CoN cells by 34‐fold relative to non‐B 12 ‐functionalized control nanogels. These findings establish covalently engineered vitamin B 12 ‐nanogels as a promising platform for selective and stimuli‐responsive anticancer drug delivery.

works.title: Violet Phosphorus Nanodots for Long‐Term Cell Imaging With Persistent Intracellular Stability
works.abstract: Long‐term cellular imaging probes with high photoluminescence intensity/stability and high biocompatibility are crucial for advanced in vitro cell imaging and long‐term cell tracing. However, conventional organic fluorescent dyes are prone to photobleaching and require assistance to enter cells. Here, NH 2 ‐PEG‐NH 2 was adopted to modify violet phosphorus quantum dots to obtain PEG‐VPNDs with strong and stable photoluminescence, where bond contacts were built between NH 2 ‐PEG‐NH 2 and phosphorus through P─N and P─O to keep robust structures. The PEG‐VPNDs have been demonstrated to have outstanding photoluminescence stability both in solution and intracellular environments. No photoluminescence decay was observed after 60 days of storage under ambient conditions or after continuous irradiation with a 300 W xenon lamp for 3 h, in contrast to the photobleaching observed in organic fluorescent dyes. The PEG‐VPNDs were also demonstrated to easily enter A2780 and SKOV3 cells and stay outside the nucleus without any assistance, where no decay was observed for photoluminescence of PEG‐VPNDs even for 96 h. The PEG‐VPNDs have been demonstrated to have high viability in A2780 and SKOV3 cells with concentration of 144 ppm. The photoluminescence performance with high intracellular stability and high biocompatibility makes PEG‐VPNDs a promising candidate for long‐term bioimaging, cell tracing and other biomedical applications.

works.title: A Biocompatible Cu(I)-Catalyzed Click Chemistry Framework for Long-Term Cell Tracking
works.abstract: Cellular immunotherapies have transformed oncologic treatment in recent years, yet the inability to monitor cell migration post-transfusion remains a significant barrier to their development. Here, we explore the feasibility of a non-invasive cell-tracking method utilizing Cu(I)-catalyzed click chemistry in which cells are first labeled with alkynes and, after 1-2 weeks, are selectively targeted via an azide-conjugated fluorescent probe. We developed Click1, a novel tris-Cu-chelating azide capable of a rapid, robust click reaction directly on live cell surfaces with minimal cytotoxicity. When paired with Click1, two distinct alkyne-labeling reagents, N-(4-pentynoyl)-mannosamine-tetraacylated (Ac4ManNAl) and propargyl choline, were capable of detecting human T cells for over two weeks. Our findings elucidate the metabolic turnover of biochemical handles in primary immune cells, providing a potential framework for long-term cell tracking in immunotherapies.

works.title: A Modular Optogenetic Split-Small GTPase Platform Reveals Long-Range RhoA Signaling
works.abstract: Small GTPases are critical regulators of cellular processes such as cell migration. However, no generalizable method exists for directly controlling their activity with subcellular precision, limiting the ability to dissect long-range signaling effects. To address this, we pair fragmented small GTPases with improved light-inducible dimerization (iLID) domains, optimizing for low dark-state background and efficient light-induced reassembly, affording spLIT-small GTPases. Demonstrating modularity, we control filopodia formation (spLIT-Cdc42), cell movement (spLIT-Rac1), and membrane retraction (spLIT-RhoA) with subcellular precision. Applying this platform to long-range signaling, we provide the first demonstration that localized RhoA activation is sufficient to drive membrane retraction at the opposite cell pole, with a directional dependence set by actin cytoskeleton polarization, a result inaccessible to global perturbations used previously. These results suggest a mechanism for coordinated establishment of cell polarity and highlight spLIT-small GTPases as a versatile platform for the direct, spatial control of small GTPase signaling in living cells.

works.title: A Comparative Biophysical Study of Conserved Ubiquitin-like Protein Folds
works.abstract: Ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like proteins (Ubls) constitute a conserved protein family that shares a common β-grasp structural fold despite substantial sequence and functional divergence. How this highly conserved fold is maintained while accommodating diverse biological functions remains an open question in protein structural biology. In this study, we provide atomistic insights into the structural features that determine the stability of these conserved ubiquitin-like folds. Using an integrated biophysical approach combining solution NMR spectroscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, and chemical denaturation experiments, we systematically compare the protein dynamics and thermodynamic stability of ubiquitin and representative Ubls, including SUMO1, SUMO2, NEDD8, and Hub1. Our results reveal that ubiquitin exhibits exceptional thermodynamic stability relative to other Ubls, whereas Ubls display a broad range of stability profiles without a uniform trend toward destabilization. Biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses show that the reduced stability of Ubls is not associated with the loss of the conserved fold but is accompanied by differences in local structural flexibility. Together, these findings indicate that the conserved ubiquitin fold has been maintained despite sequence divergence and variation in stability and dynamics, supporting functional diversity while preserving structural integrity.

works.title: From productive coupling to catalytic commitment: An evolutionarily tuned interdomain connector in Leishmania Aha1 orchestrates Hsp90 activation
works.abstract: Hsp90 activation depends on cochaperones that couple binding to catalytic commitment, yet some structural elements mediating this transition remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the molecular mechanism by which the cochaperone Aha1 from Leishmania braziliensis activates Hsp90 and present evidence supporting a linker-mediated disorder-to-order transition associated with this process. Thermodynamic analyses show that, while the Aha1 N-domain mediates Hsp90 binding, only the full-length Aha1 containing its wild-type interdomain linker exhibits a distinct enthalpy-dominated interaction and robust ATPase stimulation. Structural and kinetic measurements indicate that the wild-type linker modulates the conformational distribution of the Aha1 N-domain, promoting productive docking with Hsp90. Structural modeling suggests that the Aha1 linker adopts an α-helical conformation in the activated complex, whereas the corresponding synthetic linker peptide displays inducible helicity under structure-promoting conditions, consistent with a binding-coupled disorder-to-order transition. This transition appears evolutionarily tuned, as linker properties vary across species. Collectively, these findings support a model in which the Aha1 linker actively couples binding to activation, providing a new framework for Hsp90 regulation and highlighting a potential target for selective intervention in protozoan Aha1:Hsp90 systems.

works.title: Conserved IQ motifs, divergent apo‐calmodulin recognition in UBE3B and UBE3C
works.abstract: -free CaM (apo-CaM). The homologous to E6AP carboxyl terminus (HECT) E3 ubiquitin ligases ubiquitin protein ligase E3B (UBE3B) and ubiquitin protein ligase E3C (UBE3C) are closely related enzymes that both contain N-terminal IQ motifs, yet whether these motifs encode conserved modes of apo-CaM recognition has remained unclear. Here, we combined isothermal titration calorimetry, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and computational modeling to compare apo-CaM binding by the UBE3B and UBE3C IQ motifs. The UBE3B IQ motif bound apo-CaM with high affinity and preferentially engaged the CaM C-lobe, whereas the UBE3C IQ motif interacted more weakly under the same conditions. NMR titrations revealed distinct molecular recognition modes-UBE3B IQ binding occurred in slow exchange and produced a localized C-lobe interaction surface, while UBE3C IQ binding occurred in fast exchange and generated smaller, more distributed chemical shift perturbations. Structural models and molecular dynamics simulations provide a framework for interpreting these divergent apo-CaM engagement modes despite conservation of canonical IQ motif features. Phylogenetic analysis further suggests that the UBE3B and UBE3C IQ motifs have followed divergent evolutionary trajectories within the broader IQ motif family. Together, these findings show that conserved IQ motifs in related HECT ligases can encode different apo-CaM binding modes, providing a molecular basis for divergent CaM-mediated regulation of UBE3B and UBE3C.

works.title: Revealing protein structural transitions in the era of generative artificial intelligence
works.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and deep generative models have greatly accelerated the generation of protein conformational ensembles. Moving beyond isolated structural states to reconstruct continuous, physically realistic transition pathways further provides mechanistic understanding to guide molecular design but remains a significant challenge. This review examines emerging computational approaches for modeling protein conformational transitions, from classical molecular dynamics simulations to deep learning-based latent space interpolation. Recent developments in capturing natural molecular motions are discussed, particularly via internal coordinate representations and physics-informed models. We also examine the complexity of modeling highly dynamic systems, such as intrinsically disordered proteins, and the role of the cellular environment. Integrating experimental data with simulated structural ensembles represents a promising direction for future methodologies. Nonetheless, key challenges remain, including maintaining physical realism throughout transition trajectories, capturing environment-dependent energy landscapes, and predicting dynamically consistent pathways with accurate transition kinetics.

works.title: Dynamic residue–residue contact reorganization in protein allostery
works.abstract: Allostery is increasingly recognized as a transition-aware process in which local perturbations reshape conformational ensembles monitored by the reorganization of residue-residue contacts, leading to biased functions. This review highlights ensemble-comparison approaches to dissecting allosteric mechanisms, including those based on simulations, integration of simulation and experiment, and emerging machine learning-based predictions. These approaches provide mechanistic views of allostery that link ensemble redistribution to functional regulation. We argue that useful allosteric models should explain not only which residues connect distal sites but also which residue-residue contacts are reorganized, which regions respond cooperatively, and how these changes alter function. Understanding detailed allosteric mechanisms may help identify new allosteric pockets and guide the design of novel modulators to fine-tune biological processes for therapeutic benefit.

works.title: Editorial overview: Theory and Simulation/Computational Methods (2026): Combining simulations and machine learning to model the structure and dynamics of complex biomolecules
Neurotoxic effects of heavy metals on synaptic organization
Ultrafast MAS and Deuteration for High‐Resolution Proton Detected Solid‐State NMR of Intact Fungal Cell Walls
works.abstract: Glycans are the main components of the fungal cell wall and play a central role in fungal pathogenesis, making atomic‐level structural and dynamic insight into these biopolymers essential for the development of new antifungal therapeutics. 1 H‐detected solid‐state NMR (ssNMR) at fast magic‐angle spinning (MAS) offers an unprecedented opportunity to study glycan site, specifically at atomic resolution in intact fungal cell walls. However, the 1 H resolution and sensitivity in ssNMR are often limited for detailed studies, especially for rigid and highly heterogeneous samples, such as intact fungal cells. Here, we conducted a detailed study on 1 H line width and 1 H T ′ 2 coherence times in the rigid core of the human pathogenic Candida albicans fungal glycans at 60–150 kHz MAS rates and partial fungal cell wall deuteration schemes. We showcased the possibilities and limitations of 1 H‐detected multidimensional 1 H/ 13 C chemical shift assignment experiments for rigid cell wall glycans. Furthermore, we probed dynamics using relaxation measurements, providing access to motions spanning from nanoseconds to microseconds. Overall, we demonstrated significant methodological advances in 1 H‐detected ssNMR spectroscopy, achieving unprecedented 1 H resolution of rigid glycans in intact fungal cell walls. These developments could be applicable for ssNMR detailed studies of intact cell walls in other human pathogens.

works.title: Cytoplasmic Lipid Membrane Biogenesis in Prokaryotes: From Soluble Lipid Building Blocks to a Dynamic and Functional Boundary Layer
works.abstract: Prokaryotic membranes are fundamental to cellular organization and function, serving as dynamic platforms for transport, energy conservation, signaling, environmental adaptation, etc. This review provides an overview of prokaryotic membrane architecture, highlighting the structural diversity of bacterial and archaeal cell envelopes, focusing on the cytoplasmic membranes and the distinct lipid chemistries that define them. By describing the general pathways for fatty acid and phospholipid biosynthesis, we emphasize the universal role for the lipid intermediates lysophosphatidic acid and phosphatidic acid, as well as the major lipid species phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylglycerol, and cardiolipin of the diderm bacteria Escherichia coli. Besides synthesis, lipid membrane insertion is described, highlighting recent findings regarding lipid leaflet distribution, asymmetry, and intermembrane transport. Altogether, these processes provide a general overview of lipid composition and function of proliferating cells.

works.title: From Dysbiosis to Disease: How Vaginal Microbiota Shape Group B Streptococcus Pathogenesis
works.abstract: Host-microbe interactions refer to the dynamic relationships between hosts, such as humans, and the microorganisms present on or inside them. These associations can be beneficial, like gut bacteria facilitating digestion, or harmful, such as pathogens leading to disease. This review focuses on the reproductive tract, specifically the vaginal microbiome. Typically, a healthy vaginal microbiome is dominated by Lactobacillus species, which help protect against infections by pathogens. Dysbiosis, or a microbial imbalance, allows pathogens to invade. One such pathogen is Streptococcus agalactiae (group B Streptococcus, GBS), which can colonize the vaginal microbiome and cause infections. GBS infection during pregnancy is particularly concerning and is a major cause of adverse pregnancy outcomes. This review will explore host-microbe interactions in the vaginal microbiome, with an emphasis on GBS infection, its virulence, and current treatment strategies.

works.title: Putting the Warburg effect in reverse
Chemogenetic activation of mitochondria counteracts the Warburg effect in tumor cells
Characterization of Chromone Biosynthetic Pathway Reveals a Noncanonical Mode of Fungal Polyketide Cyclization
works.abstract: Fungal nonreducing polyketide synthases (NRPKSs) produce therapeutically and ecologically important aromatic polyketides. The product template (PT) domain of fungal NRPKSs catalyzes the regioselective aldol cyclization of the reactive poly-β-ketone chain during polyketide maturation and is essential for product fidelity of the NRPKSs. Herein, we discovered the fungal NRPKS MecA of which the polyketide cyclization steps do not involve a functional PT domain. MecA is encoded in the biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) responsible for the formation of 5-hydroxy-7-methoxy-2,3-dimethylchromone (1) from the biocontrol fungus Trichoderma afroharzianum T22. Heterologous expression and in vitro enzymatic assays fully established a biosynthetic pathway of 1 that involves three enzymes: MecA, dehydratase MecB, and methyltransferase MecC. The PT domain of MecA does not contain the conserved catalytic histidine that is essential for aldol cyclization activity. Consistent with the predicted inactive PT domain, MecA was demonstrated to catalyze a C1-C6 Claisen condensation as the first cyclization step of the pentaketide precursor, instead of the canonical aldol cyclization. Reconstitution of dissected MecA domains further demonstrated that the activity of MecA was not affected when the PT domain was removed. A Claisen Cyclase (CLC) domain that typically catalyzes Claisen cyclization in NRPKSs is also absent in MecA, implying the observed C1-C6 cyclization step is catalyzed by the remaining domains. This work contributes to the diversity of NRPKS cyclization chemistry and enables further genome mining and engineering of NRPKSs that may lead to biosynthesis of new aromatic polyketides.

works.title: Indirect Readout Drives Cre- loxP Recognition Thermodynamics
works.abstract: Cre, a site-specific tyrosine DNA recombinase, enables targeted manipulation of genetic material without the production of cytotoxic double-strand DNA breaks. Though widely deployed in biotechnology, an incomplete understanding of how Cre recognizes its cognate loxP target limits its broader application in human health. Cre is highly specific for its cognate loxP sites, comprising an inverted pair of recombinase binding elements (RBEs) and an asymmetric spacer. Structural studies have shown that Cre protomers make few direct base-specific contacts to each RBE, suggesting that specificity arises through indirect readout, wherein noncognate sites are unable to adopt favorable binding-coupled conformations. We designed a set of loxP half-site variants predicted to alter local DNA shape characteristics, including minor-groove geometry and base-step parameters, and measured the thermodynamics of Cre binding by isothermal titration calorimetry. Variable-temperature thermograms and nuclear magnetic resonance spectra reveal that unfavorable mutations at noncontacted positions in the RBE reduce signatures of binding-coupled conformational changes. Moreover, mass photometry of Cre binding to oligonucleotides containing two properly spaced RBEs revealed that noncontacted positions in the intervening 8-base pair spacer influence cooperative dimerization of two Cre protomers at loxP sites and their synapsis to form catalytically active Cre4-loxP2 complexes. These results demonstrate that noncontacted positions contribute to specificity by encoding favorable DNA mechanics, offering new design principles for engineering Cre variants that target alternative DNA sequences.

works.title: Histidine-51 Facilitates the Conformational Change and Deprotonation of Horse Liver Alcohol Dehydrogenase–NAD+ Complexes
works.abstract: Structural studies suggest that His-51 in wild-type horse liver alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH1E) facilitates proton transfer between the hydroxyl group of a ligand bound to the catalytic zinc and bulk solvent. Previous work showed that the Gln-51 substitution increases the pK values for pH dependencies for various enzymatic reactions by about 1.5 units, and stopped-flow studies on the binding of NAD+ and pyrazole suggested that the equilibrium position for the global conformational change of the enzyme-NAD+ complex became disfavored by 1000-fold. That conclusion needed confirmation. Here, X-ray crystallography of six ternary complexes of H51Q ADH with NAD+ and pyrazole, caprate, 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol, or 2,3,4,5,6-pentafluorobenzyl alcohol, and NADH and water or N-cyclohexylformamide shows that all complexes have the same closed conformation as wild-type ADH. Gln-51 fits in the region occupied by His-51 and does not affect the positions of bound coenzymes or inhibitors that coordinate to the catalytic zinc. Stopped-flow studies show that the rate-limiting formation of ternary complexes with H51Q ADH and NAD+ depends upon deprotonation of the ligands that bind to the catalytic zinc (pyrazole or 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol). Furthermore, the binding of NAD+ and trifluoroethanol monitored by fluorescence and proton release show that the H51Q substitution disfavors the conformational change by about 3-fold as compared to wild-type ADH. The pK values of the enzyme-NAD+ complexes with water and other zinc ligands increase because His-51 no longer facilitates the deprotonation. The roles of the zinc-water and His-51 in the mechanism are exposed.

works.title: Fuzzy Interactions Open Perspectives toward Drugging Conformational Heterogeneity
works.abstract: Abstract Fuzzy interactions enable specific biomolecular recognition while maintaining conformational freedom of the interacting partners. Here, we propose that fuzziness can be exploited for allosteric regulation to provide context-specific functional outputs. Using receptor signaling as an illustrative example, we demonstrate how heterogeneous binding modes with ligands can be fine-tuned through transient interactions. Fuzzy interactions interfere with alternative positions or modulate the mobility to mimic the landscapes of specific functional states that are linked with certain environmental conditions. Furthermore, using allosteric drugs targeting the ABL1 tyrosine kinase, KRAS oncogene, and IDH2 enzyme as examples, we demonstrate how fuzzy interaction mechanisms can affect allosteric couplings in a functionally meaningful manner through rewiring heterogeneous contact patterns. These notions could be helpful for drug development, targeting dynamic conformational ensembles and biasing them toward context-specific functional states.

works.title: Structure and Dynamics of Burkholderia pseudomallei OXA-57, a Distinctive Low-Efficiency Class D β-Lactamase with Carbapenem-Hydrolyzing Activity
works.abstract: The Gram-negative bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei causes the severe disease melioidosis. β-Lactams, including carbapenems, are the primary treatment for B. pseudomallei infections, but are susceptible to chromosomal serine β-lactamases (SBLs), including the class D enzyme OXA-57. Here we show that recombinant OXA-57 is active toward penicillins and first-generation cephalosporins, slowly hydrolyzes carbapenems, including imipenem and meropenem, but is inactive toward oxyimino-cephalosporins (e.g., ceftazidime). Unlike many OXA enzymes, OXA-57 is sensitive to the mechanism-based SBL inhibitor clavulanic acid, but less so to the diazabicyclooctane avibactam and not to the cyclic boronate vaborbactam. Crystal structures of covalent OXA-57:avibactam and OXA-57:meropenem complexes reveal limited hydrogen-bonding interactions with bound ligands. In molecular dynamics simulations, the bound meropenem acyl-enzyme is mobile, with the 6α-hydroxyethyl group able to sample different orientations, while the water molecule necessary for deacylation is bound only transiently. These observations are consistent with the low level of meropenem turnover, supporting proposals that limited carbapenemase activity is a general property of OXA β-lactamases, and highlight the potential importance of OXA-57 in B. pseudomallei β-lactam resistance.

works.title: Covalent Labeling of Human Neuroglobin with a 19F-Probe to Study its Conformational Changes Using 19F NMR
works.abstract: It is of interest to develop new approaches to probing protein conformational changes and protein-protein interactions. In this study, we covalently labeled human neuroglobin (Ngb) with a 19F-probe containing a Ph-OCF3 group at Cys120 and by introducing cysteine residues at specific positions in the C120S Ngb mutant. 19F NMR provides valuable insights into its conformational changes upon cleavage of the intramolecular disulfide bond of Cys46-Cys55, as well as its interactions with protein partners such as cytochrome c (Cyt c) through the formation of the Ngb-Cyt c complex. This study presents a convenient approach to investigating the dynamic properties of heme globins regulated by disulfide bonds and protein-protein interactions.

works.title: A guide to host genetic determinants of female microbiome composition across distinct anatomical niches
works.abstract: The female microbiome is a complex, dynamic and site-specific ecosystem that plays a vital role in maintaining host health, influencing immune regulation, metabolism, reproductive function and dermatological health. While significant attention has been directed towards modifiable lifestyle and environmental influences, host genetics, including inherited genetic variants in immune, cell signalling, metabolic, hormonal pathways and epithelial structure/barrier integrity, are increasingly recognised as contributors to microbial composition across distinct anatomical niches in individuals. It is theorised that these factors influence core microbial communities, predisposing individuals to dysbiosis or enhanced resilience against potential pathogens. This review integrates current evidence on how host genetics shape the female vaginal, gut, oral and skin microbiomes. By evaluating these influences across body sites, critical research gaps limiting our understanding of inherited microbe-host interactions and their contribution to disease susceptibility and persistence are identified. Addressing these gaps is essential for advancing insights into microbial composition and for informing personalised health strategies to identify populations contributing to greater risk of microbiome-associated negative health outcomes.

works.title: Architecture of the Norrin signaling complex and structure-guided surrogate design
Molecular control of bacterial immunity
Improving PROTAC-Mediated Degradation in Mouse Models: BRD9 as a Case Study
works.abstract: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) have emerged as powerful chemical tools and therapeutics, yet their translation from preclinical models to humans remains inconsistent. Here, we systematically evaluate the activity of BRD9-targeting PROTACs in human and mouse systems to elucidate a key limitation in preclinical studies. Widely used CRBN- and VHL-recruiting degraders, including dBRD9 and VZ185, exhibit markedly reduced potency in mouse cells despite high sequence conservation of BRD9. Mechanistic interrogation reveals that species-specific differences in E3 ligases, particularly the Crbn I391 residue and structural variations in VHL, likely impair productive ternary complex formation. Expression of human CRBN or VHL, or introduction of the CrbnI391V mutation, increases degradation potency in mouse cells. Importantly, in vivo studies demonstrate enhanced BRD9 degradation in CrbnI391V mice using clinically relevant degraders. These findings highlight a critical barrier in PROTAC evaluation and establish humanized E3 ligase models as tools for more accurate assessment of on-target efficacy and toxicity.

works.title: What Computational Simulations Tell Us about Cryptochromes in Magnetoreception
works.abstract: The ability of migratory birds to orient using the Earth's magnetic field has been proposed to rely on a radical-pair mechanism operating within Cryptochrome 4, a blue-light flavoprotein. In this perspective, we review how computational approaches have shaped our molecular understanding of cryptochrome-based magnetoreception. We organize the discussion around the three steps that connect light absorption to a cellular signal: the photochemical step, in which light absorption by FAD drives a hole-hopping electron-transfer cascade along a conserved tryptophan tetrad; the spin-dependent step, in which the resulting radical pair interconverts between singlet and triplet states under the influence of the magnetic field; and the structural step, in which this transient information is converted into a long-lived signaling state. The early electron-transfer events are now described with growing confidence and appear conserved across avian orthologs, although the relative stability of the final radical-pair states remains debated. The spin-dependent step remains more problematic: once the fluctuations of the hyperfine couplings and a realistic number of nuclear spins are included, the predicted magnetic sensitivity at geomagnetic field intensities becomes very small, and explaining the magnitude of the effect is still a central open problem. The postactivation conformational dynamics, involving intrinsically disordered regions, remains the principal challenge. We suggest that atomistic multiscale modeling, integrated with artificial intelligence-based approaches, has become indispensable for connecting the conserved photochemistry to this downstream process.

works.title: Biocatalytic synthesis of S ‐adenosyl‐ l ‐methionine analogues for allosteric activation of cystathionine‐β‐synthase
works.abstract: Cystathionine-β-synthase (CBS) is the key regulatory enzyme of the transsulfuration pathway and plays a crucial role in eliminating homocysteine. Homocysteine, a by-product of methylation reactions, is a known risk factor for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders, all of which are among the leading causes of death worldwide. CBS represents a promising therapeutic target due to its allosterically inducible capacity to redirect homocysteine into sulfur metabolism, yielding the protective antioxidants cysteine, hydrogen sulfide and glutathione. Although the therapeutic benefit of CBS activation was established more than a decade ago, there are as yet no drug-like small-molecule allosteric activators of CBS. Therefore, we establish a framework for the development of CBS activators. Starting from S-adenosyl-l-methionine (SAM), the endogenous allosteric activator of CBS as a template, we rationally designed 15 analogues and synthesized them using biocatalysis. We characterized their action on isolated recombinant human CBS and cell lysate and their metabolic breakdown in DNA methylation. Besides SAM, three analogues enhanced the catalytic activity of CBS and stabilized CBS during thermal denaturation, suggesting binding. Thermodynamic parameters were quantified using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). All active compounds participated in the methylation of lambda DNA. We confirmed S-adenosyl-l-ethionine, an established CBS activator, and seleno-adenosyl-l-methionine, recently reported by us. Additionally, we introduce a novel CBS activator, S-2-amino-adenosyl-l-methionine. Taken together, CBS allosteric activation required compounds that do not deviate far from the structure of SAM. Nevertheless, we discovered a new allosteric activator of CBS and propose that our work represents a structural framework for further development of small-molecule activators of CBS.

works.title: Structural features of ZAK kinase regulation at the ribosome
works.abstract: ZAKα is a MAP3K that interacts with ribosomes and autophosphorylates upon widespread ribosome collisions mediating the ribotoxic stress response pathway. While activation of ZAKα determines downstream cell fate outcomes such as cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, the exact nature of ribosome binding and the mechanism of activation have not been fully understood. Our recent cryo-EM structures contribute to bridging this gap by visualizing ZAKα bound to ribosomes in various states (hibernating, translating, and colliding) providing a clear molecular blueprint for ZAKα kinase regulation at the ribosome.

works.title: Spermine is an endogenous small‐molecule 20S proteasome activator synergistically coupling chymotrypsin‐like active‐site modulation with α‐ring gate opening
works.abstract: The biogenic polyamine spermine accumulates to millimolar concentrations in proliferating cells, yet its direct effect on the 20S proteasome ( EC3.4.25.1 ) has remained mechanistically obscure. Here, we show that spermine directly binds and activates the human 20S proteasome through two mechanistically distinct, kinetically separable events. At low millimolar concentrations, spermine selectively stimulates the chymotrypsin‐like β5 site up to 14‐fold over the basal rate, whereas above ~1.7 m m it triggers a highly cooperative (Hill n = 8) opening of the α‐ring channel that additionally engages the trypsin‐ and caspase‐like sites. Simultaneous occupancy of both regions generates a hybrid enzyme form for which the catalytic constant is super‐additive, 163‐fold over k cat . The α‐ring transition is intrinsically slow, with channels reaching only 44% of equilibrium opening within the first 5 min. Abolition of this hysteresis by SDS or by PA28αβ preloading confirms that gate opening is the rate‐limiting step. The combination of a high cooperative threshold ( K ch ~ 1.7 m m ) and slow gating kinetics defines a kinetic filter that allows the proteasome to respond selectively to sustained elevations of free polyamines, such as those characteristic of proliferating and malignant cells, while remaining insensitive to transient metabolic fluctuations. Finally, we show that spermine enhances hydrolysis of unfolded substrates by the 20S proteasome in vitro and in mammalian cells. Spermine thus emerges as the first endogenous small‐molecule activator that engages both the catalytic and gating layers of 20S regulation, linking polyamine metabolism directly to proteolytic capacity.

works.title: Mitochondrial iron homeostasis is required for azole tolerance in Candida albicans
works.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is an escalating global concern with the human fungal pathogen, Candida albicans, increasingly exhibiting resistance to fluconazole (FLC). Together with the high mortality associated with bloodstream infections, this growing resistance contributed to the classification of C. albicans as a critical priority pathogen by the World Health Organisation (WHO). Notably, C. albicans can survive high concentrations of fluconazole (FLC) through a phenomenon termed tolerance, which is different from resistance as tolerant cells grow slowly. Tolerance is considered a precursor to resistance development. Previous work from our laboratory demonstrated that intracellular iron homeostasis, particularly the mobilisation of vacuolar iron stores, modulates the synergistic interaction between doxycycline, an iron chelator, and FLC. Building on this, we hypothesised that mitochondrial iron plays a central role in determining FLC susceptibility, supported by emerging links between mitochondrial function, iron metabolism, and azole response. Mitochondrial iron import is mediated by MRS4, after which iron is primarily incorporated into iron-sulfur clusters and haem. Here, we investigated the role of mitochondrial iron import via MRS4 in azole susceptibility phenotypes, including tolerance, synergy and cidality. We demonstrate that MRS4 is essential for FLC tolerance under iron-chelating conditions, despite minimal effects on minimal inhibitory concentration or drug synergy. Absence of MRS4 results in mitochondrial dysfunction and accumulation of toxic sterol intermediates during FLC treatment. Collectively, our findings reveal that mitochondrial iron homeostasis critically governs azole tolerance and highlights toxic sterol accumulation as a driver of fungicidal outcomes.

works.title: Automated reconstruction of reproducible protein databases with RepDBmaker
works.abstract: RepDBmaker is a reproducible Snakemake pipeline designed for the automated construction of large-scale protein sequence databases. It enables the seamless downloading of sequences from different public databases and the integration of user-specified proteomes. The pipeline also performs standardized taxonomic annotations to all compiled sequences and contamination screening in eukaryotic proteomes. In addition, RepDBmaker generates queryable database files for Basic Local Alignment Search Tool Program (BLASTP), DIAMOND, and MMseqs2, with the option of taxonomy-aware sequence clustering to produce less redundant datasets. To showcase its utility, we used RepDBmaker to build a Tree-of-Life-scale database comprising 482 million protein sequences from 160,045 publicly available genomes and transcriptomes. RepDBmaker offers an off-the-shelf but customizable solution for researchers undertaking large-scale evolutionary projects that require extensive, well-annotated protein databases. The pipeline is available at https://github.com/Gabaldonlab/RepDBmaker.

works.title: Mechanism of M18BP1-mediated activation of condensin II for mitotic DNA compaction
works.abstract: DNA compaction by human condensin II is crucial for the correct organization of mitotic chromosomes. Mitotic activation of condensin II is a multilayered process, controlled mainly by the opposing activity of the MCPH1 and M18BP1 proteins, acting as an interphase inhibitor and a mitotic activator, respectively. Mitotic phosphorylation favors M18BP1 binding to condensin II, resulting in effective and timely chromosome compaction. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying condensin II activation in driving DNA compaction remain uncharacterized. Here, combining cryo-electron microscopy with single-molecule imaging, we unravel the mechanism of condensin II activation by M18BP1 and elucidate their role in DNA compaction. The specific interaction with phosphorylated M18BP1 induces conformational changes in the condensin II complex, relieving an autoinhibitory conformation and allowing stable DNA binding and DNA compaction. Beyond the activity of isolated condensin II complexes on DNA, we observe the emergence of multimeric species that withstand the forces applied by optical tweezers, suggesting that condensin II multimerization might contribute to the mechanical reinforcement of mitotic chromosomes. Here, the authors show that phosphorylated M18BP1 activates condensin II by relieving an autoinhibitory interface, enabling stable DNA binding and compaction. Additionally, the M18BP1–condensin II complex forms clusters that might mechanically reinforce mitotic chromosomes.
