works.abstract: -(5-phospho-β-d-ribosyl)-ATP with the release of inorganic pyrophosphate. L-Histidine allosterically inhibits ATPPRT as a mechanism to regulate this energy-intensive pathway in histidine-synthesising organisms, such as bacteria, archaea and plants. Absent in humans and essential in many disease-causing bacteria, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Acinetobacter baumannii, ATPPRT is a promising drug target for novel antibiotic development. Furthermore, ATPPRT is a target of synthetic biology efforts to maximise L-histidine production in bacteria. Here we provide a brief overview of allosteric concepts and review the structure, catalysis and allosteric mechanism of bacterial ATPPRTs, which exist in two forms in nature, a long and a short form. We highlight recent findings on ATPPRT catalysis, allosteric regulation, inhibition and activation, discuss open questions in the field, and possible industrial and biomedical applications.

works.title: Brief encounters and lasting impressions—How target protein half‐life affects reactive metabolite signaling
works.abstract: Cellular stress signaling conveys vital messages to the cell's machinery to respond dynamically to internal and external environmental cues. One prevailing hypothesis for such signaling is to bring about crucial downstream functional changes in the cell's ability to withstand intra- and extra-cellular stress, as exemplified by the NRF2-ARE pathway. Reactive electrophilic metabolites (REMs)-exemplified by the lipid-derived electrophile, 4-hydroxynonenal-are often generated from membrane lipids or respiratory metabolites in inflammatory and stress signaling contexts. REMs harbor an innate ability to irreversibly bind protein-cysteines and form DNA and RNA adducts. Our work has led us to propose a new hypothesis regarding the role of locale-specific REM build-up in stress signaling; whereby, they can label both the majority stable protein residents in a given locale and the minority guests transiently existing within a subcellular compartment at a kinetically significant rate to trigger a 'gain of function' signaling cascade. Much like the NRF2 signaling pathway, such downstream signaling messages could assist the cell's ability to survive against microenvironment-specific stress and adapt on demand. As REMs accumulate in several disease-specific cells, especially age-related disorders such as cancer and neurodegeneration, understanding the functional signal propagation mechanisms shaped by specific REMs engaging with specific biomolecular targets will prove vital for future therapeutic interventions with enhanced precision and context.

works.title: Dark energy: the cost of function in protein evolution
Beyond structural cycles: computational mechanisms of biomolecular machines
Characterization and Crystal Structure Elucidation of the l ‐Homoserine O ‐Succinyltransferase MetXS From Cupriavidus necator H16
works.abstract: Among the promising microbial platforms to produce value‐added products from CO 2 , chemolithoautotrophic bacteria, such as Cupriavidus necator H16 ( C. necator ), stand out due to their ability to fix CO 2 via the Calvin–Benson–Bassham (CBB) cycle. Although C. necator has been extensively studied as a biotechnological production host, several of its biosynthetic pathways remain incompletely characterized at the biochemical level. This includes l ‐methionine biosynthesis, for which genome‐based functional annotations of key enzymes have not been validated experimentally. In this study, we identified and characterized Cn MetXS, a homoserine O ‐succinyltransferase involved in l ‐methionine biosynthesis in C. necator . Biochemical characterization demonstrated that Cn MetXS catalyzes the transsuccinylation of l ‐homoserine to O ‐succinyl‐ l ‐homoserine but exhibits no transacetylase activity. Additionally, we determined the apo crystal structure of Cn MetXS at 1.86 Å resolution, revealing a homodimer with a MetX‐G2 active‐site architecture and distinct conformations of the active‐site lid region. Structural analysis and docking suggest that Arg335 stabilizes the succinylated enzyme intermediate and explains the observed succinyl‐CoA specificity. Together, these results establish the function of Cn MetXS and pave the way for metabolic engineering strategies to produce l ‐methionine in C. necator .

works.title: Investigation of the DSF/Cu Reaction Using HR LCMS and Reactivity Studies
works.abstract: Cuprotosis is a unique mode of cell death being explored in many new therapeutic anticancer studies. A widely used approach is the combination of Cu(II) salts with diethyldithiocarbamate disulfide, disulfiram (DSF), also known as the alcohol‐sensitizing drug Antabuse, which generates the toxic Cu(II)bis(diethyldithiocarbamate), Cu(DTC) 2 , in a complex redox reaction. The mechanism for the generation of Cu(DTC) 2 in this reaction, which we term the DSF/Cu reaction, has been examined using high‐resolution liquid chromatography‐mass spectroscopy (HR LCMS) by monitoring the reaction at different sampling times to determine sequential speciation of reaction intermediates. Other intermediates of this reaction are characterized by the addition of adduct‐forming “traps” used to characterize thiol and sulfenic acid species generated throughout the reaction. The time‐resolved spectra reveal that one initial reaction is a 2‐electron oxidation of a thione moiety in DSF to a sulfine (DSF‐O), which implies a concurrent reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(0). Other results suggest the involvement of Cu(I) in the titled reaction, most likely formed by comproportionation of Cu(0) with Cu(II) in the MeCN/H 2 O solutions used. Additional intermediate products indicate a variety of sulfur oxidation, hydrolysis, and insertion/extrusion reactions forming species that also feed into pathways generating Cu(DTC) 2 .

works.title: Discovery and Engineering of a Flavin‐Containing Monooxygenase From Bradyrhizobium sp. 200 for the Asymmetric Synthesis of an Indoxacarb Intermediate
works.abstract: Indoxacarb is an oxadiazine insecticide bearing a single stereogenic center, of which only the ( S )‐enantiomer exhibits insecticidal activity. Therefore, the synthesis of the key intermediate ( S )‐5‐chloro‐2‐methoxycarbonyl‐2‐hydroxy‐1‐indanone ( 2 ) is crucial for the enantioselective total synthesis of Indoxacarb. In this study, a flavin‐containing monooxygenase from Bradyrhizobium sp. 200 ( Bj FMO) was employed for the asymmetric synthesis of this chiral intermediate, offering a biocatalytic approach as a potential complement to conventional chemical routes. Based on molecular docking and sequence alignment, several amino acid residues located in the FAD and NADPH‐binding domains were selected for site‐saturation mutagenesis. In combination with rational design, additional positions potentially affecting catalytic activity and stability were subjected to site‐directed mutagenesis. Beneficial single mutations were iteratively combined to generate the final variant, Bj FMO M9 . Under optimal conditions, Bj FMO M9 displayed a twofold increase in specific activity compared with the wild type. Its half‐life at 40 °C was extended from 1.3 to 3.0 h, and its tolerance toward isopropanol, ethanol, and acetone was markedly enhanced. In a preparative synthesis, Bj FMO M9 consistently outperformed the wild type, achieving >80% conversion within 10 h and >90% ee for the ( S )‐product.

works.title: Affinity Engineering Modulates Soluble Antigen Degrader Activity
works.abstract: Soluble extracellular proteins drive many physiological and pathological signaling pathways, and targeted degradation offers a potential strategy for their therapeutic modulation. Here, we engineered bispecific targeting chimeras (TACs) that couple soluble proteins to constitutively internalizing cell-surface effectors for clearance. Using transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) as an initial effector, we find that uptake depends on both binding arms. Rapid target association facilitates extracellular antigen capture, while increased intracellular dissociation can improve uptake when overall binding strength is maintained. Introducing pH-sensitive target binders enhances internalization, but only when neutral-pH affinity remains high. We also find that atypical chemokine receptor 5 (ACKR5) can serve as an alternative internalizing effector. Applying these principles to tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), an optimized TAC more effectively inhibits its signaling than FDA-approved anti-TNF-α therapy adalimumab. These findings identified molecular determinants for engineering TACs targeting soluble extracellular proteins.

works.title: Isolation of Tritonicysteinolic Acid From a Marine Bacterium and Its Evaluation as a PGAM5 Inhibitor
works.abstract: The new sulfolipid-like natural product tritonicysteinolic acid (TTC) was isolated from an extract of the marine bacterium Tritonibacter and exhibited inhibitory activity against PGAM5, a protein phosphatase that localizes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The full stereochemistry of TTC was elucidated through total synthesis, thereby enabling the synthesis of various derivatives. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) studies were conducted, which revealed that the derivatives exhibited higher inhibitory activity against PGAM5 phosphatase relative to the parent natural product.

works.title: Alkyl Chain‐Functionalized Nitronyl Nitroxide Radicals: Structure‐Microenvironment Effects on Thiol Kinetics and Dual Antioxidant Behavior
works.abstract: Radical reactivity can be modulated through structural and microenvironmental control, thereby representing an important challenge in the design of redox-active systems. In this study, an alkyl chain-functionalized series of nitronyl nitroxide (NN) radicals designed and synthesized by varying their amphiphilic character. Subsequently, their thiol-based reactivity and microenvironment accessibility, along with antioxidant profile, were investigated. Radical behavior was monitored in aqueous media and sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) micelles. Accessibility properties and micellar partitioning of all radicals were evaluated in a concentration-dependent manner, using electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR). Glutathione (GSH) reactivity and quantitative EPR kinetic analysis revealed that the reduction rate constants systematically decrease with increasing alkyl chain length, leading to the formation of diamagnetic hydroxylamine species. In the presence of SDS, the reactivity of NN derivatives with GSH was dramatically suppressed, confirming the protection of the nitroxide center from thiol reduction. The NN-functionalized derivatives displayed a dual antioxidant mechanism, based on electron transfer and hydrogen atom transfer (HAT). The limited superoxide scavenging and pro-oxidant effects indicated radical-specific selectivity under single-electron transfer (SET) conditions. Notably, all derivatives exhibited pronounced inhibition of lipid peroxidation, confirming their effectiveness in chain-breaking antioxidant activity and rendering them competitive agents in targeted therapeutics and stress-based pathologies.

works.title: A DNA Platform‐Assisted Cooperative Probe Addresses the Affinity–Selectivity Trade‐Off in Hybridization‐Based Nucleic Acid Detection at Room Temperature
works.abstract: Hybridization-based nucleic acid detection remains central to molecular diagnostics but is often limited by slow kinetics, diminished sensitivity toward structured or double-stranded targets and low selectivity in recognizing single-nucleotide variation (SNV) at ambient temperatures. Here we introduce a DNA platform-assisted cooperative probe (PCP) that enhances the performance of conventional molecular beacon (MB) probes through cooperative analyte binding mediated by a DNA scaffold. The PCP architecture spatially organizes two analyte-binding arms (F and U) on a dsDNA platform for cooperative tight binding of nucleic acid analytes, which enables the use of a short platform-detached strand m for highly selective SNV recognition. Using clinically relevant targets from Mycoplasma genitalium (23S rRNA fragment) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (penA gene fragment), we demonstrate that PCP improves SNV selectivity from 10% to 14% for MB probe up to 99%, and lowers the limit of detection by up to an order of magnitude but does not significantly improve hybridization rate. The PCP sensor further enables room-temperature detection of double-stranded polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplicons. These results establish DNA platform-based probe organization as an advantageous strategy to resolve the affinity/specificity trade-off in hybridization-based diagnostics.

works.title: Being N sync
Sensing red light
Reduction reporter
Finding signal in the noise
Let’s degrade
Developing phenylalanine decaging
Thermophilic Adaptation of a Minimal Hammerhead Ribozyme Comes with a Functional Penalty
works.abstract: Life has adapted to extreme environments, such as elevated pH, extreme temperatures, and environments with a lack of oxygen. The biomolecules made by organisms that live in extreme environments must adapt to remain folded and functional. Recent computational studies have shown that rRNA, tRNA, and certain mRNAs adapt in thermophilic organisms through an increased GC content. However, few previous studies have assessed the efficiency of adapted thermophilic RNAs. The work presented herein uses minimal hammerhead ribozymes as a model system to determine the effects of high-temperature adaptation, through increased GC base pairing in the ribozyme secondary structure. Two hammerhead ribozymes were designed based upon the minimal hammerhead 16 (HH16) ribozyme, a well-characterized model system. The mesophilic ribozyme has a moderate GC content (44%) in stems I, II, and III, while the thermophilic ribozyme has nearly double the GC content (76%) in those same stems. Both ribozymes share a conserved catalytic core and loop. Thermal denaturation experiments show that the model thermophilic ribozyme is more thermostable with a higher single (cooperative) melting temperature than the model mesophilic ribozyme. However, thermostability is accompanied by a functional penalty. While at certain temperatures, the thermophilic ribozyme reaches the lower observed rates of the mesophilic ribozyme, the thermophilic ribozyme never reaches the same maximal rate of catalysis as the mesophilic ribozyme.

works.title: Beyond the Active Site: Allosteric Tail of HIV-1 Protease Is a Potential Target for Inhibiting Dimerization
works.abstract: HIV protease (HIVPR) is one of the key targets in AIDS therapy. All ten FDA-approved drugs targeting this enzyme compete with the substrates in binding to its active site. However, the emergence of drug-resistant mutants in active and nonactive sites of HIVPR has compromised the efficacy of these drugs. Nonetheless, darunavir (DRV) and tipranavir (TPV) have exhibited greater success than the other eight drugs, presumably due to their dual mode of action: (i) inhibiting protease activity and (ii) blocking protease dimerization. Although crystal structures have explained the inhibitory mechanism of protease activity, the mechanism of inhibiting the dimerization process is poorly understood. In this study, we employ advanced molecular dynamics simulation methods to identify the precise binding motifs of DRV and TPV with monomeric HIVPR. Our results suggest that both inhibitors bind stably to an allosteric pocket located in the tail region of the enzyme. Results also elucidate reversible association-dissociation of the drugs between the conventional active site and the newly identified tail cavity through surface diffusion. Structural analysis revealed that drug binding to the tail pocket induces a conformational extension of the C-terminal α-helix, a change that sequesters the terminal residues required for stable dimer formation. Our finding aligns very well with the reported ESI-MS spectra showing the tail interface as a crucial domain in forming a stable HIV protease dimer. Our result paves the way for designing a new class of HIVPR drugs that could target the C-terminal to effectively lock it in the monomeric form, potentially bypassing the cross-resistance due to active-site mutations.

works.title: No lysine? No problem: the surprising roles of WNK kinases in physiology and disease
works.abstract: WNK (With No lysine K) protein kinases gained early attention because gain-of-function mutations in genes encoding two of them cause hypertension. They differ from other kinases due to the unusual location of the catalytic lysine, hence the name WNK. These kinases control many aspects of ion transport in the kidney and are essential for development and maintenance of the cardiovascular system. In the present review, we describe WNK proteins and selected substrates, in particular, the kinases oxidative stress-responsive kinase 1 and SPS1-related proline/alanine-rich kinase, and their regulation. We spotlight findings that emphasize the broad relevance of WNKs in normal physiology and disease. Our overview focuses on basic aspects of ion transport that occur in many cell types and tissues, functions in the endothelial system, interactions with insulin-dependent and metabolic pathways, the importance in the brain in part through controlling chloride ion balance, and the whirlwind of findings in cancer that reveal how WNK signaling can be repurposed. Other actions that may be of equal importance, e.g., influences on the immune system, are touched on only briefly. We also note a few genome-wide association studies that have uncovered multiple SNPs in genes encoding WNKs and downstream effectors in an array of diseases, in anticipation of more to come in the future.

works.title: Chemical and Genetically Encoded Strategies for Spatiotemporal Control of Lipid Generation in Living Cells
works.abstract: Mammalian cells synthesize thousands of distinct lipids, and lipid metabolism fundamentally influences signaling in both homeostatic and disease states. Despite considerable interest in the biological functions of diverse lipid species, direct study of their effects in biological systems has historically been limited by a lack of methods to modulate discrete lipid species with precise spatiotemporal control. Several efforts in lipid chemical biology focus on the development of technologies to generate individual lipid species with spatial and temporal control in living cells. Emerging strategies are enabling the on-demand generation of lipids in response to various stimuli. In this Perspective, we discuss three mechanistic approaches for controlled lipid generation: light-triggered production of lipids from modified precursors, orthogonal chemical release, and triggerable chemoenzymatic or genetically encoded enzymatic generation of lipids. We highlight the strengths and weaknesses of each platform, and we outline the design strategies that will shape the next generation of tools.

works.title: Beyond the obvious pocket
Tryptoline stereoprobe elaboration identifies inhibitors of the GRPEL1–HSPA9 complex
works.abstract: Activity-based protein profiling has identified hundreds of human proteins from diverse classes that react at cysteine residues with stereochemically defined electrophilic compounds (stereoprobes). The structure-activity relationships underlying these stereoprobe-protein interactions, however, remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the protein interaction landscape of tryptoline acrylamide stereoprobes can be profoundly altered by structural modifications distal to the acrylamide reactive group. Most stereoprobe liganding events occurred at nonorthosteric sites and evaded assignment by the machine learning-based cofolding model Boltz-2, which instead tended to misplace stereoprobes in orthosteric pockets (an outcome we term 'orthostery burnout'). We found that stereoprobes reacting with C124 in the nucleotide exchange factor GRPEL1 disrupt interactions with the mitochondrial HSP70 chaperone HSPA9/mortalin, leading to impairments in mitochondrial protein import and mitophagy induction. Our results highlight tryptoline acrylamides as a versatile source of covalent ligands targeting nonorthosteric sites on proteins, including tool compounds that perturb the mitochondrial HSP70 chaperone system.

works.title: Issue Editorial Masthead
Issue Publication Information
Randomization of the Damaged Base-Capping Loop Rewires Substrate Specificity in Formamidopyrimidine–DNA Glycosylase
works.abstract: Formamidopyrimidine-DNA glycosylase (Fpg) is a bacterial base excision repair enzyme that removes 8-oxoguanine (8-oxoG) and some other oxidatively damaged nucleobases from DNA. Fpg hydrolyzes the N-glycosidic bond of the damaged nucleotide and nicks DNA at the resulting apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site by β-elimination. Together with bacterial endonuclease VIII and eukaryotic homologues, more specific for damaged pyrimidines, Fpg belongs to a helix-two-turn-helix (H2TH) superfamily of DNA glycosylases. Crystal structures of Fpg reveal that the enzyme recognizes 8-oxoG by flipping it out of the DNA duplex and capping it with a flexible tetrapeptide loop. However, this loop is poorly conserved and contacts 8-oxoG only through the main-chain amides, raising questions about the enzyme specificity determinants. To clarify the mechanism of 8-oxoG recognition, we have produced and characterized five variants of Fpg from Lactococcus lactis with a randomized capping loop. All of these mutants were deficient in 8-oxoG repair, both in vitro and in the E. coli complementation assay, yet retained the ability to bind AP site-containing DNA, form a Schiff base covalent reaction intermediate, and catalyze β-elimination. The mutants were still active in the removal of 5-hydroxyuracil (OHU), an alternative Fpg substrate. All loop mutants showed relaxed opposite-base specificity, processing AP sites and OHU opposite either C or A. Thus, whereas the general architecture of the active site in H2TH DNA glycosylases is permissive for the excision of a wide range of oxidized bases, the capping loop endows Fpg with the specificity for its biologically relevant substrate, 8-oxoguanine.

works.title: Mapping Ligand-Induced Conformational Changes during the Enzymatic Cycle of Human Geranylgeranyl Diphosphate Synthase
works.abstract: Geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGDPS) catalyzes the condensation reaction between two isoprenoid substrates: farnesyl diphosphate (FDP) and isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), to form geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGDP). Due to the flexible nature of the GGDPS active site and its capacity to bind multiple ligands during the reaction coordinate, understanding the structural changes that enable it to accommodate different ligands and catalyze the reaction is essential. While structures exist of substrate and product-bound GGDPS, a lack of high-resolution apo or Mg2+-only structures prevents complete understanding of the enzyme active site. Here, we report apo and Mg2+-only structures of human GGDPS, investigating the key differences between them and published GGDPS structures relating to the enzymatic cycle. A crystal structure resolved to 1.82 Å, the highest-resolution structure of human GGDPS to date, contains five product-bound subunits and one Mg2+-only subunit. The first cryo-EM structure of apo GGDPS is also reported, which exhibited an open hexamer conformation. Comparing the Mg2+-only and apo structures shows that the active site is posed and ready to bind Mg2+ without significant conformational changes. Comparing Mg2+-only to structures with either of the substrates or product bound, we observe changes in residues that actively obstruct or encourage the binding of certain ligands. We also propose an enzymatic mechanism for the structural states of GGDPS and highlight the possibility of Asp188 as the general base in the condensation reaction. These findings enhance our understanding of GGDPS ligand binding, which will improve the knowledge base for rational, structure-based design of future GGDPS inhibitors.

works.title: The GndA Microprotein Promotes Cell Growth during Heat Shock in Escherichia coli
works.abstract: Hundreds of bacterial small open reading frames (sORFs) encoding microproteins of fewer than 50 amino acids have recently been identified. Biological functions have been ascribed to an increasing number of microproteins, some of which play roles in bacterial stress responses. In this work, we provide evidence that GndA, a frameshifted 36-amino acid microprotein encoded in an internal open reading frame overlapping the 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (6PGD) coding sequence (CDS), functions in the response to heat shock. We demonstrate independent contributions of GndA and 6PGD to cell growth at a high temperature. GndA is hydrophobic and associates with the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and the inner membrane. Consistent with a role in cellular homeostasis, GndA mutations alter the transcriptional response to heat shock. These results demonstrate that GndA promotes bacterial cell growth at high temperatures independently of the 6PGD protein that it overlaps. GndA thus expands the paradigm of bacterial microproteins that function in cellular stress responses.

works.title: Single Staphylococcus aureus SauUSI restriction enzyme motors fragment methylated DNA
works.abstract: SauUSI is a dimeric, ATP-dependent type IV restriction enzyme that protects Staphylococcus aureus by cleaving nonself DNA containing 5-methylcytosine or 5-hydroxymethylcytosine. Using biophysical, single-molecule and nanopore sequencing methods, we show that 5-methylcytosine recognition first induces ATP-driven unidirectional translocation by one helicase-like subunit, displacing its target recognition domain (TRD). In half of events, the partner TRD can then bind the liberated modified site, stabilizing a growing DNA loop. On symmetrically methylated DNA, looping is more frequent and both motors can engage in bidirectional loop translocation. Cleavage occurs stochastically throughout translocation but events that increase dwell time such as rebinding methylated sites elevate the chance of cleavage. Interactions with other SauUSI dimers or protein roadblocks influence cleavage distributions but are not required for nuclease activation. While the first cleavages principally generate 1-nt 3' overhangs or blunt ends, multiple binding-translocation-cleavage cycles by individual enzymes ultimately fragment the modified nonself DNA, neutralizing its threat.

works.title: Short-term methionine starvation reshapes diurnal hepatic m6A RNA methylation
works.abstract: Dietary methionine restriction improves metabolic health and has therapeutic potential in multiple disease contexts. Methionine metabolism regulates transmethylation reactions, including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation, by modulating availability of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM). Both m6A methylation and methionine metabolism have separately been linked to circadian regulation, but whether dietary methionine influences circadian rhythms through m6A remains unknown. Here we show that short-term methionine deprivation induces diurnal variation in serum methionine and SAM and reprograms diurnal expression of m6A writers, erasers, and readers in mouse liver. Methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (MeRIP-seq) at two timepoints (ZT9, ZT21) revealed that a methionine-deficient (MD) diet was associated with a roughly 10-fold increase in differentially methylated m6A peaks between timepoints relative to control, despite no change in methylation at core clock transcripts. These diet-induced oscillations arose at sites already methylated under the control diet, indicating that methionine restriction alters the rhythmicity of existing m6A marks rather than inducing new methylation, and were enriched in transcripts involved in RNA processing, translation, ubiquitination, and mTORC1 signaling. Integrating RNA-seq and proteomics, we found that a subset of these m6A changes co-occurred with altered mRNA and/or protein abundance, indicating gene-specific rather than global effects. Notably, reduced m6A methylation of Mat2a and Cbs, encoding enzymes central to methionine homeostasis, was associated with increased MAT2A and decreased CBS protein levels, respectively. These findings identify diet-induced, diurnally rhythmic m6A methylation as a candidate mechanism linking methionine metabolism to circadian biology and nominate specific m6A sites and pathways for future investigation.

works.title: Phospholipase Fluorogenic Probes and Molecular Determinants of Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate–Adenosine Monophosphate Binding to Cyclic Oligonucleotide-Based Antiphage Signaling System CapV
works.abstract: Cyclic oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling systems (CBASS) protect bacteria from bacteriophage infection by producing cyclic nucleotide second messengers that activate downstream effector proteins. Cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate (cGAMP)-activated phospholipase in Vibrio (CapV) is a prevalent CBASS effector whose activity is commonly monitored using the commercially available fluorogenic substrate resorufin butyrate; however, this probe is hydrolyzed by both basal and activated CapV, limiting its usefulness in CapV-related studies. Here, we report the rational design and evaluation of a series of resorufin ester probes with varying acyl chain lengths to improve the fluorogenic assay used to monitor CapV (from Acinetobacter baumannii and Vibrio cholerae) activation. While resorufin butyrate and pentanoate exhibited substantial cGAMP-independent hydrolysis, resorufin octanoate and decanoate provided an optimal balance between catalytic turnover and activation-dependent discrimination, displaying over 5-fold and approximately 10-fold increases in hydrolysis, respectively, upon 3',3'-cGAMP activation. Using resorufin octanoate as a fluorogenic reporter, we systematically investigated the effects of cyclic dinucleotide structural modifications on CapV activation. Phosphorothioate analogues with nonbridging sulfur (exo-S linkages) retained partial agonist activity, whereas the corresponding bridging 5'-phosphorothioester (endo-S) analogues was inactive, highlighting the importance of the native phosphodiester moiety in activating CapV. Replacement of the ribose 2'-hydroxyl groups with fluorine preserved CapV activation, whereas 2'-deoxy substitutions reduced activity, with modifications on the adenosine moiety having a greater detrimental effect than those on guanosine. These findings using the fluorogenic probes were validated using phospholipid hydrolysis and activity-based protein labeling assays. Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the observed activity trends arise from differential disruption of key hydrogen-bonding interactions and ligand conformations required for productive CapV activation. Together, these fluorogenic probes provide a robust, high-throughput-compatible platform for studying CapV activation and defining cyclic dinucleotide structure-activity relationships.

works.title: Benzo[ c ]acridine Dimer Cyclization as a Route toward a Small Bicationic Heteroaromatic Compound with Unprecedented G-Quadruplex Stabilization Properties
works.abstract: G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures are key regulatory elements in genome stability and gene expression, with a pronounced role in cancer biology due to their selective formation in oncogenic genomic regions and abundance in tumor cells. Their structural uniqueness makes them compelling targets for therapeutic intervention. Thus, targeting G4s with small molecule ligands offers a promising approach for modulating gene expression and inducing replication stress, particularly in DNA damage response-deficient malignancies such as ovarian and breast cancers. However, the structural diversity of G4s has hindered the development of ligands capable of broad-spectrum, topology-independent stabilization. Here, we introduce a novel dimeric N-methylbenzo[c]acridinium derivative, engineered as a visible-light-absorbing cationic G4 ligand. Compared to previously reported diazonia derivatives, this compound demonstrates red-shifted optical properties, superior luminescence quantum efficiency, and outstanding G4-stabilizing activity. It exhibits high preferential binding for G4s over dsDNA, induces conformational transitions between hybrid and antiparallel G4s, stalls DNA replication, and disrupts DNA duplex formation. Notably, its broad, topology-independent recognition enables stabilization of a range of G4 targets. Crucially, it surpasses benchmark G4 ligands, including PhenDC3 and CX-5461, in both selectivity and/or efficacy. These results support the dimeric benzo[c]acridinium scaffold as a versatile platform for the development of G4-targeted therapeutic strategies.

works.title: Characterization of a Unique Carbohydrate-Binding Module from Akkermansia muciniphila that Binds Ganglioside-Associated Glycans
works.abstract: Akkermansia muciniphila is a mucin-degrading gut symbiont that promotes host metabolic health through its ability to utilize host-derived glycans. Central to this microbe is its diverse set of glycoside hydrolases (GHs), specifically GHs involved in degrading host glycans like mucin. Here, we characterize an A. muciniphila GH from family 123 (AmGH123), that has β-N-acetyl-d-galactosaminidase activity, removing terminal β-linked GalNAc from ganglioside-associated glycans similar to other GH123s. In addition, we identify and characterize a unique carbohydrate-binding module from family 32 associated with AmGH123 (AmGH123CBM32), representing the first CBM characterized from A. muciniphila. AmGH123CBM32 selectively binds GalNAc-terminated ganglioside-associated glycans, revealing previously unrecognized ligand specificity for CBM32 members. Structural analysis and site-directed mutagenesis reveal a distinct ligand-binding pocket in AmGH123CBM32, highlighting diverse strategies for glycan recognition within this family.

works.title: Targeting Tyrosine-Anchored Nonapeptides for Lipid-Binding Events
works.abstract: Short polypeptides are increasingly used in cancer research as modular systems for selectively targeting cellular environments, including membrane interfaces that regulate signaling and trafficking. These applications rely on the ability of short sequences to encode specific interactions with defined biological targets. One such target class is angiomotins (Amots), adaptor proteins that regulate cell proliferation and differentiation through selective binding to phosphatidylinositol-containing membranes, followed by membrane deformation and lipid reorganization. Because this activity depends on sequence-specific membrane recognition, angiomotin provides a useful model for determining how local peptide structure drives selective membrane interaction. However, the structural basis for this interaction and the role of individual tyrosine residues within the Amot80/130 coiled-coil homology domain remain unclear. To address this, nine-amino-acid peptides (nonapeptides) centered on the five native tyrosines were studied to determine how local sequence context influences membrane interaction. Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy in solution indicates that these peptides adopt defined structural features, including restricted tyrosine ring motion and inter-residue contacts. Absorbance and fluorescence measurements in hydrophobic solvent systems and lipid-containing vesicle preparations show sequence-dependent differences consistent with variations in hydrophobic partitioning and lipid headgroup interactions. Computational modeling using solution NMR structural models further identifies sequence- and conformation-dependent differences in lipid-headgroup contacts, membrane orientation, and predicted membrane insertion. Together, these results support a model that local sequence context surrounding individual tyrosines governs selective interaction with hydrophobic environments and phosphatidylinositol-containing membranes, providing a framework for peptide-based membrane targeting in cancer-relevant systems.

works.title: Stacking Up: The Expanding Catalog of Filament-Forming Enzymes
works.abstract: Enzyme filamentation has emerged as a widespread and functionally important mode of macromolecular organization. Once viewed as an unusual property of a few metabolic enzymes, reversible filament formation is now known for more than 50 enzymes across bacteria, archaea, plants, fungi, and animals. This review summarizes recent progress in the field, expanding substantially on our 2019 analysis and incorporating more than 300 new publications. We survey the known filament-forming enzymes, their catalytic activities, biological contexts, filament architectures, and available structural information from X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, and in cellulo imaging approaches. Filamenting enzymes span five major enzyme classes and function in metabolism, stress responses, signaling, replication, and host defense. In many cases, polymerization occurs at critical metabolic branch points and appears to regulate enzyme activity, allostery, substrate channeling, localization, or sequestration. Distinct filament geometries, including linear stacks, solenoidal coils, tubes, and rings, are associated with specific functional outcomes and cellular roles. We also highlight emerging in cellulo structural studies of enzyme filaments, summarizing the insights they provide into filament organization and cellular assembly when available. Together, these findings highlight enzyme filamentation as a common mode of macromolecular organization with consequences for structure, assembly, and function in diverse biological contexts.

works.title: CerS2-mediated lipotoxicity and calcium signaling: a novel sequential mechanism of apoptosis in cancer
works.abstract: The classical paradigm of the sphingolipid rheostat-balancing pro-apoptotic ceramide against pro-survival sphingosine-1-phosphate-has evolved into a complex signaling landscape where N-acyl chain length serves as the fundamental determinant of biological outcomes. This perspective explores the pivotal role of ceramide synthase 2 (CerS2) in synthesizing very-long-chain (VLC) ceramides (C22-C26) and its function as a central regulator of cellular stress responses. While CerS2 typically acts as a tumor suppressor, its activity is frequently attenuated in aggressive malignancies through alternative splicing or protein inhibition. The emergence of DH20931, a first-in-class small-molecule CerS2 agonist, is discussed as a paradigm-shifting tool for re-engaging suppressed apoptotic pathways. The present paper outlines a sequential-mechanism model for pharmacological CerS2 activation, which drives lipotoxic endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress via the PERK-ATF4-CHOP axis and tightens the ER-mitochondria synapse through direct IP3R1 interaction. The latter mechanism facilitates lethal calcium influx, triggering the mitochondrial caspase-dependent apoptotic pathway. Furthermore, the preclinical performance of DH20931 is evaluated in models of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) relative to standard-of-care therapeutics. The conclusion examines the future of CerS2 as a major druggable target, emphasizing the need for companion diagnostics to identify patients most likely to benefit from agonist therapy based on specific splice variants and metabolic profiles. Combining CerS2 activation with existing chemo- or immunotherapies represents a promising synergistic strategy for treating resistant solid tumors.

works.title: Recent advances in coarse-grained simulations of nucleic acid condensation
works.abstract: Biomolecular condensates, formed through phase separation of multivalent biomolecules, play essential roles in cellular processes such as stress response, RNA processing, transcriptional control, and genome organization. Nucleic acids are increasingly recognized as important drivers and regulators of condensate formation and dynamics. This review examines recent advances in coarse-grained molecular simulations of dynamic nucleic acids and their phase transitions. We survey established computational frameworks validated against experimental data and discuss emerging applications that address increasingly complex systems. Existing studies reveal that base-mediated interactions emerge as dominant drivers in homotypic nucleic acid condensation and that simulation resolution fundamentally determines which physical phenomena are accessible and observable. We underscore that different modeling approaches at various resolutions provide complementary insights into nucleic acid condensation mechanisms and the driving forces. We emphasize the opportunities and challenges in extending these frameworks to capture the complexity of nucleic acid-mediated phase separation in biological contexts, while identifying important gaps in current modeling capabilities. Overall, molecular simulations at multiple scales have proven to be powerful tools for elucidating the mechanistic principles underlying nucleic acid condensates and their cellular functions.

works.title: PDBe‐SIFTS: An open‐source tool for Structure Integration with Function, Taxonomy, and Sequences, featuring improved alignment, scoring scheme, and accelerated search
works.abstract: Abstract Structure integration with function, taxonomy and sequences (SIFTS) provides residue‐level mappings between UniProt Knowledgebase sequences and Protein Data Bank structures and has historically been generated through internal Protein Data Bank in Europe (PDBe) pipelines. Here, PDBe‐SIFTS is presented as a fully open‐source, locally deployable implementation of this mapping framework. The pipeline combines fast, scalable sequence search using MMseqs2, an improved bounded scoring scheme for ranking candidate mappings, and residue‐level mapping refinement based on backbone connectivity. PDBe‐SIFTS is distributed as a Python package with command‐line tools for (1) building a sequence search database, (2) identifying the best sequence‐structure match, (3) one‐to‐one mapping at the residue level, and (4) generating SIFTS annotations in PDBx/mmCIF format. Benchmarking on the complete Protein Data Bank archive showed that MMseqs2 reduced archive‐scale UniProtKB searches from hours with BLASTP to minutes, approximately 22–36 times faster, while curated mappings were recovered at top rank in 93.1% of cases. The remaining discrepancies mainly involved biologically ambiguous cases such as highly conserved proteins, chimeric constructs, or closely related orthologs. These results show that PDBe‐SIFTS enables fast mapping, improving structural coherence in residue‐level alignments while delivering the most up‐to‐date and accurate mappings, comparable to expert curation. Tool: https://github.com/PDBeurope/SIFTS . Quick start notebook with example: https://github.com/PDBeurope/SIFTS/tree/master/notebooks .

works.title: Structural and mechanistic basis of selective inhibition of the fungal‐specific histone deacetylase Hos3 from the pathogenic fungus Aspergillus fumigatus
works.abstract: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are critical epigenetic regulators of fungal growth and pathogenicity and constitute promising targets for antifungal drug development. Hos3 defines a fungal-specific HDAC subclass that lacks a clear mammalian ortholog; however, the structural determinants underlying its selective inhibition remain poorly characterized. Here, we integrated x-ray crystallography with biochemical and biophysical analyses to comprehensively characterize the catalytic properties of Hos3 from the pathogenic fungus Aspergillus fumigatus (AfHos3) and its inhibition by the hydroxamate-based compound T2383. Despite high conservation of catalytic residues, AfHos3 displayed significantly higher intrinsic catalytic activity and markedly enhanced sensitivity to T2383 compared with its yeast homolog ScHos3. The crystal structure of the AfHos3-T2383 complex revealed a canonical zinc-dependent inhibitor-binding mode, coupled with a distinct, fungal-specific architecture of the substrate and inhibitor binding pocket. Structural and functional studies identified an aromatic clamp, comprising residues F371 and F443, that is indispensable for both catalytic activity and ligand stabilization. Furthermore, fungal-specific residues M538 and V205, together with structural elements loopA and α12, shape the catalytic-pocket environment and differentially influence enzymatic activity and T2383 responsiveness. Notably, the dimeric assembly of AfHos3 was associated with optimal enzymatic activity but did not influence inhibitor recognition. Collectively, these findings elucidate how fungal-specific structural elements synergize with the evolutionarily conserved catalytic core to govern selective inhibitor recognition, providing a robust structural and mechanistic framework for the rational design of fungal-selective HDAC inhibitors.

works.title: A generalizable method for the purification and biophysical characterization of bacterial membrane receptors
works.abstract: Membrane-embedded bacterial receptors are challenging to express and purify in soluble form, yet their isolated domains are essential tools for structural and ligand-discovery studies. Pseudomonas aeruginosa relies on the TonB-dependent heme receptor HasR for iron acquisition, a process central to its pathogenicity. Here, we report a robust strategy for the recombinant expression, purification, and biophysical characterization of the two soluble HasR domains directly involved in heme uptake: the N-terminal plug and the Secretin/TonB short N-terminal domain. Each domain was expressed individually in Escherichia coli and purified to homogeneity, adopting well-folded conformations as confirmed by circular dichroism, NMR spectroscopy, and mass spectrometry. We then engineered a fusion construct containing both domains and systematically evaluated multiple solubilization tags. A GST-His dual-affinity strategy enabled efficient purification of the construct, whereas His6-tag alone resulted in insoluble protein and HLT-tag fusions suffered from non-specific proteolysis. Biophysical analyses revealed that the Secretin/TonB short N-terminal domain remains stably folded within the fusion construct, while the N-terminal plug domain becomes partially disordered, a finding further supported by hydrogen/deuterium exchange mass spectrometry. Together, these results establish a generalizable workflow for producing soluble receptor domains from membrane proteins and provide validated HasR constructs suitable for downstream ligand-screening applications, including aptamer and nanobody discovery.

works.title: NuXLApp : Interactive data analysis and visualization for protein‐nucleic acid crosslinking mass spectrometry
works.abstract: Protein-nucleic acid (protein-Nu) interactions are crucial for many cellular processes and biological functions. Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) has emerged as a powerful method for identifying these interactions. However, the analysis of protein-Nu XL-MS data requires an integrated workflow from raw data processing to results inspection and validation. Existing workflows for protein-Nu XL-MS often require switching between tools and considerable manual processing. Here, we introduce NuXLApp, an interactive web-based application for data processing and results visualization in protein-Nu XL-MS studies. NuXLApp integrates the protein-Nu crosslink search engine "NuXL," machine-learning models for peptide property prediction, and interactive result visualization within a reproducible workflow. It enables rapid validation of false discovery rate-controlled crosslink spectrum match-level identifications and facilitates collaboration and intuitive exploration of experimental results. In addition, NuXLApp generates a spectral library from identified protein-Nu crosslinks to enable quantitative analysis of crosslinks using data-independent acquisition (DIA). NuXLApp supports discovery-driven identification of protein-nucleic acid crosslinks and enables DIA-based follow-up experiments for their quantitative analysis. NuXLApp is open-source and available via the OpenMS WebApps platform at https://nuxl.webapps.openms.de/.
